paragraphs: MURPHY is a neural controller and path planner implemented with a video camera and a Rhino XR-series robot arm. Its internal representation uses four populations of simple units to describe static and changing aspects of the sensory and motor environment. This organization is inspired by the arrangement of sensory and motor maps in cerebral cortex.

Earlier work taught MURPHY a direct kinematic model through extended practice: a model of how its camera-arm system behaves. It then used that model to guide reaching toward unobstructed visual targets through heuristic search. The present work adds learning of inverse differential kinematics, allowing the controller to turn a desired direction of hand movement into corresponding arm changes.

This extension lets MURPHY move its hand directly toward a visible target without searching for that movement. A second extension addresses reaching when obstacles are present. The two developments expand different aspects of the controller: one provides a more direct route from visual goals to movement, while the other extends planning to environments where the route itself matters.
summary.tldr: MURPHY adds learned inverse differential kinematics for direct visually guided movement and extends reaching to environments with obstacles.

title: Further Explorations in Visually-Guided Reaching: Making MURPHY Smarter

Within a statistical mechanics frame(cid:173) work, numerical studies show that this model has features which do not exist in previously studied two-layer network models with(cid:173) out adjustable biases, e.g., attractive suboptimal symmetric phases even for realizable cases and noiseless data.

paragraphs: A model's ability to represent a target does not determine how learning will proceed. This paper studies that distinction in a universal approximator called a normalized committee machine with adjustable biases. The network is trained through online back-propagation, so its behavior is examined as learning unfolds over successive examples.

The authors use a statistical-mechanics framework and numerical studies to investigate the training dynamics. They find attractive, suboptimal symmetric phases: learning can be drawn toward states that preserve symmetry but do not provide the best solution. Such phases appear even when the target is realizable by the model and the data contain no noise.

These behaviors distinguish the model from previously studied two-layer networks without adjustable biases. The important implication concerns the relationship between flexibility and learning: adding adjustable biases changes the dynamics as well as what the network can represent. Even in the favorable setting of noiseless, representable data, the training process can encounter an attracting suboptimal phase.
summary.tldr: A universal approximator with adjustable biases can exhibit attracting suboptimal learning phases even with noiseless, realizable data.

title: The Learning Dynamcis of a Universal Approximator

abstract: We describe a new iterative method for parameter estimation of Gaus(cid:173) sian mixtures. The new method is based on a framework developed by Kivinen and Warmuth for supervised on-line learning. In contrast to gra(cid:173) dient descent and EM, which estimate the mixture's covariance matrices, the proposed method estimates the inverses of the covariance matrices. Furthennore, the new parameter estimation procedure can be applied in both on-line and batch settings. We show experimentally that it is typi(cid:173) cally faster than EM, and usually requires about half as many iterations as EM.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an iterative method for estimating the parameters of Gaussian mixture models. Its starting point is a framework developed by Kivinen and Warmuth for supervised online learning. The authors adapt that framework to mixture estimation, producing a procedure that can operate either on a batch of observations or in an online setting.

The distinctive design choice concerns the matrices describing each mixture component's spread and relationships among variables. Gradient descent and expectation maximization, or EM, estimate covariance matrices. The proposed method instead estimates their inverses. This changes which mathematical quantities the iterative procedure updates while retaining the goal of fitting a Gaussian mixture.

Experiments indicate that the method is typically faster than EM and usually needs about half as many iterations. These are qualified empirical findings, so they support a practical advantage in the reported comparisons rather than a universal speed guarantee. The combination of fewer iterations and support for both batch and online estimation is the paper's stated practical appeal.
summary.tldr: An iterative Gaussian-mixture estimator updates inverse covariance matrices and typically converges faster than EM in the reported experiments.

title: Batch and On-Line Parameter Estimation of Gaussian Mixtures Based on the Joint Entropy

abstract: We attempt to understand visual classiﬁcation in humans using both psy- chophysical and machine learning techniques. Frontal views of human faces were used for a gender classiﬁcation task. Human subjects classi- ﬁed the faces and their gender judgment, reaction time and conﬁdence rating were recorded. Several hyperplane learning algorithms were used on the same classiﬁcation task using the Principal Components of the texture and shape representation of the faces. The classiﬁcation perfor- mance of the learning algorithms was estimated using the face database with the true gender of the faces as labels, and also with the gender es- timated by the subjects. We then correlated the human responses to the distance of the stimuli to the separating hyperplane of the learning algo- rithms. Our results suggest that human classiﬁcation can be modeled by some hyperplane algorithms in the feature space we used. For classiﬁca- tion, the brain needs more processing for stimuli close to that hyperplane than for those further away.

paragraphs: This paper compares human visual judgments with machine-learning classifiers to investigate how people classify faces. Human participants perform a gender-classification task using frontal face views. The researchers record their judgments, reaction times, and confidence ratings, giving several measures of how each face is processed.

Several algorithms learn separating hyperplanes using principal components of face texture and shape representations. Their performance is evaluated using both the database's gender labels and the labels supplied by participants. The authors then relate human responses to each face's distance from the learned decision boundary. This connects classifier geometry with behavioral measures of the human decision process.

The results suggest that some hyperplane algorithms, operating in the chosen feature space, can model human classification. Faces near the separating boundary require more processing than faces farther away. The finding gives boundary distance an interpretation beyond the predicted label: it relates to the effort involved in deciding. The support remains specific to some algorithms and the representation used in this task.
summary.tldr: Human face-classification responses suggest that some learned decision boundaries capture both judgments and increased processing near ambiguous boundaries.

title: Insights from Machine Learning Applied to Human Visual Classification

abstract: Alternative splicing (AS) is an important and frequent step in mammalian gene expression that allows a single gene to specify multiple products, and is crucial for the regulation of fundamental biological processes. The extent of AS regulation, and the mechanisms involved, are not well understood. We have developed a custom DNA microarray platform for surveying AS levels on a large scale. We present here a generative model for the AS Array Platform (GenASAP) and demonstrate its utility for quantifying AS levels in different mouse tissues. Learning is performed using a variational expectation maximization algorithm, and the parameters are shown to correctly capture expected AS trends. A comparison of the results obtained with a well-established but low through-put experimental method demonstrate that AS levels obtained from GenASAP are highly predictive of AS levels in mammalian tissues.

paragraphs: Alternative splicing allows a single gene to produce multiple products and contributes to the regulation of biological processes. The paper addresses the challenge of measuring splicing levels at scale, against a background of incomplete understanding of their regulation. The authors develop a custom DNA microarray platform for surveying these levels across many events.

They introduce GenASAP, a generative model for the platform, to infer alternative splicing levels from the measurements. Model learning uses variational expectation maximization. The method is demonstrated on different mouse tissues, and the learned parameters capture expected splicing trends, providing evidence that the model reflects meaningful biological variation.

The authors also compare the inferred levels with results from an established experimental method that has lower throughput. They find that GenASAP's estimates are highly predictive of splicing levels in mammalian tissues. This supports the model's usefulness for interpreting large-scale array measurements. The contribution combines a measurement platform with probabilistic analysis and checks the resulting estimates against a separate experimental approach.
summary.tldr: GenASAP uses a generative model of custom microarray measurements to estimate alternative splicing levels that agree closely with an established experimental method.

title: Probabilistic Inference of Alternative Splicing Events in Microarray Data

abstract: We present a method for nonparametric regression that performs bandwidth selection and variable selection simultaneously. The approach is based on the technique of incrementally decreasing the bandwidth in directions where the gradient of the estimator with respect to bandwidth is large. When the unknown function satisfies a sparsity condition, our approach avoids the curse of dimensionality, achieving the optimal minimax rate of convergence, up to logarithmic factors, as if the relevant variables were known in advance. The method--called rodeo (regularization of derivative expectation operator)--conducts a sequence of hypothesis tests, and is easy to implement. A modified version that replaces hard with soft thresholding effectively solves a sequence of lasso problems.

When the unknown function satisfies a sparsity condition, our approach avoids the curse of dimensionality, achieving the optimal minimax rate of convergence, up to logarithmic factors, as if the relevant variables were known in advance. paragraphs: Rodeo addresses regression when many input variables are available but the unknown function satisfies a sparsity condition. It combines two decisions: which variables matter and how much smoothing to apply along each input direction. Making these decisions together allows the regression procedure to adapt its attention to relevant parts of a high-dimensional input.

The method gradually decreases bandwidths in directions where the estimator changes strongly with bandwidth. It uses a sequence of hypothesis tests to guide these reductions. This sensitivity-based mechanism connects variable selection to the behavior of the regression estimator itself, rather than treating selection as a separate preliminary operation.

Under the stated sparsity condition, the authors show that rodeo avoids the curse of dimensionality and achieves the optimal minimax convergence rate up to logarithmic factors, as though the relevant variables were known beforehand. The guarantee is conditional on that sparsity. A modified version uses soft rather than hard thresholding and effectively solves a sequence of Lasso problems, linking the procedure to another approach to sparse estimation.
summary.tldr: Rodeo jointly selects variables and smoothing bandwidths, achieving near-optimal regression rates under a sparsity condition.

title: Rodeo: Sparse Nonparametric Regression in High Dimensions

abstract: We present a sequence of unsupervised, nonparametric Bayesian models for clustering complex linguistic objects. In this approach, we consider a potentially infinite number of features and categorical outcomes. We evaluate these models for the task of within- and cross-document event coreference on two corpora. All the models we investigated show significant improvements when compared against an existing baseline for this task.
originalAbstract: We present a sequence of unsupervised, nonparametric Bayesian models for clustering complex linguistic objects. In this approach, we consider a potentially infinite number of features and categorical outcomes. We evaluate these models for the task of within- and cross-document event coreference on two corpora. All the models we investigated show significant improvements when compared against an existing baseline for this task.

paragraphs: Event coreference resolution groups linguistic references that describe the same event. The grouping may be needed within a single document or across separate documents. This paper approaches that task through unsupervised clustering, developing a sequence of Bayesian nonparametric models for complex linguistic objects rather than relying on supervised training for the clustering task.

The models allow potentially infinite collections of features and categorical outcomes. This is the flexibility emphasized in the proposed representation: the modeling framework does not require those possibilities to be confined to a fixed finite inventory in advance. Features and outcomes are part of the probabilistic treatment of the objects being clustered.

The authors evaluate the models on two corpora, considering both within-document and cross-document event coreference. Every investigated model shows significant improvement over an existing baseline for the task. This supports the usefulness of the proposed modeling approach in the evaluated settings, while keeping the reported comparison tied to the baseline and corpora actually studied.
summary.tldr: Unsupervised Bayesian nonparametric models improve event coreference clustering over an existing baseline on two corpora.

title: Nonparametric Bayesian Models for Unsupervised Event Coreference Resolution

abstract: Recent studies compare gene expression data across species to identify core and species specific genes in biological systems. To perform such comparisons researchers need to match genes across species. This is a challenging task since the correct matches (orthologs) are not known for most genes. Previous work in this area used deterministic matchings or reduced multidimensional expression data to binary representation. Here we develop a new method that can utilize soft matches (given as priors) to infer both, unique and similar expression patterns across species and a matching for the genes in both species. Our method uses a Dirichlet process mixture model which includes a latent data matching variable. We present learning and inference algorithms based on variational methods for this model. Applying our method to immune response data we show that it can accurately identify common and unique response patterns by improving the matchings between human and mouse genes.

paragraphs: Comparing gene expression across species requires deciding which genes correspond to one another. Those correspondences, called ortholog matches, are unknown for many genes. Fixing uncertain matches in advance can therefore complicate the search for expression patterns shared across species and patterns specific to one species.

The paper develops a method that accepts uncertain, or soft, matches as prior information and jointly infers gene matching and expression patterns. It uses a Dirichlet process mixture model with an additional latent variable representing the matching. This lets uncertainty about correspondence participate in the analysis instead of requiring a single predetermined assignment or reducing multidimensional expression measurements to binary values.

The authors provide variational methods for learning and inference, then apply the model to immune-response data from humans and mice. They report accurate identification of shared and distinct response patterns through improved gene matchings. The result illustrates the value of treating correspondence and pattern discovery as connected inference problems, allowing expression evidence to help refine the cross-species comparison.
summary.tldr: A mixture model jointly refines uncertain cross-species gene matches and discovers shared or species-specific expression patterns.

title: Cross Species Expression Analysis using a Dirichlet Process Mixture Model with Latent Matchings

abstract: Budgeted optimization involves optimizing an unknown function that is costly to evaluate by requesting a limited number of function evaluations at intelligently selected inputs. Typical problem formulations assume that experiments are selected one at a time with a limited total number of experiments, which fail to capture important aspects of many real-world problems. This paper defines a novel problem formulation with the following important extensions: 1) allowing for concurrent experiments; 2) allowing for stochastic experiment durations; and 3) placing constraints on both the total number of experiments and the total experimental time. We develop both offline and online algorithms for selecting concurrent experiments in this new setting and provide experimental results on a number of optimization benchmarks. The results show that our algorithms produce highly effective schedules compared to natural baselines.

paragraphs: When a function is expensive to evaluate, optimization must choose carefully which inputs to test. Standard budgeted formulations often select one experiment at a time and limit only the total number of evaluations. This paper broadens the problem to include scheduling concerns that arise when experiments can overlap and take uncertain amounts of time.

The formulation allows concurrent experiments, treats their durations as stochastic, and constrains both the experiment count and total experimental time. These features make the schedule part of the optimization problem. A useful collection of evaluations must fit the available time as well as the evaluation budget, while accounting for uncertainty about when experiments will finish.

The authors develop offline and online algorithms for selecting concurrent experiments in this setting. Tests on multiple optimization benchmarks show highly effective schedules compared with natural baselines. The stated result supports treating experiment selection and scheduling together: the new formulation captures resource constraints that a purely sequential evaluation budget leaves out, and the proposed algorithms perform well in the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: A broader optimization framework schedules parallel experiments with uncertain durations under both evaluation-count and time budgets.

title: Budgeted Optimization with Concurrent Stochastic-Duration Experiments

abstract: Several recent advances to the state of the art in image classification benchmarks have come from better configurations of existing techniques rather than novel approaches to feature learning. Traditionally, hyper-parameter optimization has been the job of humans because they can be very efficient in regimes where only a few trials are possible. Presently, computer clusters and GPU processors make it possible to run more trials and we show that algorithmic approaches can find better results. We present hyper-parameter optimization results on tasks of training neural networks and deep belief networks (DBNs). We optimize hyper-parameters using random search and two new greedy sequential methods based on the expected improvement criterion. Random search has been shown to be sufficiently efficient for learning neural networks for several datasets, but we show it is unreliable for training DBNs. The sequential algorithms are applied to the most difficult DBN learning problems from [Larochelle et al., 2007] and find significantly better results than the best previously reported. This work contributes novel techniques for making response surface models P (y|x) in which many elements of hyper-parameter assignment (x) are known to be irrelevant given particular values of other elements.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose the settings that determine how a learning algorithm is trained. Its motivation is that better configurations of existing methods can produce substantial improvements without changing the underlying feature-learning approach. As computing resources permit more trials, automated search becomes an increasingly useful alternative to manual tuning.

The authors evaluate random search and introduce two greedy sequential methods based on expected improvement. These methods select further configurations using a model of how settings relate to performance. A central contribution is handling conditional relevance: some settings matter only when other settings take particular values, so the search model must represent that structure.

The experiments concern neural networks and deep belief networks. Although random search had proved sufficiently efficient for neural networks on several datasets, the authors find it unreliable for deep belief networks. Their sequential methods obtain significantly better results on difficult deep-belief-network problems than those previously reported. These findings show why a search strategy that works in one training setting may need a more structured replacement in another.
summary.tldr: Two sequential hyper-parameter search methods handle conditional settings and improve difficult deep-belief-network results where random search is unreliable.

title: Algorithms for Hyper-Parameter Optimization

abstract: Our central goal is to quantify the long-term progression of pediatric neurological diseases, such as a typical 10-15 years progression of child dystonia. To this purpose, quantitative models are convincing only if they can provide multi-scale details ranging from neuron spikes to limb biomechanics. The models also need to be evaluated in hyper-time, i.e. significantly faster than real-time, for producing useful predictions. We designed a platform with digital VLSI hardware for multi-scale hyper-time emulations of human motor nervous systems. The platform is constructed on a scalable, distributed array of Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) devices. All devices operate asynchronously with 1 millisecond time granularity, and the overall system is accelerated to 365x real-time. Each physiological component is implemented using models from well documented studies and can be flexibly modified. Thus the validity of emulation can be easily advised by neurophysiologists and clinicians. For maximizing the speed of emulation, all calculations are implemented in combinational logic instead of clocked iterative circuits. This paper presents the methodology of building FPGA modules in correspondence to components of a monosynaptic spinal loop. Results of emulated activities are shown. The paper also discusses the rationale of approximating neural circuitry by organizing neurons with sparse interconnections. In conclusion, our platform allows introducing various abnormalities into the neural emulation such that the emerging motor symptoms can be analyzed. It compels us to test the origins of childhood motor disorders and predict their long-term progressions.

Its motivating goal is to quantify the long-term progression of childhood neurological disorders such as dystonia. Because that progression can span 10–15 years, useful model exploration requires running substantially faster than biological time.

The platform allows researchers to introduce abnormalities and examine the resulting motor symptoms. This establishes a tool for investigating possible origins and progression of motor disorders, with long-term disease prediction serving as the motivating research objective.
summary.tldr: An FPGA platform emulates motor-system components at 365 times real time to support investigations of childhood motor disorders.

title: Multi-scale Hyper-time Hardware Emulation of Human Motor Nervous System Based on Spiking Neurons using FPGA

abstract: In categorical data there is often structure in the number of variables that take on each label. For example, the total number of objects in an image and the number of highly relevant documents per query in web search both tend to follow a structured distribution. In this paper, we study a probabilistic model that explicitly includes a prior distribution over such counts, along with a count-conditional likelihood that deﬁnes probabilities over all subsets of a given size. When labels are binary and the prior over counts is a Poisson-Binomial distribution, a standard logistic regression model is recovered, but for other count distributions, such priors induce global dependencies and combinatorics that appear to complicate learning and inference. However, we demonstrate that simple, efﬁcient learning procedures can be derived for more general forms of this model. We illustrate the utility of the formulation by exploring applications to multi-object classiﬁcation, learning to rank, and top-K classiﬁcation.

paragraphs: This paper models structure in how many variables receive a particular label. In an image, the number of objects can carry information; in search, the number of highly relevant documents can do the same. The proposed framework makes such counts an explicit part of a probabilistic model.

It combines a prior distribution over counts with a likelihood over subsets of a specified size. The count describes how many items receive a label, while the conditional likelihood describes which items they are. With binary labels and a Poisson–Binomial count prior, the formulation recovers standard logistic regression. Other count distributions introduce dependencies across labels.

Those dependencies create apparent combinatorial difficulties because possible subsets must be accounted for. The authors nevertheless derive simple, efficient learning procedures for more general versions of the model. Applications to multi-object classification, learning to rank, and top-K classification illustrate its utility. The contribution is a way to include knowledge about label totals while retaining practical learning procedures beyond the logistic-regression special case.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic count priors extend classification and ranking models to capture dependencies in how many items receive each label.

title: Probabilistic n-Choose-k Models for Classification and Ranking

abstract: In this paper we consider the problem of learning online what is the information to consider when making sequential decisions. We formalize this as a contextual multi-armed bandit problem where a high dimensional ($D$-dimensional) context vector arrives to a learner which needs to select an action to maximize its expected reward at each time step. Each dimension of the context vector is called a type. We assume that there exists an unknown relation between actions and types, called the relevance relation, such that the reward of an action only depends on the contexts of the relevant types. When the relation is a function, i.e., the reward of an action only depends on the context of a single type, and the expected reward of an action is Lipschitz continuous in the context of its relevant type, we propose an algorithm that achieves $\tilde{O}(T^{\gamma})$ regret with a high probability, where $\gamma=2/(1+\sqrt{2})$. Our algorithm achieves this by learning the unknown relevance relation, whereas prior contextual bandit algorithms that do not exploit the existence of a relevance relation will have $\tilde{O}(T^{(D+1)/(D+2)})$ regret. Our algorithm alternates between exploring and exploiting, it does not require reward observations in exploitations, and it guarantees with a high probability that actions with suboptimality greater than $\epsilon$ are never selected in exploitations. Our proposed method can be applied to a variety of learning applications including medical diagnosis, recommender systems, popularity prediction from social networks, network security etc., where at each instance of time vast amounts of different types of information are available to the decision maker, but the effect of an action depends only on a single type.

We formalize this as a contextual multi-armed bandit problem where a high dimensional ($D$-dimensional) context vector arrives to a learner which needs to select an action to maximize its expected reward at each time step. Each dimension of the context vector is called a type. We assume that there exists an unknown relation between actions and types, called the relevance relation, such that the reward of an action only depends on the contexts of the relevant types. When the relation is a function, i.e., the reward of an action only depends on the context of a single type, and the expected reward of an action is Lipschitz continuous in the context of its relevant type, we propose an algorithm that achieves $\tilde{O}(T^{\gamma})$ regret with a high probability, where $\gamma=2/(1+\sqrt{2})$. Our algorithm achieves this by learning the unknown relevance relation, whereas prior contextual bandit algorithms that do not exploit the existence of a relevance relation will have $\tilde{O}(T^{(D+1)/(D+2)})$ regret. Our algorithm alternates between exploring and exploiting, it does not require reward observations in exploitations, and it guarantees with a high probability that actions with suboptimality greater than $\epsilon$ are never selected in exploitations. Our proposed method can be applied to a variety of learning applications including medical diagnosis, recommender systems, popularity prediction from social networks, network security etc., where at each instance of time vast amounts of different types of information are available to the decision maker, but the effect of an action depends only on a single type.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions with many available contextual features, when only a small part of that information determines an action’s reward. It assumes an unknown relationship connecting actions to relevant context dimensions. The learner must discover that relationship while choosing actions, so identifying useful information becomes part of learning how to act.

The main guarantee concerns the case where each action depends on just one context dimension and its expected reward changes smoothly in the Lipschitz sense along that dimension. Under those assumptions, the algorithm achieves a high-probability regret bound with time exponent 2/(1+√2), up to logarithmic factors. Unlike the comparison bound for methods that ignore relevance, this exponent does not depend on the full context dimension.

The algorithm alternates exploration with exploitation and does not require reward observations during exploitation. It also guarantees, with high probability, that exploitation never chooses an action whose suboptimality exceeds ε. The contribution shows how discovering relevance can reduce the difficulty of learning from abundant information, with the stated guarantees tied to the single-relevant-dimension and smoothness assumptions.
summary.tldr: Learning which single context dimension matters for each action yields dimension-independent regret exponents under the paper’s smoothness assumptions.

title: Discovering, Learning and Exploiting Relevance

abstract: In this paper, we propose a generalized Unsupervised Manifold Alignment (GUMA) method to build the connections between different but correlated datasets without any known correspondences. Based on the assumption that datasets of the same theme usually have similar manifold structures, GUMA is formulated into an explicit integer optimization problem considering the structure matching and preserving criteria, as well as the feature comparability of the corresponding points in the mutual embedding space. The main benefits of this model include: (1) simultaneous discovery and alignment of manifold structures; (2) fully unsupervised matching without any pre-specified correspondences; (3) efficient iterative alignment without computations in all permutation cases. Experimental results on dataset matching and real-world applications demonstrate the effectiveness and the practicability of our manifold alignment method.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to connect different but related datasets when no matching examples are known in advance. Its starting assumption is that datasets concerning the same theme usually have similar manifold structures. Those shared structural patterns provide a basis for discovering correspondences without supplied pairs.

The proposed GUMA method expresses alignment as an explicit integer optimization problem. Its criteria combine matching the datasets' structures, preserving those structures, and making corresponding points' features comparable in a shared embedding space. Structure discovery and alignment occur together, so the method jointly determines the manifolds and how they should correspond.

The algorithm uses iterative alignment without evaluating every possible permutation of matches. This makes the search for correspondences more practical while retaining a fully unsupervised formulation. Experiments on dataset matching and real-world applications support the method's effectiveness and practical use. The stated structural assumption is central to understanding the approach: related datasets are connected through similarities in their organization, which serve as evidence in the absence of predefined correspondences.
summary.tldr: GUMA jointly discovers and aligns related datasets' manifold structures without known correspondences, assuming similarity in their underlying organization.

title: Generalized Unsupervised Manifold Alignment

abstract: Active learning methods automatically adapt data collection by selecting the most informative samples in order to accelerate machine learning. Because of this, real-world testing and comparing active learning algorithms requires collecting new datasets (adaptively), rather than simply applying algorithms to benchmark datasets, as is the norm in (passive) machine learning research. To facilitate the development, testing and deployment of active learning for real applications, we have built an open-source software system for large-scale active learning research and experimentation. The system, called NEXT, provides a unique platform for real-world, reproducible active learning research. This paper details the challenges of building the system and demonstrates its capabilities with several experiments. The results show how experimentation can help expose strengths and weaknesses of active learning algorithms, in sometimes unexpected and enlightening ways.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which samples to collect based on what would be most informative for the learner. This makes evaluation different from applying several algorithms to one fixed benchmark: each algorithm's choices help determine the data it receives. Real-world comparison therefore requires an adaptive data-collection process as part of the experiment.

NEXT is an open-source system built to support that process at large scale. It provides a platform for developing, testing, and deploying active-learning methods in real applications, with reproducible research as a central purpose. The paper describes the challenges involved in building this infrastructure and demonstrates its capabilities through several experiments.

The experimental results show that testing active-learning algorithms in this way can expose strengths and weaknesses that are sometimes unexpected. The contribution is therefore a research and application platform that makes adaptive experimentation possible, alongside evidence of what such experimentation can reveal. It supports evaluating algorithms through the data-collection behavior that defines active learning, rather than treating sample selection as separate from evaluation.
summary.tldr: NEXT provides open-source infrastructure for reproducible active-learning experiments in which algorithms adaptively collect their own data.

title: NEXT: A System for Real-World Development, Evaluation, and Application of Active Learning

abstract: There is renewed interest in formulating integration as an inference problem, motivated by obtaining a full distribution over numerical error that can be propagated through subsequent computation. Current methods, such as Bayesian Quadrature, demonstrate impressive empirical performance but lack theoretical analysis. An important challenge is to reconcile these probabilistic integrators with rigorous convergence guarantees. In this paper, we present the first probabilistic integrator that admits such theoretical treatment, called Frank-Wolfe Bayesian Quadrature (FWBQ). Under FWBQ, convergence to the true value of the integral is shown to be exponential and posterior contraction rates are proven to be superexponential. In simulations, FWBQ is competitive with state-of-the-art methods and out-performs alternatives based on Frank-Wolfe optimisation. Our approach is applied to successfully quantify numerical error in the solution to a challenging model choice problem in cellular biology.

paragraphs: The paper treats numerical integration as an inference problem. Alongside an estimate of an integral, a probabilistic integrator supplies a distribution describing numerical uncertainty, which can be carried into later computations. The authors aim to connect this useful uncertainty representation with rigorous guarantees about convergence.

They introduce Frank-Wolfe Bayesian Quadrature, or FWBQ, as a probabilistic integration method amenable to such analysis. For FWBQ, they establish exponential convergence to the true integral and superexponential posterior contraction rates. These results address two related questions: how rapidly the numerical estimate approaches its target, and how rapidly the posterior uncertainty concentrates.

In simulations, FWBQ is competitive with leading methods and outperforms alternatives based on Frank-Wolfe optimization. The authors also apply it to quantify numerical error in a challenging cellular-biology model-choice problem. The contribution combines theoretical treatment of probabilistic integration with evidence that the method can remain useful in practice when numerical uncertainty matters to a subsequent scientific calculation.
summary.tldr: Frank-Wolfe Bayesian Quadrature combines numerical uncertainty estimates with proven rapid convergence and posterior contraction.

title: Frank-Wolfe Bayesian Quadrature: Probabilistic Integration with Theoretical Guarantees

abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) stand at the forefront of many recent developments in deep learning. Yet a major difficulty with these models is their tendency to overfit, with dropout shown to fail when applied to recurrent layers. Recent results at the intersection of Bayesian modelling and deep learning offer a Bayesian interpretation of common deep learning techniques such as dropout. This grounding of dropout in approximate Bayesian inference suggests an extension of the theoretical results, offering insights into the use of dropout with RNN models. We apply this new variational inference based dropout technique in LSTM and GRU models, assessing it on language modelling and sentiment analysis tasks. The new approach outperforms existing techniques, and to the best of our knowledge improves on the single model state-of-the-art in language modelling with the Penn Treebank (73.4 test perplexity). This extends our arsenal of variational tools in deep learning.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks can overfit their training data, and the abstract identifies ordinary applications of dropout to recurrent layers as unsuccessful. This creates a practical problem: a regularization technique useful elsewhere in deep learning cannot simply be carried over without considering the recurrent model's structure.

The paper derives a dropout technique from a Bayesian interpretation of neural-network training. In this view, dropout relates to approximate Bayesian inference, and extending that reasoning to recurrent models suggests a variational inference approach to regularization. The theory therefore serves as a guide for constructing the method, rather than only as an explanation after its design.

The authors evaluate the approach in LSTM and GRU networks on language modelling and sentiment analysis. They report improvements over existing techniques and a Penn Treebank test perplexity of 73.4, described, to their knowledge, as an improvement on the single-model state of the art. These results support the usefulness of the proposed Bayesian grounding for recurrent-network regularization in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: A variational inference interpretation of dropout yields a recurrent-network regularizer that improves the evaluated language and sentiment models.

title: A Theoretically Grounded Application of Dropout in Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: We consider the problem of recommending relevant labels (items) for a given data point (user). In particular, we are interested in the practically important setting where the evaluation is with respect to non-decomposable (over labels) performance metrics like the $F_1$ measure, \emph{and} training data has missing labels. To this end, we propose a generic framework that given a performance metric $\Psi$, can devise a regularized objective function and a threshold such that all the values in the predicted score vector above and only above the threshold are selected to be positive. We show that the regret or generalization error in the given metric $\Psi$ is bounded ultimately by estimation error of certain underlying parameters. In particular, we derive regret bounds under three popular settings: a) collaborative filtering, b) multilabel classification, and c) PU (positive-unlabeled) learning. For each of the above problems, we can obtain precise non-asymptotic regret bound which is small even when a large fraction of labels is missing. Our empirical results on synthetic and benchmark datasets demonstrate that by explicitly modeling for missing labels and optimizing the desired performance metric, our algorithm indeed achieves significantly better performance (like $F_1$ score) when compared to methods that do not model missing label information carefully.

paragraphs: Recommending relevant labels becomes difficult when training labels are missing and evaluation uses a metric such as F1. Such a metric evaluates the selected labels jointly rather than adding independent scores for each label. The paper addresses missing supervision and the desired evaluation criterion within one framework.

Given a performance metric, the framework constructs a regularized training objective and a threshold for selecting positive predictions from a score vector. The analysis connects regret in that metric to errors in estimating underlying parameters. It provides precise finite-sample bounds for collaborative filtering, multilabel classification, and positive-unlabeled learning, with bounds that can remain small even when many labels are missing.

Experiments on synthetic and benchmark datasets report significantly better performance, including F1, than methods that do not carefully model missing labels. The findings support jointly designing training and prediction around the actual metric and incomplete observations. The theoretical contribution explains how parameter estimation quality translates into the performance measure that ultimately determines whether the selected labels are useful.
summary.tldr: A framework combines missing-label modeling with metric-specific training and thresholding, backed by finite-sample regret bounds.

title: Regret Bounds for Non-decomposable Metrics with Missing Labels

abstract: We consider a transfer-learning problem by using the parameter transfer approach, where a suitable parameter of feature mapping is learned through one task and applied to another objective task. Then, we introduce the notion of the local stability of parametric feature mapping and parameter transfer learnability, and thereby derive a learning bound for parameter transfer algorithms. As an application of parameter transfer learning, we discuss the performance of sparse coding in self-taught learning. Although self-taught learning algorithms with plentiful unlabeled data often show excellent empirical performance, their theoretical analysis has not been studied. In this paper, we also provide the first theoretical learning bound for self-taught learning.

As an application of parameter transfer learning, we discuss the performance of sparse coding in self-taught learning. Although self-taught learning algorithms with plentiful unlabeled data often show excellent empirical performance, their theoretical analysis has not been studied. In this paper, we also provide the first theoretical learning bound for self-taught learning.

paragraphs: Parameter transfer learning reuses a feature mapping learned through one task when solving another. The transferred object is a parameter controlling how inputs become features, so the target task depends partly on a representation learned elsewhere. This paper develops a theoretical account of that process by deriving a learning bound for parameter-transfer algorithms.

The analysis introduces local stability of a parametric feature mapping and a notion of parameter transfer learnability. These concepts provide the framework for relating the transferred representation to learning on the objective task. Their role is to make the behavior of parameter transfer amenable to a formal guarantee, beyond observing that reuse sometimes works well.

As an application, the authors analyze sparse coding in self-taught learning, where plentiful unlabeled data can support strong empirical performance. They provide what they describe as the first theoretical learning bound for self-taught learning. The contribution is therefore both a general framework for studying transferred feature parameters and a concrete theoretical treatment of an empirically successful learning setting.
summary.tldr: A stability-based theory provides learning bounds for parameter transfer and an application to sparse-coding-based self-taught learning.

title: Learning Bound for Parameter Transfer Learning

abstract: Spectral clustering and co-clustering are well-known techniques in data analysis, and recent work has extended spectral clustering to square, symmetric tensors and hypermatrices derived from a network. We develop a new tensor spectral co-clustering method that simultaneously clusters the rows, columns, and slices of a nonnegative three-mode tensor and generalizes to tensors with any number of modes. The algorithm is based on a new random walk model which we call the super-spacey random surfer. We show that our method out-performs state-of-the-art co-clustering methods on several synthetic datasets with ground truth clusters and then use the algorithm to analyze several real-world datasets.

We show that our method out-performs state-of-the-art co-clustering methods on several synthetic datasets with ground truth clusters and then use the algorithm to analyze several real-world datasets.

paragraphs: This paper develops a clustering method for data organized along several dimensions. Its starting point is a nonnegative three-mode tensor, which can be understood as an array with rows, columns, and slices. The task is to group entries along all three modes together, so the resulting clusters reflect relationships across the different dimensions of the data.

The proposed method extends spectral co-clustering through a new random-walk model called the super-spacey random surfer. This walk provides the basis for an algorithm that simultaneously clusters the tensor’s modes. Although the initial description uses three modes, the method generalizes to tensors with any number of modes, extending its scope beyond the square, symmetric tensor settings discussed in earlier work.

The authors report better clustering results than state-of-the-art co-clustering methods on several synthetic datasets with known clusters. They also apply the algorithm to real-world datasets. The synthetic experiments support its ability to recover planted group structure, while the real-data applications demonstrate its use for analyzing higher-order observations.
summary.tldr: A new random-walk-based spectral method jointly clusters every mode of nonnegative tensor data and outperforms comparison methods on several synthetic datasets.

title: General Tensor Spectral Co-clustering for Higher-Order Data

abstract: In this work we derive a variant of the classic Glivenko-Cantelli Theorem, which asserts uniform convergence of the empirical Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) to the CDF of the underlying distribution. Our variant allows for tighter convergence bounds for extreme values of the CDF. We apply our bound in the context of revenue learning, which is a well-studied problem in economics and algorithmic game theory. We derive sample-complexity bounds on the uniform convergence rate of the empirical revenues to the true revenues, assuming a bound on the k'th moment of the valuations, for any (possibly fractional) k > 1. For uniform convergence in the limit, we give a complete characterization and a zero-one law: if the first moment of the valuations is finite, then uniform convergence almost surely occurs; conversely, if the first moment is infinite, then uniform convergence almost never occurs.

paragraphs: The classical Glivenko-Cantelli theorem describes how an empirical cumulative distribution function approaches the true distribution uniformly. This paper derives a variant that gives tighter convergence bounds near extreme values of the cumulative distribution function. It then applies the result to learning revenues from observed valuations.

For revenue learning, the authors obtain sample-complexity bounds describing how quickly empirical revenues approach true revenues uniformly. These bounds assume a bound on the kth moment of valuations, with k allowed to be any real value greater than one, including fractional values. The moment condition is therefore an explicit part of the finite-sample guarantee.

The paper also gives a complete characterization of uniform convergence in the limit. If valuations have a finite first moment, uniform convergence occurs almost surely; if the first moment is infinite, it almost surely does not occur. This zero-one law identifies a precise dividing line for eventual convergence, while the higher-moment results provide quantitative control over how much data is needed.
summary.tldr: Sharper distribution convergence bounds yield revenue-learning sample guarantees and characterize almost-sure uniform convergence by finiteness of the first valuation moment.

title: Submultiplicative Glivenko-Cantelli and Uniform Convergence of Revenues

abstract: Dealing with uncertainty is essential for efficient reinforcement learning. There is a growing literature on uncertainty estimation for deep learning from fixed datasets, but many of the most popular approaches are poorly-suited to sequential decision problems. Other methods, such as bootstrap sampling, have no mechanism for uncertainty that does not come from the observed data. We highlight why this can be a crucial shortcoming and propose a simple remedy through addition of a randomized untrainable `prior' network to each ensemble member. We prove that this approach is efficient with linear representations, provide simple illustrations of its efficacy with nonlinear representations and show that this approach scales to large-scale problems far better than previous attempts.

Other methods, such as bootstrap sampling, have no mechanism for uncertainty that does not come from the observed data. We highlight why this can be a crucial shortcoming and propose a simple remedy through addition of a randomized untrainable `prior' network to each ensemble member. We prove that this approach is efficient with linear representations, provide simple illustrations of its efficacy with nonlinear representations and show that this approach scales to large-scale problems far better than previous attempts.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning requires decisions while knowledge is still incomplete, so uncertainty affects which experiences an agent gathers next. Methods designed to estimate uncertainty from a fixed dataset may be poorly suited to this sequential setting. The paper highlights a particular gap in bootstrap approaches: they have no mechanism for expressing uncertainty that does not originate in observed data.

The proposed remedy adds a randomly initialized, untrainable prior network to each member of an ensemble. These fixed random functions provide a source of uncertainty alongside the component learned from observations. The change is simple at the architectural level, but directly addresses the absence of uncertainty supplied independently of the collected dataset.

The authors prove efficiency for linear representations and give illustrative evidence of effectiveness with nonlinear representations. They also report substantially better scaling to large problems than previous attempts. The distinction between these findings matters: the formal efficiency result covers the linear setting, while nonlinear usefulness and large-scale behavior are supported by the reported demonstrations.
summary.tldr: Adding a fixed random prior network to each ensemble member supplies uncertainty beyond observed data for reinforcement learning.

title: Randomized Prior Functions for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The problem of estimating an unknown discrete distribution from its samples is a fundamental tenet of statistical learning. Over the past decade, it attracted significant research effort and has been solved for a variety of divergence measures. Surprisingly, an equally important problem, estimating an unknown Markov chain from its samples, is still far from understood. We consider two problems related to the min-max risk (expected loss) of estimating an unknown k-state Markov chain from its n sequential samples: predicting the conditional distribution of the next sample with respect to the KL-divergence, and estimating the transition matrix with respect to a natural loss induced by KL or a more general f-divergence measure. For the first measure, we determine the min-max prediction risk to within a linear factor in the alphabet size, showing it is \Omega(k\log\log n/n) and O(k^2\log\log n/n). For the second, if the transition probabilities can be arbitrarily small, then only trivial uniform risk upper bounds can be derived. We therefore consider transition probabilities that are bounded away from zero, and resolve the problem for essentially all sufficiently smooth f-divergences, including KL-, L_2-, Chi-squared, Hellinger, and Alpha-divergences.

paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately an unknown Markov chain can be learned from a single sequence of observations. It distinguishes two goals: predicting the next observation’s conditional distribution and estimating the whole transition matrix. Both are evaluated through minimax risk, which asks about expected loss under the most difficult chain in the considered class.

For next-step prediction measured by KL divergence, the authors establish lower and upper risk bounds of order k log log n/n and k² log log n/n. Here k is the number of states and n is the sequence length. The bounds therefore locate the minimax prediction risk within a factor linear in the number of states.

Transition-matrix estimation behaves differently. If transition probabilities may be arbitrarily small, the authors obtain only trivial uniform upper bounds on risk. They therefore impose a positive lower bound on those probabilities and resolve the estimation problem for essentially all sufficiently smooth f-divergences. The covered measures include KL, L2, chi-squared, Hellinger, and alpha divergences, showing why the transition-probability assumption matters.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds Markov-chain prediction risk and characterizes transition estimation when probabilities are bounded away from zero.

title: On Learning Markov Chains

abstract: Experimental data has revealed that in addition to feedforward connections, there exist abundant feedback connections in a neural pathway. Although the importance of feedback in neural information processing has been widely recognized in the field, the detailed mechanism of how it works remains largely unknown. Here, we investigate the role of feedback in hierarchical information retrieval. Specifically, we consider a hierarchical network storing the hierarchical categorical information of objects, and information retrieval goes from rough to fine, aided by dynamical push-pull feedback from higher to lower layers. We elucidate that the push (positive) and pull (negative) feedbacks suppress the interferences due to neural correlations between different and the same categories, respectively, and their joint effect improves retrieval performance significantly. Our model agrees with the push-pull phenomenon observed in neural data and sheds light on our understanding of the role of feedback in neural information processing.

paragraphs: Neural pathways contain abundant feedback connections as well as connections carrying information forward. This paper investigates what feedback can contribute to retrieving information organized into categories at multiple levels. The authors study a hierarchical network that stores categorical information about objects and retrieves it progressively, moving from coarse categories toward finer distinctions.

The model uses dynamic positive and negative feedback from higher layers to lower layers. These two forms of feedback serve different roles: positive feedback suppresses interference associated with correlations between different categories, while negative feedback suppresses interference associated with correlations within the same category. Their combined action improves retrieval performance significantly.

This account gives push and pull complementary functions within one retrieval process. The model agrees with a push-pull phenomenon observed in neural data, linking its proposed mechanism to an experimental observation. The contribution is a mechanistic explanation within the studied network of how feedback can reduce interference and improve hierarchical retrieval, offering insight into the broader role of feedback in neural information processing.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical neural model shows how positive and negative feedback jointly suppress interference and improve information retrieval.

title: Push-pull Feedback Implements Hierarchical Information Retrieval Efficiently

abstract: The softmax bottleneck has been shown to limit the expressiveness of neural lan- guage models. Mixture of Softmaxes (MoS) is an effective approach to address such a theoretical limitation, but are expensive compared to softmax in terms of both memory and time. We propose Mixtape, an output layer that breaks the softmax bottleneck more efficiently with three novel techniques—logit space vector gating, sigmoid tree decomposition, and gate sharing. On four benchmarks including language modeling and machine translation, the Mixtape layer substantially improves the efficiency over the MoS layer by 3.5x to 10.5x while obtaining similar performance. A network equipped with Mixtape is only 20% to 34% slower than a softmax-based network with 10-30K vocabulary sizes, and outperforms softmax in perplexity and translation quality.

A network equipped with Mixtape is only 20% to 34% slower than a softmax-based network with 10-30K vocabulary sizes, and outperforms softmax in perplexity and translation quality.

paragraphs: A standard softmax output layer can limit the expressiveness of neural language models. Mixture of Softmaxes addresses that bottleneck but increases memory and computational costs. This paper introduces Mixtape, an alternative output layer designed to retain the expressive benefit with less overhead.

Mixtape combines logit-space vector gating, sigmoid-tree decomposition, and gate sharing. The authors evaluate it on four benchmarks spanning language modeling and machine translation, comparing both predictive quality and efficiency with Mixture of Softmaxes and ordinary softmax output layers.

The reported efficiency improvement over Mixture of Softmaxes ranges from 3.5x to 10.5x at similar performance. For vocabularies of 10–30K, a Mixtape-equipped network is 20% to 34% slower than a softmax-based network while improving perplexity and translation quality. These figures describe the tested configurations, illustrating a practical tradeoff between output-layer expressiveness and its computational cost.
summary.tldr: Mixtape addresses the softmax bottleneck with much lower overhead than Mixture of Softmaxes.

title: Mixtape: Breaking the Softmax Bottleneck Efficiently

abstract: For optimization of a large sum of functions in a distributed computing environment, we present a novel communication efficient Newton-type algorithm that enjoys a variety of advantages over similar existing methods. Our algorithm, DINGO, is derived by optimization of the gradient's norm as a surrogate function. DINGO does not impose any specific form on the underlying functions and its application range extends far beyond convexity and smoothness. The underlying sub-problems of DINGO are simple linear least-squares, for which a plethora of efficient algorithms exist. DINGO involves a few hyper-parameters that are easy to tune and we theoretically show that a strict reduction in the surrogate objective is guaranteed, regardless of the selected hyper-parameters.

paragraphs: DINGO addresses optimization when an objective is a large sum of functions distributed across computing resources. In this setting, communication is part of the computational challenge. The paper proposes a communication-efficient Newton-type algorithm whose organizing objective is the norm of the gradient, used as a surrogate for the original optimization problem.

This choice turns the algorithm's underlying subproblems into linear least-squares problems, for which many efficient solution methods already exist. The abstract emphasizes that DINGO does not require a particular form for the component functions and has an application range extending beyond convexity and smoothness. Its few hyperparameters are also described as easy to tune.

The theoretical result guarantees a strict decrease in the surrogate objective regardless of the chosen hyperparameters. The quantity guaranteed to decrease is therefore the gradient-norm surrogate. This provides a concrete progress property for the proposed method, while remaining distinct from a claim that every update reduces the original objective or reaches its global minimum.
summary.tldr: DINGO uses gradient-norm optimization and linear least-squares subproblems to provide communication-efficient distributed updates with guaranteed surrogate decrease.

title: DINGO: Distributed Newton-Type Method for Gradient-Norm Optimization

abstract: This paper introduces a structured memory which can be easily integrated into a neural network. The memory is very large by design and significantly increases the capacity of the architecture, by up to a billion parameters with a negligible computational overhead. Its design and access pattern is based on product keys, which enable fast and exact nearest neighbor search. The ability to increase the number of parameters while keeping the same computational budget lets the overall system strike a better trade-off between prediction accuracy and computation efficiency both at training and test time. This memory layer allows us to tackle very large scale language modeling tasks. In our experiments we consider a dataset with up to 30 billion words, and we plug our memory layer in a state-of-the-art transformer-based architecture. In particular, we found that a memory augmented model with only 12 layers outperforms a baseline transformer model with 24 layers, while being twice faster at inference time. We release our code for reproducibility purposes.

In the reported comparison, a memory-augmented model with 12 layers outperforms a 24-layer baseline transformer and runs twice as fast at inference. title: Large Memory Layers with Product Keys

abstract: We consider active learning of deep neural networks. Most active learning works in this context have focused on studying effective querying mechanisms and assumed that an appropriate network architecture is a priori known for the problem at hand. We challenge this assumption and propose a novel active strategy whereby the learning algorithm searches for effective architectures on the fly, while actively learning. We apply our strategy using three known querying techniques (softmax response, MC-dropout, and coresets) and show that the proposed approach overwhelmingly outperforms active learning using fixed architectures.

We apply our strategy using three known querying techniques (softmax response, MC-dropout, and coresets) and show that the proposed approach overwhelmingly outperforms active learning using fixed architectures.

paragraphs: Active learning asks a learning system to choose which examples should receive labels. For deep neural networks, much of the work in this area has concentrated on that selection rule while treating the network architecture as already settled. This paper challenges the assumption that an appropriate architecture is known before the active learning process begins.

The proposed strategy searches for effective architectures during active learning itself. Architecture choice becomes part of the ongoing learning procedure alongside the choice of examples to query. This matters because selecting informative training data and selecting a network to learn from those data are separate decisions; improving the query mechanism alone leaves the architecture decision fixed.

The authors apply their strategy with three established querying techniques: softmax response, MC-dropout, and coresets. They report that the resulting approach overwhelmingly outperforms active learning with fixed architectures in their evaluation. Testing several query techniques supports the value of revisiting architecture selection across different active learning setups, rather than tying the reported improvement to a single querying rule.
summary.tldr: Searching for neural architectures during active learning substantially outperforms fixed architectures across three tested querying techniques.

title: Deep Active Learning with a Neural Architecture Search

abstract: Frequency estimation is a fundamental problem in signal processing, with applications in radar imaging, underwater acoustics, seismic imaging, and spectroscopy. The goal is to estimate the frequency of each component in a multisinusoidal signal from a finite number of noisy samples. A recent machine-learning approach uses a neural network to output a learned representation with local maxima at the position of the frequency estimates. In this work, we propose a novel neural-network architecture that produces a significantly more accurate representation, and combine it with an additional neural-network module trained to detect the number of frequencies. This yields a fast, fully-automatic method for frequency estimation that achieves state-of-the-art results. In particular, it outperforms existing techniques by a substantial margin at medium-to-high noise levels.

paragraphs: A signal can contain several sinusoidal components, each with its own frequency. Frequency estimation seeks to identify those frequencies from a limited collection of noisy measurements. The problem appears in applications such as radar imaging, underwater acoustics, seismic imaging, and spectroscopy, where the observed samples must reveal the signal’s underlying components.

The paper builds on a learning approach that represents candidate frequencies through peaks in a neural network’s output. It introduces a new architecture that produces a substantially more accurate representation. A second neural network module estimates how many frequencies are present, addressing a separate part of the task needed to turn the representation into a complete estimate.

Together, the two modules form a fast, fully automatic frequency estimation method. The authors report state-of-the-art results, with particularly substantial improvements over existing techniques at medium-to-high noise levels. The contribution combines better identification of frequency locations with a learned estimate of component count, allowing the system to address both questions within one method.
summary.tldr: Two neural network modules jointly estimate sinusoid frequencies and their number, with especially strong reported results under medium-to-high noise.

title: Data-driven Estimation of Sinusoid Frequencies

abstract: In many scientific settings there is a need for adaptive experimental design to guide the process of identifying regions of the search space that contain as many true positives as possible subject to a low rate of false discoveries (i.e. false alarms). Such regions of the search space could differ drastically from a predicted set that minimizes 0/1 error and accurate identification could require very different sampling strategies. Like active learning for binary classification, this experimental design cannot be optimally chosen a priori, but rather the data must be taken sequentially and adaptively in a closed loop. However, unlike classification with 0/1 error, collecting data adaptively to find a set with high true positive rate and low false discovery rate (FDR) is not as well understood. In this paper, we provide the first provably sample efficient adaptive algorithm for this problem. Along the way, we highlight connections between classification, combinatorial bandits, and FDR control making contributions to each.

paragraphs: In scientific discovery, the goal is often to identify a region containing many genuine positives while keeping false discoveries low. That objective differs from minimizing the total number of binary classification mistakes. A set that works well under ordinary classification error can therefore be poorly suited to discovery, and the most useful observations can differ as well.

The paper treats data collection as a sequential decision process. Each new observation informs the choice of what to examine next, creating a closed loop between evidence and experimental design. This adaptivity matters because the best sequence of observations cannot be selected optimally before seeing any data.

The authors provide what they describe as the first provably sample-efficient adaptive algorithm for finding a set with high true-positive rate and low false-discovery rate. They also establish connections among classification, combinatorial bandits, and false-discovery control. The central contribution is to give discovery-oriented sampling its own theoretical treatment, with guarantees aligned to the scientific objective.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a provably sample-efficient adaptive method for finding many true positives while controlling false discoveries.

title: A New Perspective on Pool-Based Active Classification and False-Discovery Control

abstract: Encouraged by the success of deep convolutional neural networks on a variety of visual tasks, much theoretical and experimental work has been aimed at understanding and interpreting how vision networks operate. At the same time, deep neural networks have also achieved impressive performance in audio processing applications, both as sub-components of larger systems and as complete end-to-end systems by themselves. Despite their empirical successes, comparatively little is understood about how these audio models accomplish these tasks.In this work, we employ a recently developed statistical mechanical theory that connects geometric properties of network representations and the separability of classes to probe how information is untangled within neural networks trained to recognize speech. We observe that speaker-specific nuisance variations are discarded by the network's hierarchy, whereas task-relevant properties such as words and phonemes are untangled in later layers. Higher level concepts such as parts-of-speech and context dependence also emerge in the later layers of the network. Finally, we find that the deep representations carry out significant temporal untangling by efficiently extracting task-relevant features at each time step of the computation. Taken together, these findings shed light on how deep auditory models process their time dependent input signals to carry out invariant speech recognition, and show how different concepts emerge through the layers of the network.

paragraphs: Speech recognition networks perform well, but their internal treatment of sound is less understood than the operation of many vision models. This paper investigates how speech information changes across network layers. It uses a statistical mechanical theory linking the geometry of internal representations to how easily different classes can be separated.

The analysis finds that the network hierarchy discards speaker-specific variation that is irrelevant to recognition, while later layers make words and phonemes more separable. Higher-level properties, including parts of speech and context dependence, also emerge in later layers. These observations describe a progression in which representations increasingly organize information around the recognition task.

The paper additionally examines the temporal dimension of speech processing. It finds substantial temporal untangling, with deep representations efficiently extracting task-relevant features at each computation step. Together, the findings explain aspects of invariant recognition: the studied networks reduce nuisance variation while reorganizing useful linguistic and time-dependent information. The contribution is an account of observed internal processing, connecting representation geometry to the emergence of recognizable concepts.
summary.tldr: A geometric analysis finds that speech networks discard speaker-specific nuisance variation while separating linguistic concepts and extracting relevant temporal features.

title: Untangling in Invariant Speech Recognition

abstract: Current deep neural networks(DNNs) can easily overfit to biased training data with corrupted labels or class imbalance. Sample re-weighting strategy is commonly used to alleviate this issue by designing a weighting function mapping from training loss to sample weight, and then iterating between weight recalculating and classifier updating. Current approaches, however, need manually pre-specify the weighting function as well as its additional hyper-parameters. It makes them fairly hard to be generally applied in practice due to the significant variation of proper weighting schemes relying on the investigated problem and training data. To address this issue, we propose a method capable of adaptively learning an explicit weighting function directly from data. The weighting function is an MLP with one hidden layer, constituting a universal approximator to almost any continuous functions, making the method able to fit a wide range of weighting function forms including those assumed in conventional research. Guided by a small amount of unbiased meta-data, the parameters of the weighting function can be finely updated simultaneously with the learning process of the classifiers. Synthetic and real experiments substantiate the capability of our method for achieving proper weighting functions in class imbalance and noisy label cases, fully complying with the common settings in traditional methods, and more complicated scenarios beyond conventional cases. This naturally leads to its better accuracy than other state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Training examples can be misleading when labels are corrupted or some classes dominate the data. Assigning different weights to examples can help, but choosing how training loss should translate into weight usually requires a manually designed rule and additional hyperparameters. The appropriate rule can vary substantially between datasets and problems.

Meta-Weight-Net learns that loss-to-weight mapping directly. It represents the weighting function with a neural network containing one hidden layer, whose approximation flexibility allows it to express many continuous weighting rules. A small amount of unbiased meta-data guides updates to this function while the classifier itself is being trained. The weighting strategy can therefore adapt alongside the model it supports.

Synthetic and real-data experiments show that the method learns suitable weighting functions for class imbalance, noisy labels, and more complicated scenarios. The authors report better accuracy than competing state-of-the-art methods in these evaluations. The contribution is an explicit, learned weighting rule with broad functional flexibility; access to the small unbiased meta-dataset is a stated part of how the method learns which rules are useful.
summary.tldr: Meta-Weight-Net uses a small unbiased meta-dataset to learn how strongly each training example should influence the classifier.

title: Meta-Weight-Net: Learning an Explicit Mapping For Sample Weighting

abstract: Human intelligence is characterized not only by the capacity to learn complex skills, but the ability to rapidly adapt and acquire new skills within an ever-changing environment. In this work we study how the learning of modular solutions can allow for effective generalization to both unseen and potentially differently distributed data. Our main postulate is that the combination of task segmentation, modular learning and memory-based ensembling can give rise to generalization on an exponentially growing number of unseen tasks. We provide a concrete instantiation of this idea using a combination of: (1) the Forget-Me-Not Process, for task segmentation and memory based ensembling; and (2) Gated Linear Networks, which in contrast to contemporary deep learning techniques use a modular and local learning mechanism. We demonstrate that this system exhibits a number of desirable continual learning properties: robustness to catastrophic forgetting, no negative transfer and increasing levels of positive transfer as more tasks are seen. We show competitive performance against both offline and online methods on standard continual learning benchmarks.
