paragraphs: This paper studies how learning reusable parts of solutions can help a system handle new tasks, including tasks whose data may follow different distributions. Its central proposal combines identifying task boundaries, learning modular components, and retaining previous knowledge through memory-based ensembles. The authors postulate that these ingredients could support generalization to an exponentially growing collection of unseen tasks.

Their concrete system combines the Forget-Me-Not Process with Gated Linear Networks. The former handles task segmentation and memory-based ensembling, while the latter supplies modular, local learning. Together, these components connect the organization of experience with the organization of the learned solution: experience can be separated into tasks while useful learned components remain available for subsequent learning.

The reported system resists catastrophic forgetting, exhibits no negative transfer, and gains more positive transfer as it encounters additional tasks. It also performs competitively against offline and online methods on standard continual learning benchmarks. These findings support the usefulness of the proposed combination; the broader exponential generalization claim is presented as the motivating postulate.
summary.tldr: Combining modular learning, task segmentation, and memory-based ensembles supports transfer and resistance to forgetting across continual learning tasks.

title: A Combinatorial Perspective on Transfer Learning

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (RL), which finds an optimal policy using an empirical model, has long been recognized as one of the cornerstones of RL. It is especially suitable for multi-agent RL (MARL), as it naturally decouples the learning and the planning phases, and avoids the non-stationarity problem when all agents are improving their policies simultaneously using samples. Though intuitive and widely-used, the sample complexity of model-based MARL algorithms has been investigated relatively much less often. In this paper, we aim to address the fundamental open question about the sample complexity of model-based MARL. We study arguably the most basic MARL setting: two-player discounted zero-sum Markov games, given only access to a generative model of state transition. We show that model-based MARL achieves a sample complexity of $\tilde \cO(|\cS||\cA||\cB|(1-\gamma)^{-3}\epsilon^{-2})$ for finding the Nash equilibrium (NE) \emph{value} up to some $\epsilon$ error, and the $\epsilon$-NE \emph{policies}, where $\gamma$ is the discount factor, and $\cS,\cA,\cB$ denote the state space, and the action spaces for the two agents. We also show that this method is near-minimax optimal with a tight dependence on $1-\gamma$ and $|\cS|$ by providing a lower bound of $\Omega(|\cS|(|\cA|+|\cB|)(1-\gamma)^{-3}\epsilon^{-2})$. Our results justify the efficiency of this simple model-based approach in the multi-agent RL setting.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning first estimates an environment and then plans using that estimate. In multi-agent settings, separating these stages avoids the moving learning problem created when agents simultaneously change their policies while collecting samples. This paper studies how much transition data that approach needs in two-player discounted zero-sum Markov games, assuming access to a generative model of transitions.

The authors establish a sample bound for approximating both the Nash equilibrium value and equilibrium policies. Ignoring logarithmic factors, the bound scales with the number of states times the product of the players' action counts, with inverse squared target error, and with the inverse cube of one minus the discount factor. This quantifies the data needed as the game or effective planning horizon grows.

A corresponding lower bound matches the state-count and discount-factor dependence but involves the sum of action counts rather than their product. Thus, the near-minimax optimality claim retains a distinction in action-space dependence. The results give theoretical support to a simple model-based approach in this specific game setting and under the stated transition-sampling access.
summary.tldr: Model-based learning has near-optimal sample guarantees for two-player discounted zero-sum Markov games with generative transition access.

title: Model-Based Multi-Agent RL in Zero-Sum Markov Games with Near-Optimal Sample Complexity

abstract: We study the role of $L_2$ regularization in deep learning, and uncover simple relations between the performance of the model, the $L_2$ coefficient, the learning rate, and the number of training steps. These empirical relations hold when the network is overparameterized. They can be used to predict the optimal regularization parameter of a given model. In addition, based on these observations we propose a dynamical schedule for the regularization parameter that improves performance and speeds up training. We test these proposals in modern image classification settings. Finally, we show that these empirical relations can be understood theoretically in the context of infinitely wide networks. We derive the gradient flow dynamics of such networks, and compare the role of $L_2$ regularization in this context with that of linear models.

paragraphs: L2 regularization interacts with how a network is trained, including its learning rate and training duration. This paper investigates those interactions and finds simple empirical relationships linking the regularization coefficient, learning rate, number of training steps, and model performance. The reported relationships hold in the overparameterized setting.

The authors use these observations to predict an optimal regularization parameter for a given model. They also propose changing the regularization parameter during training according to a dynamic schedule. Tests in modern image classification settings show that the proposed schedule improves performance and accelerates training, connecting the empirical relationships to practical choices in optimization.

To explain the observations, the paper studies infinitely wide networks and derives their gradient-flow dynamics. This theoretical setting provides an account of the empirical patterns and allows comparison with the role of L2 regularization in linear models. The contribution joins observed training behavior with a mathematical explanation, while keeping the empirical overparameterized setting and the infinite-width theoretical setting distinct.
summary.tldr: Empirical relationships between L2 regularization and training dynamics motivate parameter selection and a schedule that improves image-classification training.

title: On the training dynamics of deep networks with $L_2$ regularization

abstract: A major challenge in current optimization research for deep learning is to automatically find optimal step sizes for each update step. The optimal step size is closely related to the shape of the loss in the update step direction. However, this shape has not yet been examined in detail. This work shows empirically that the sample loss over lines in negative gradient direction is mostly convex and well suited for one-dimensional parabolic approximations. Exploiting this parabolic property we introduce a simple and robust line search approach, which performs loss-shape dependent update steps. Our approach combines well-known methods such as parabolic approximation, line search and conjugate gradient, to perform efficiently. It successfully competes with common and state-of-the-art optimization methods on a large variety of experiments without the need of hand-designed step size schedules. Thus, it is of interest for objectives where step-size schedules are unknown or do not perform well. Our excessive evaluation includes multiple comprehensive hyperparameter grid searches on several datasets and architectures. We provide proof of convergence for an adapted scenario. Finally, we give a general investigation of exact line searches in the context of sample losses and exact losses, including their relation to our line search approach.

paragraphs: Choosing an update direction does not by itself determine how far a neural-network optimizer should move. This paper studies the loss along the negative-gradient direction to guide that choice. Empirically, the sample loss along these lines is mostly convex and can be approximated well by a one-dimensional parabola.

The proposed line-search method uses this observed shape to select update sizes. It combines parabolic approximation, line search, and conjugate-gradient methods to make the procedure efficient. Step sizes therefore respond to the measured loss shape, removing the need for hand-designed step-size schedules in the reported experiments.

These distinctions matter: the empirical parabolic behavior is qualified as typical, and the convergence proof applies to the adapted setting. The approach is especially relevant when useful step-size schedules are unknown or ineffective.
summary.tldr: A line-search optimizer uses empirical parabolic loss structure to choose step sizes and competes well without hand-designed schedules.

title: Parabolic Approximation Line Search for DNNs

abstract: In this paper, we introduce variational semantic memory into meta-learning to acquire long-term knowledge for few-shot learning. The variational semantic memory accrues and stores semantic information for the probabilistic inference of class prototypes in a hierarchical Bayesian framework. The semantic memory is grown from scratch and gradually consolidated by absorbing information from tasks it experiences. By doing so, it is able to accumulate long-term, general knowledge that enables it to learn new concepts of objects. We formulate memory recall as the variational inference of a latent memory variable from addressed contents, which offers a principled way to adapt the knowledge to individual tasks. Our variational semantic memory, as a new long-term memory module, confers principled recall and update mechanisms that enable semantic information to be efficiently accrued and adapted for few-shot learning. Experiments demonstrate that the probabilistic modelling of prototypes achieves a more informative representation of object classes compared to deterministic vectors. The consistent new state-of-the-art performance on four benchmarks shows the benefit of variational semantic memory in boosting few-shot recognition.

paragraphs: Few-shot recognition requires learning object concepts from limited examples. This paper introduces a long-term semantic memory into meta-learning so that experience from earlier tasks can support later ones. The memory starts from scratch and gradually consolidates semantic information across the tasks the learner encounters.

The method places class prototypes within a hierarchical Bayesian framework. Instead of treating a class representation as a single fixed vector, it infers prototypes probabilistically using accumulated memory. Recall is formulated as variational inference over a latent memory variable based on addressed contents. This provides a mechanism for adapting general stored knowledge to the particular task currently being learned.

The experiments find that probabilistic prototypes give more informative object-class representations than deterministic vectors. The method also achieves new state-of-the-art results consistently across four benchmarks. These findings support the combination of long-term knowledge accumulation and task-specific probabilistic recall as a way to improve recognition when each new task provides few examples.
summary.tldr: A learned probabilistic semantic memory accumulates knowledge across tasks and adapts it to improve few-shot object recognition.

title: Learning to Learn Variational Semantic Memory

abstract: We propose here a generalization of regression trees, referred to as Probabilistic Regression (PR) trees, that adapt to the smoothness of the prediction function relating input and output variables while preserving the interpretability of the prediction and being robust to noise. In PR trees, an observation is associated to all regions of a tree through a probability distribution that reflects how far the observation is to a region. We show that such trees are consistent, meaning that their error tends to 0 when the sample size tends to infinity, a property that has not been established for similar, previous proposals as Soft trees and Smooth Transition Regression trees. We further explain how PR trees can be used in different ensemble methods, namely Random Forests and Gradient Boosted Trees. Lastly, we assess their performance through extensive experiments that illustrate their benefits in terms of performance, interpretability and robustness to noise.

paragraphs: Regression trees organize prediction around regions of the input space. This paper generalizes that structure into Probabilistic Regression trees, aiming to adapt to the smoothness of the relationship between inputs and outputs while preserving interpretability and robustness to noise. The key change is how an observation participates in the regions defined by a tree.

Each observation is associated with all regions through a probability distribution that reflects its distance from them. This probabilistic association provides a way to express smoother predictive relationships within a tree-based model. The authors establish consistency: the relevant prediction error tends to zero as the sample size grows without bound. They note that comparable results had not been established for earlier soft-tree and smooth-transition proposals.

The paper also explains how to use these trees within random forests and gradient-boosted trees, extending the construction to familiar ensemble methods. Extensive experiments illustrate benefits in prediction performance, interpretability, and noise robustness. Together, the results connect a smoother region-assignment mechanism with both an asymptotic guarantee and empirical evidence of practical usefulness.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic Regression trees associate observations with multiple regions to support smooth predictions, consistency guarantees, and robust tree ensembles.

title: Smooth And Consistent Probabilistic Regression Trees

abstract: Recent works on One-Shot Neural Architecture Search (NAS) mostly adopt a bilevel optimization scheme to alternatively optimize the supernet weights and architecture parameters after relaxing the discrete search space into a differentiable space. However, the non-negligible incongruence in their relaxation methods is hard to guarantee the differentiable optimization in the continuous space is equivalent to the optimization in the discrete space. Differently, this paper utilizes a variational graph autoencoder to injectively transform the discrete architecture space into an equivalently continuous latent space, to resolve the incongruence. A probabilistic exploration enhancement method is accordingly devised to encourage intelligent exploration during the architecture search in the latent space, to avoid local optimal in architecture search. As the catastrophic forgetting in differentiable One-Shot NAS deteriorates supernet predictive ability and makes the bilevel optimization inefficient, this paper further proposes an architecture complementation method to relieve this deficiency. We analyze the effectiveness of the proposed method, and a series of experiments have been conducted to compare the proposed method with state-of-the-art One-Shot NAS methods.

paragraphs: Differentiable architecture search makes discrete network designs accessible to gradient-based optimization by replacing them with continuous choices. The paper identifies a mismatch in common relaxations: optimizing those continuous choices need not correspond to optimizing the original architectures. This matters because the search ultimately needs to select a discrete network.

The authors use a variational graph autoencoder to map architectures injectively into a continuous latent space, meaning distinct architectures receive distinct representations. They present this space as an equivalent setting for optimization. A probabilistic exploration mechanism encourages the search to investigate alternatives, with the aim of avoiding locally attractive but inferior architecture choices.

A further component addresses catastrophic forgetting in the shared supernet used during search. The proposed architecture complementation method is intended to reduce forgetting that harms predictions and makes alternating optimization inefficient. The paper analyzes the approach and compares it experimentally with existing one-shot search methods. Its contribution combines a revised search representation, enhanced exploration, and an intervention on the shared model's training behavior.
summary.tldr: The method searches an equivalent continuous architecture representation while adding exploration and reducing supernet forgetting.

title: Differentiable Neural Architecture Search in Equivalent Space with Exploration Enhancement

abstract: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have made great achievements for sequential prediction tasks. In practice, the target sequence often follows certain model properties or patterns (e.g., reasonable ranges, consecutive changes, resource constraint, temporal correlations between multiple variables, existence, unusual cases, etc.). However, RNNs cannot guarantee their learned distributions satisfy these model properties. It is even more challenging for predicting large-scale and complex Cyber-Physical Systems. Failure to produce outcomes that meet these model properties will result in inaccurate and even meaningless results. In this paper, we develop a new temporal logic-based learning framework, STLnet, which guides the RNN learning process with auxiliary knowledge of model properties, and produces a more robust model for improved future predictions. Our framework can be applied to general sequential deep learning models, and trained in an end-to-end manner with back-propagation. We evaluate the performance of STLnet using large-scale real-world city data. The experimental results show STLnet not only improves the accuracy of predictions, but importantly also guarantees the satisfaction of model properties and increases the robustness of RNNs.

The experimental results show STLnet not only improves the accuracy of predictions, but importantly also guarantees the satisfaction of model properties and increases the robustness of RNNs.

paragraphs: Sequential predictions often need to obey known properties, such as reasonable value ranges, resource restrictions, or temporal relationships between variables. A recurrent neural network trained from data alone does not guarantee that its predictions will satisfy these requirements. Violations can make predictions inaccurate or meaningless, particularly in complex cyber-physical systems.

STLnet introduces a temporal-logic learning framework that uses knowledge of these properties to guide training. It incorporates requirements about how sequences should behave into the learning process. The framework supports general sequential deep learning models and can be trained end to end with backpropagation, connecting explicit model knowledge with standard neural training.

Evaluation on large-scale real-world city data reports improved prediction accuracy and robustness, together with guaranteed satisfaction of model properties. The relevant properties are those supplied to the framework, which gives the satisfaction claim a concrete target. The results show the value of evaluating sequence predictions by whether they follow known system requirements as well as whether they match observed values.
summary.tldr: STLnet uses temporal logic to guide sequential neural models toward accurate, robust predictions that satisfy specified model properties.

title: STLnet: Signal Temporal Logic Enforced Multivariate Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: We study the statistical guarantees for the Imitation Learning (IL) problem in episodic MDPs.Rajaraman et al. (2020) show an information theoretic lower bound that in the worst case, a learner which can even actively query the expert policy suffers from a suboptimality growing quadratically in the length of the horizon, $H$. We study imitation learning under the $\mu$-recoverability assumption of Ross et al. (2011) which assumes that the difference in the $Q$-value under the expert policy across different actions in a state do not deviate beyond $\mu$ from the maximum. We show that the reduction proposed by Ross et al. (2010) is statistically optimal: the resulting algorithm upon interacting with the MDP for $N$ episodes results in a suboptimality bound of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}} \left( \mu |\mathcal{S}| H / N \right)$ which we show is optimal up to log-factors. In contrast, we show that any algorithm which does not interact with the MDP and uses an offline dataset of $N$ expert trajectories must incur suboptimality growing as $\gtrsim |\mathcal{S}| H^2/N$ even under the $\mu$-recoverability assumption. This establishes a clear and provable separation of the minimax rates between the active setting and the no-interaction setting. We also study IL with linear function approximation. When the expert plays actions according to a linear classifier of known state-action features, we use the reduction to multi-class classification to show that with high probability, the suboptimality of behavior cloning is $\widetilde{O}(dH^2/N)$ given $N$ rollouts from the optimal policy. This is optimal up to log-factors but can be improved to $\widetilde{O}(dH/N)$ if we have a linear expert with parameter-sharing across time steps. In contrast, when the MDP transition structure is known to the learner such as in the case of simulators, we demonstrate fundamental differences compared to the tabular setting in terms of the performance of an optimal algorithm, Mimic-MD (Rajaraman et al. (2020)) when extended to the function approximation setting. Here, we introduce a new problem called confidence set linear classification, that can be used to construct sample-efficient IL algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper asks when interacting with an environment improves imitation learning's statistical efficiency. Its analysis uses a recoverability assumption: at any state, action values under the expert policy are within mu of the maximum. This bounds how much the choice of action can change value when subsequent behavior follows the expert.

Under this assumption, an interactive algorithm achieves suboptimality scaling as mu times the number of states times horizon H, divided by N episodes, up to logarithmic factors. The authors show this is optimal to that precision. Offline learners using N expert trajectories still face a worst-case lower bound proportional to the number of states times H squared over N, establishing a separation in horizon dependence.

For experts represented by linear classifiers with known features, behavior cloning has a high-probability bound scaling as dH squared over N, up to logarithms. Sharing expert parameters across time improves this to dH over N. The paper also studies known transitions and introduces confidence-set linear classification as a tool for sample-efficient imitation learning.
summary.tldr: Under recoverability, interaction improves imitation learning's optimal horizon dependence, while linear expert structure and parameter sharing yield additional statistical guarantees.

title: On the Value of Interaction and Function Approximation in Imitation Learning

abstract: We present a scalable post-processing algorithm for debiasing trained models, including deep neural networks (DNNs), which we prove to be near-optimal by bounding its excess Bayes risk. We empirically validate its advantages on standard benchmark datasets across both classical algorithms as well as modern DNN architectures and demonstrate that it outperforms previous post-processing methods while performing on par with in-processing. In addition, we show that the proposed algorithm is particularly effective for models trained at scale where post-processing is a natural and practical choice.
originalAbstract: We present a scalable post-processing algorithm for debiasing trained models, including deep neural networks (DNNs), which we prove to be near-optimal by bounding its excess Bayes risk. We empirically validate its advantages on standard benchmark datasets across both classical algorithms as well as modern DNN architectures and demonstrate that it outperforms previous post-processing methods while performing on par with in-processing. In addition, we show that the proposed algorithm is particularly effective for models trained at scale where post-processing is a natural and practical choice.

paragraphs: This paper addresses debiasing after a machine learning model has already been trained. It proposes a scalable post-processing algorithm that applies to both classical models and deep neural networks. Working at this stage makes the approach relevant when a trained model is already available, particularly for the large-scale models emphasized in the abstract.

The theoretical contribution is a near-optimality guarantee expressed through a bound on excess Bayes risk. This gives the method a formal assessment of how far its predictive risk can be from the relevant optimum. The claim is therefore more specific than simply saying that the algorithm reduces bias: it also controls the predictive cost associated with its solution.

Experiments on standard benchmark datasets cover classical learning algorithms and modern neural architectures. The authors report better results than earlier post-processing methods and performance comparable to methods that address debiasing during training. They also find the approach particularly effective for models trained at scale. Together, these findings support post-processing as a practical route to debiasing with both theoretical and empirical backing.
summary.tldr: A scalable post-processing method debiases trained models with a near-optimal risk guarantee and strong benchmark results.

title: A Near-Optimal Algorithm for Debiasing Trained Machine Learning Models

abstract: Very recently, a variety of vision transformer architectures for dense prediction tasks have been proposed and they show that the design of spatial attention is critical to their success in these tasks. In this work, we revisit the design of the spatial attention and demonstrate that a carefully devised yet simple spatial attention mechanism performs favorably against the state-of-the-art schemes. As a result, we propose two vision transformer architectures, namely, Twins- PCPVT and Twins-SVT. Our proposed architectures are highly efficient and easy to implement, only involving matrix multiplications that are highly optimized in modern deep learning frameworks. More importantly, the proposed architectures achieve excellent performance on a wide range of visual tasks including image-level classification as well as dense detection and segmentation. The simplicity and strong performance suggest that our proposed architectures may serve as stronger backbones for many vision tasks.

paragraphs: The paper revisits spatial attention in vision Transformers, focusing on a design choice the authors identify as central to dense prediction performance. It shows that a carefully designed, simple attention mechanism can compare favorably with state-of-the-art schemes. This investigation leads to two architectures, Twins-PCPVT and Twins-SVT.

The proposed architectures emphasize both computational efficiency and ease of implementation. Their operations involve matrix multiplications that modern deep-learning frameworks already optimize heavily. That connection matters because the design's computational ingredients fit established execution machinery, making simplicity part of the practical case for the architectures alongside their prediction performance.

The authors report strong results across image classification, object detection, and segmentation. These tasks span whole-image decisions and spatially detailed predictions, giving the evaluation a broad visual scope. The combination of simplicity, efficiency, and reported performance suggests that the architectures may serve as stronger backbones for multiple vision tasks, with the findings supporting that possibility across the evaluated applications.
summary.tldr: Twins-PCPVT and Twins-SVT use simple, efficient spatial attention and achieve strong results across classification, detection, and segmentation.

title: Twins: Revisiting the Design of Spatial Attention in Vision Transformers

abstract: We give relative error coresets for training linear classifiers with a broad class of loss functions, including the logistic loss and hinge loss. Our construction achieves $(1\pm \epsilon)$ relative error with $\tilde O(d \cdot \mu_y(X)^2/\epsilon^2)$ points, where $\mu_y(X)$ is a natural complexity measure of the data matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ and label vector $y \in \{-1,1\}^n$, introduced by Munteanu et al. 2018. Our result is based on subsampling data points with probabilities proportional to their $\ell_1$ $Lewis$ $weights$. It significantly improves on existing theoretical bounds and performs well in practice, outperforming uniform subsampling along with other importance sampling methods. Our sampling distribution does not depend on the labels, so can be used for active learning. It also does not depend on the specific loss function, so a single coreset can be used in multiple training scenarios.

Our result is based on subsampling data points with probabilities proportional to their $\ell_1$ $Lewis$ $weights$. It significantly improves on existing theoretical bounds and performs well in practice, outperforming uniform subsampling along with other importance sampling methods. Our sampling distribution does not depend on the labels, so can be used for active learning. It also does not depend on the specific loss function, so a single coreset can be used in multiple training scenarios.

paragraphs: Training a linear classifier on a large dataset can be simplified if a smaller representative collection preserves the training objective. This paper constructs such collections, called coresets, for a broad family of losses that includes logistic and hinge loss. Its guarantee concerns relative error in the objective, rather than merely selecting examples that appear representative.

The construction samples examples according to their ℓ1 Lewis weights. It achieves a multiplicative approximation within 1 ± ε using roughly d times the square of a data-complexity measure, divided by ε squared, with additional logarithmic factors suppressed. Thus, the required coreset size depends on feature dimension, approximation accuracy, and the structure of the labeled dataset.

The authors report stronger theoretical size bounds and practical improvements over uniform sampling and other importance-sampling approaches. The sampling probabilities themselves require neither labels nor a particular loss function. This supports use in active learning and reuse across multiple training scenarios. The distinction is useful: the sampling rule is label-independent, even though the stated size bound involves a complexity measure of both data and labels.
summary.tldr: Lewis-weight sampling produces reusable small datasets with relative-error guarantees for training several kinds of linear classifiers.

title: Coresets for Classification – Simplified and Strengthened

abstract: Recognizing and localizing objects in the 3D space is a crucial ability for an AI agent to perceive its surrounding environment. While significant progress has been achieved with expensive LiDAR point clouds, it poses a great challenge for 3D object detection given only a monocular image. While there exist different alternatives for tackling this problem, it is found that they are either equipped with heavy networks to fuse RGB and depth information or empirically ineffective to process millions of pseudo-LiDAR points. With in-depth examination, we realize that these limitations are rooted in inaccurate object localization. In this paper, we propose a novel and lightweight approach, dubbed {\em Progressive Coordinate Transforms} (PCT) to facilitate learning coordinate representations. Specifically, a localization boosting mechanism with confidence-aware loss is introduced to progressively refine the localization prediction. In addition, semantic image representation is also exploited to compensate for the usage of patch proposals. Despite being lightweight and simple, our strategy allows us to establish a new state-of-the-art among the monocular 3D detectors on the competitive KITTI benchmark. At the same time, our proposed PCT shows great generalization to most coordinate-based 3D detection frameworks.

paragraphs: Locating objects in three dimensions from a single image is difficult. Existing approaches may require heavy networks to combine image and depth information or struggle to use very large pseudo-LiDAR point sets effectively. The authors identify inaccurate object localization as a root cause of these limitations.

Their proposed Progressive Coordinate Transforms approach improves the learning of coordinate representations through successive localization refinement. A localization-boosting mechanism uses a confidence-aware loss to guide this process. The method also incorporates semantic image representations to compensate for its use of patch proposals, combining information about image content with coordinate-based localization.

Despite its lightweight design, the method achieves a new state-of-the-art result among monocular 3D detectors on the KITTI benchmark, according to the reported evaluation. The authors also report broad generalization to most coordinate-based detection frameworks. These findings support progressive localization refinement as a useful intervention for monocular detection. The approach emphasizes improving the quality of object-position estimates while remaining simple enough to fit into other coordinate-based detection systems.
summary.tldr: Progressive Coordinate Transforms refine object localization to improve lightweight monocular 3D detection.

title: Progressive Coordinate Transforms for Monocular 3D Object Detection

abstract: Policy gradient (PG) methods are popular reinforcement learning (RL) methods where a baseline is often applied to reduce the variance of gradient estimates. In multi-agent RL (MARL), although the PG theorem can be naturally extended, the effectiveness of multi-agent PG (MAPG) methods degrades as the variance of gradient estimates increases rapidly with the number of agents. In this paper, we offer a rigorous analysis of MAPG methods by, firstly, quantifying the contributions of the number of agents and agents' explorations to the variance of MAPG estimators. Based on this analysis, we derive the optimal baseline (OB) that achieves the minimal variance. In comparison to the OB, we measure the excess variance of existing MARL algorithms such as vanilla MAPG and COMA. Considering using deep neural networks, we also propose a surrogate version of OB, which can be seamlessly plugged into any existing PG methods in MARL. On benchmarks of Multi-Agent MuJoCo and StarCraft challenges, our OB technique effectively stabilises training and improves the performance of multi-agent PPO and COMA algorithms by a significant margin. Code is released at \url{https://github.com/morning9393/Optimal-Baseline-for-Multi-agent-Policy-Gradients}.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods learn by estimating how policy changes affect reward. With multiple agents, those estimates can become increasingly noisy as the number of agents grows. This paper analyzes that variance, separating the contributions of agent count and the agents' exploratory behavior.

Using the analysis, the authors derive a baseline that minimizes variance within the studied setting. A baseline is used in the gradient estimate to reduce noise. The paper measures the excess variance of existing methods, including vanilla multi-agent policy gradients and COMA, relative to this optimal baseline. It also proposes a surrogate version suitable for deep neural networks and integration into existing multi-agent policy-gradient methods.

Experiments on Multi-Agent MuJoCo and StarCraft challenges show more stable training and substantial performance improvements for multi-agent PPO and COMA. The contribution connects an analytical account of gradient noise with a practical intervention. The exact optimal baseline provides the theoretical reference, while the neural-network-oriented surrogate provides a way to use the idea in deep multi-agent learning.
summary.tldr: An analysis of multi-agent gradient variance yields an optimal baseline and a practical surrogate that stabilize training in experiments.

title: Settling the Variance of Multi-Agent Policy Gradients

abstract: This work concerns self-supervised video representation learning (SSVRL), one topic that has received much attention recently. Since videos are storage-intensive and contain a rich source of visual content, models designed for SSVRL are expected to be storage- and computation-efficient, as well as effective. However, most existing methods only focus on one of the two objectives, failing to consider both at the same time. In this work, for the first time, the seemingly contradictory goals are simultaneously achieved by exploiting compressed videos and capturing mutual information between two input streams. Specifically, a novel Motion Vector based Cross Guidance Contrastive learning approach (MVCGC) is proposed. For storage and computation efficiency, we choose to directly decode RGB frames and motion vectors (that resemble low-resolution optical flows) from compressed videos on-the-fly. To enhance the representation ability of the motion vectors, hence the effectiveness of our method, we design a cross guidance contrastive learning algorithm based on multi-instance InfoNCE loss, where motion vectors can take supervision signals from RGB frames and vice versa. Comprehensive experiments on two downstream tasks show that our MVCGC yields new state-of-the-art while being significantly more efficient than its competitors.

To enhance the representation ability of the motion vectors, hence the effectiveness of our method, we design a cross guidance contrastive learning algorithm based on multi-instance InfoNCE loss, where motion vectors can take supervision signals from RGB frames and vice versa. Comprehensive experiments on two downstream tasks show that our MVCGC yields new state-of-the-art while being significantly more efficient than its competitors.

This paper addresses those goals together by using information already available in compressed video. Its method, Motion Vector based Cross Guidance Contrastive learning, pairs RGB appearance information with motion vectors.

The system decodes RGB frames and motion vectors on demand. The motion vectors resemble low-resolution optical flow, providing a motion-related stream alongside the image stream. To strengthen what can be learned from them, the authors introduce a cross-guidance contrastive objective based on multi-instance InfoNCE. RGB frames supply learning signals to motion vectors, and motion vectors supply signals back to RGB frames.

This reciprocal training is intended to capture shared information while improving the motion representation. Experiments on two downstream tasks report state-of-the-art performance together with significantly greater efficiency than competing methods. The reported findings indicate that compressed video can provide a useful basis for representation learning that addresses effectiveness and resource costs at the same time.
summary.tldr: MVCGC jointly trains RGB and compressed-video motion streams through reciprocal contrastive guidance, reporting stronger representations with greater efficiency.

title: Compressed Video Contrastive Learning

abstract: Existing observational approaches for learning human preferences, such as inverse reinforcement learning, usually make strong assumptions about the observability of the human's environment. However, in reality, people make many important decisions under uncertainty. To better understand preference learning in these cases, we study the setting of inverse decision theory (IDT), a previously proposed framework where a human is observed making non-sequential binary decisions under uncertainty. In IDT, the human's preferences are conveyed through their loss function, which expresses a tradeoff between different types of mistakes. We give the first statistical analysis of IDT, providing conditions necessary to identify these preferences and characterizing the sample complexity—the number of decisions that must be observed to learn the tradeoff the human is making to a desired precision. Interestingly, we show that it is actually easier to identify preferences when the decision problem is more uncertain. Furthermore, uncertain decision problems allow us to relax the unrealistic assumption that the human is an optimal decision maker but still identify their exact preferences; we give sample complexities in this suboptimal case as well. Our analysis contradicts the intuition that partial observability should make preference learning more difficult. It also provides a first step towards understanding and improving preference learning methods for uncertain and suboptimal humans.

title: Uncertain Decisions Facilitate Better Preference Learning

abstract: The Wasserstein barycenter is a geometric construct which captures the notion of centrality among probability distributions, and which has found many applications in machine learning. However, most algorithms for finding even an approximate barycenter suffer an exponential dependence on the dimension $d$ of the underlying space of the distributions. In order to cope with this ``curse of dimensionality,'' we study dimensionality reduction techniques for the Wasserstein barycenter problem. When the barycenter is restricted to support of size $n$, we show that randomized dimensionality reduction can be used to map the problem to a space of dimension $O(\log n)$ independent of both $d$ and $k$, and that \emph{any} solution found in the reduced dimension will have its cost preserved up to arbitrary small error in the original space. We provide matching upper and lower bounds on the size of the reduced dimension, showing that our methods are optimal up to constant factors. We also provide a coreset construction for the Wasserstein barycenter problem that significantly decreases the number of input distributions. The coresets can be used in conjunction with random projections and thus further improve computation time. Lastly, our experimental results validate the speedup provided by dimensionality reduction while maintaining solution quality.

This paper studies whether the problem can be compressed before solving it while preserving the quality of the resulting solution.

When the barycenter is restricted to n support points, the authors show that randomized reduction can bring the dimension down to O(log n), independently of the original dimension and the number of input distributions. title: Dimensionality Reduction for Wasserstein Barycenter

abstract: We present an approach to encode a speech signal into a fixed-size representation which minimizes the cosine loss with the existing massively multilingual LASER text embedding space. Sentences are close in this embedding space, independently of their language and modality, either text or audio. Using a similarity metric in that multimodal embedding space, we perform mining of audio in German, French, Spanish and English from Librivox against billions of sentences from Common Crawl. This yielded more than twenty thousand hours of aligned speech translations. To evaluate the automatically mined speech/text corpora, we train neural speech translation systems for several languages pairs. Adding the mined data, achieves significant improvements in the BLEU score on the CoVoST2 and the MUST-C test sets with respect to a very competitive baseline. Our approach can also be used to directly perform speech-to-speech mining, without the need to first transcribe or translate the data. We obtain more than one thousand three hundred hours of aligned speech in French, German, Spanish and English. This speech corpus has the potential to boost research in speech-to-speech translation which suffers from scarcity of natural end-to-end training data. All the mined multimodal corpora will be made freely available.

The authors use similarity in this space to match Librivox audio in German, French, Spanish, and English against billions of Common Crawl sentences. This produces more than twenty thousand hours of aligned speech translations. Adding the mined data to speech-translation training significantly improves BLEU on CoVoST2 and MUST-C relative to a competitive baseline.

The same approach also matches speech directly to speech without first transcribing or translating it. This yields more than thirteen hundred hours of aligned multilingual audio. The findings show that shared embeddings can support large-scale collection of translation training pairs, including direct speech pairs for a research area constrained by scarce natural end-to-end data. The authors also state plans to release the mined corpora freely.
summary.tldr: A shared multilingual speech-and-text embedding space mines large translation corpora that improve evaluated speech-translation systems.

title: Multimodal and Multilingual Embeddings for Large-Scale Speech Mining

abstract: Refining low-resolution (LR) spatial fields with high-resolution (HR) information, often known as statistical downscaling, is challenging as the diversity of spatial datasets often prevents direct matching of observations. Yet, when LR samples are modeled as aggregate conditional means of HR samples with respect to a mediating variable that is globally observed, the recovery of the underlying fine-grained field can be framed as taking an "inverse" of the conditional expectation, namely a deconditioning problem. In this work, we propose a Bayesian formulation of deconditioning which naturally recovers the initial reproducing kernel Hilbert space formulation from Hsu and Ramos (2019). We extend deconditioning to a downscaling setup and devise efficient conditional mean embedding estimator for multiresolution data. By treating conditional expectations as inter-domain features of the underlying field, a posterior for the latent field can be established as a solution to the deconditioning problem. Furthermore, we show that this solution can be viewed as a two-staged vector-valued kernel ridge regressor and show that it has a minimax optimal convergence rate under mild assumptions. Lastly, we demonstrate its proficiency in a synthetic and a real-world atmospheric field downscaling problem, showing substantial improvements over existing methods.

paragraphs: Statistical downscaling aims to recover a detailed spatial field using coarse measurements and finer-resolution information. A central difficulty is that observations from different datasets may not match directly. This paper considers a setting where coarse observations are conditional averages of fine observations, connected through a mediating variable observed throughout the domain.

Under that model, recovering the detailed field becomes an inverse problem: undoing a conditional expectation, which the authors call deconditioning. They formulate this problem in Bayesian terms using Gaussian processes. Conditional averages serve as inter-domain features of the underlying field, allowing the method to construct a posterior distribution for the fine-scale field rather than only a single reconstruction.

The framework recovers an earlier kernel formulation and adds an efficient conditional mean embedding estimator for data at multiple resolutions. The solution also admits an interpretation as a two-stage, vector-valued kernel ridge regression procedure. Under mild assumptions, the authors establish a minimax-optimal convergence rate. Synthetic and real atmospheric downscaling experiments show substantial improvements over existing methods, supporting the approach for the stated aggregation setting.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian deconditioning framework reconstructs fine spatial fields from conditional averages, with convergence guarantees and improved atmospheric downscaling results.

title: Deconditional Downscaling with Gaussian Processes

abstract: Recently, a new trend of exploring sparsity for accelerating neural network training has emerged, embracing the paradigm of training on the edge. This paper proposes a novel Memory-Economic Sparse Training (MEST) framework targeting for accurate and fast execution on edge devices. The proposed MEST framework consists of enhancements by Elastic Mutation (EM) and Soft Memory Bound (&S) that ensure superior accuracy at high sparsity ratios. Different from the existing works for sparse training, this current work reveals the importance of sparsity schemes on the performance of sparse training in terms of accuracy as well as training speed on real edge devices. On top of that, the paper proposes to employ data efficiency for further acceleration of sparse training. Our results suggest that unforgettable examples can be identified in-situ even during the dynamic exploration of sparsity masks in the sparse training process, and therefore can be removed for further training speedup on edge devices. Comparing with state-of-the-art (SOTA) works on accuracy, our MEST increases Top-1 accuracy significantly on ImageNet when using the same unstructured sparsity scheme. Systematical evaluation on accuracy, training speed, and memory footprint are conducted, where the proposed MEST framework consistently outperforms representative SOTA works. A reviewer strongly against our work based on his false assumptions and misunderstandings. On top of the previous submission, we employ data efficiency for further acceleration of sparse training. And we explore the impact of model sparsity, sparsity schemes, and sparse training algorithms on the number of removable training examples. Our codes are publicly available at: https://github.com/boone891214/MEST.

It includes enhancements called Elastic Mutation and Soft Memory Bound to support accuracy at high sparsity. The paper also emphasizes that the pattern of sparsity affects both predictive performance and actual training speed on edge hardware.

A second component uses data efficiency to reduce training work. The authors' results suggest that examples identified as unforgettable can be detected during training even while the network explores changing sparsity masks. Evaluations covering accuracy, training time, and memory footprint report consistent advantages over representative leading approaches. The contribution combines decisions about which network weights remain active with decisions about which examples still need training effort, while assessing their effects on real edge devices.
summary.tldr: MEST combines memory-conscious sparse training with removal of unforgettable examples to improve reported accuracy, speed, and memory use on edge devices.

title: MEST: Accurate and Fast Memory-Economic Sparse Training Framework on the Edge

abstract: The rapid increase in sizes of state-of-the-art DNN models, and consequently the increase in the compute and memory requirements of model training, has led to the development of many execution schemes such as data parallelism, pipeline model parallelism, tensor (intra-layer) model parallelism, and various memory-saving optimizations. However, no prior work has tackled the highly complex problem of optimally partitioning the DNN computation graph across many accelerators while combining all these parallelism modes and optimizations.In this work, we introduce Piper, an efficient optimization algorithm for this problem that is based on a two-level dynamic programming approach. Our two-level approach is driven by the insight that being given tensor-parallelization techniques for individual layers (e.g., Megatron-LM's splits for transformer layers) significantly reduces the search space and makes the global problem tractable, compared to considering tensor-parallel configurations for the entire DNN operator graph.

However, no prior work has tackled the highly complex problem of optimally partitioning the DNN computation graph across many accelerators while combining all these parallelism modes and optimizations.In this work, we introduce Piper, an efficient optimization algorithm for this problem that is based on a two-level dynamic programming approach. Our two-level approach is driven by the insight that being given tensor-parallelization techniques for individual layers (e.g., Megatron-LM's splits for transformer layers) significantly reduces the search space and makes the global problem tractable, compared to considering tensor-parallel configurations for the entire DNN operator graph.

paragraphs: Training large neural networks across many accelerators involves several interacting choices. Data parallelism distributes data processing, pipeline parallelism divides model stages, and tensor parallelism splits computations within layers. Memory-saving techniques add further options. Piper addresses the difficult planning problem of combining these choices while partitioning the network's computation across the available accelerators.

The proposed optimization algorithm uses two levels of dynamic programming. Its central insight is to start with supplied tensor-parallelization techniques for individual layers. Having these layer-level choices substantially reduces the search space compared with considering tensor-parallel configurations across the entire network operator graph.

This restriction makes the global planning problem tractable within the proposed approach while still combining several parallelism modes and memory optimizations. The contribution is an efficient way to organize a complex optimization problem around useful layer-level building blocks. Its tractability argument depends on those provided techniques, such as established transformer-layer splits, being available as inputs to the planner.
summary.tldr: Piper uses two-level dynamic programming and supplied layer-level tensor splits to plan combinations of parallelism and memory optimizations.

title: Piper: Multidimensional Planner for DNN Parallelization

abstract: Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (cGANs) are implicit generative models which allow to sample from class-conditional distributions. Existing cGANs are based on a wide range of different discriminator designs and training objectives. One popular design in earlier works is to include a classifier during training with the assumption that good classifiers can help eliminate samples generated with wrong classes. Nevertheless, including classifiers in cGANs often comes with a side effect of only generating easy-to-classify samples. Recently, some representative cGANs avoid the shortcoming and reach state-of-the-art performance without having classifiers. Somehow it remains unanswered whether the classifiers can be resurrected to design better cGANs. In this work, we demonstrate that classifiers can be properly leveraged to improve cGANs. We start by using the decomposition of the joint probability distribution to connect the goals of cGANs and classification as a unified framework. The framework, along with a classic energy model to parameterize distributions, justifies the use of classifiers for cGANs in a principled manner. It explains several popular cGAN variants, such as ACGAN, ProjGAN, and ContraGAN, as special cases with different levels of approximations, which provides a unified view and brings new insights to understanding cGANs. Experimental results demonstrate that the design inspired by the proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art cGANs on multiple benchmark datasets, especially on the most challenging ImageNet. The code is available at https://github.com/sian-chen/PyTorch-ECGAN.

paragraphs: Conditional GANs generate samples associated with a requested class. Some designs use a classifier during training to discourage samples that belong to the wrong class. However, this can favor examples that are especially easy to classify, narrowing the kinds of samples produced. The paper investigates how classifiers can contribute without simply reinforcing that tendency.

The authors build a common framework by decomposing the joint probability distribution of samples and classes. They combine this view with an energy-based representation of distributions to connect classification and conditional generation. Within the framework, ACGAN, ProjGAN, and ContraGAN emerge as different approximations to related underlying objectives.

This connection provides a principled basis for a new classifier-informed design and helps explain why existing designs behave differently. Experiments report that the resulting method outperforms state-of-the-art conditional GANs on multiple benchmarks, particularly ImageNet. The contribution therefore includes both an organizing account of previously separate approaches and evidence that this account can guide improvements in conditional image generation.
summary.tldr: A unified probabilistic framework explains several conditional GAN designs and guides a classifier-based approach that improves reported benchmark performance.

title: A Unified View of cGANs with and without Classifiers

abstract: Adversarial training is the industry standard for producing models that are robust to small adversarial perturbations. However, machine learning practitioners need models that are robust to other kinds of changes that occur naturally, such as changes in the style or illumination of input images. Such changes in input distribution have been effectively modeled as shifts in the mean and variance of deep image features. We adapt adversarial training by directly perturbing feature statistics, rather than image pixels, to produce models that are robust to various unseen distributional shifts. We explore the relationship between these perturbations and distributional shifts by visualizing adversarial features. Our proposed method, Adversarial Batch Normalization (AdvBN), is a single network layer that generates worst-case feature perturbations during training. By fine-tuning neural networks on adversarial feature distributions, we observe improved robustness of networks to various unseen distributional shifts, including style variations and image corruptions. In addition, we show that our proposed adversarial feature perturbation can be complementary to existing image space data augmentation methods, leading to improved performance. The source code and pre-trained models are released at \url{https://github.com/azshue/AdvBN}.

paragraphs: Images can change in style or illumination even when their relevant content remains useful for the same task. Robustness to small adversarial pixel changes does not directly address this broader need. This paper studies training against changes in internal image features, using shifts in feature means and variances to represent changes in appearance.

The proposed Adversarial Batch Normalization layer, or AdvBN, generates worst-case perturbations of these feature statistics during training. Networks are then fine-tuned on the resulting adversarial feature distributions. The authors also visualize adversarial features to investigate how their perturbations relate to distribution shifts. This places the training intervention inside the network's representation rather than solely at the input image.

The experiments show improved robustness to several unseen shifts, including style variations and image corruptions. The authors also find that adversarial feature perturbation can complement existing image-space augmentation methods and improve performance when combined with them. These findings support feature statistics as a useful intervention point for the evaluated shifts, without implying robustness to every possible change in image distribution.
summary.tldr: AdvBN trains networks against adversarial changes in feature statistics, improving observed robustness to unseen style changes and image corruptions.

title: Encoding Robustness to Image Style via Adversarial Feature Perturbations

abstract: Decentralized optimization is an emerging paradigm in distributed learning in which agents achieve network-wide solutions by peer-to-peer communication without the central server. Since communication tends to be slower than computation, when each agent communicates with only a few neighboring agents per iteration, they can complete iterations faster than with more agents or a central server. However, the total number of iterations to reach a network-wide solution is affected by the speed at which the information of the agents is ``mixed'' by communication. We found that popular communication topologies either have large degrees (such as stars and complete graphs) or are ineffective at mixing information (such as rings and grids). To address this problem, we propose a new family of topologies, EquiTopo, which has an (almost) constant degree and network-size-independent consensus rate which is used to measure the mixing efficiency.In the proposed family, EquiStatic has a degree of $\Theta(\ln(n))$, where $n$ is the network size, and a series of time-varying one-peer topologies, EquiDyn, has a constant degree of 1. We generate EquiDyn through a certain random sampling procedure. Both of them achieve $n$-independent consensus rate. We apply them to decentralized SGD and decentralized gradient tracking and obtain faster communication and better convergence, both theoretically and empirically. Our code is implemented through BlueFog and available at https://github.com/kexinjinnn/EquiTopo.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning lets agents coordinate through peer-to-peer messages without a central server. Communicating with fewer neighbors can shorten each iteration, but information may then spread too slowly across the network. This paper addresses the tradeoff between local communication cost and the number of iterations needed to reach agreement.

The proposed EquiTopo family contains two designs. EquiStatic uses a number of neighbors that grows logarithmically with network size. EquiDyn uses time-varying connections generated through a particular random sampling procedure, with each agent communicating with one peer. Both designs achieve a consensus rate independent of network size, preserving efficient information mixing as the network grows.

The authors apply these topologies to decentralized stochastic gradient descent and decentralized gradient tracking. They report theoretical and empirical improvements in communication and convergence. The distinction between the designs matters: the static construction has slowly growing degree, whereas the dynamic construction has degree one. Their shared contribution is showing how sparse communication patterns can support effective network-wide coordination without requiring each agent to contact many others.
summary.tldr: EquiTopo provides sparse communication patterns with network-size-independent consensus rates for decentralized learning.

title: Communication-Efficient Topologies for Decentralized Learning with $O(1)$ Consensus Rate

abstract: To build an artificial neural network like the biological intelligence system, recent works have unified numerous tasks into a generalist model, which can process various tasks with shared parameters and do not have any task-specific modules. While generalist models achieve promising results on various benchmarks, they have performance degradation on some tasks compared with task-specialized models. In this work, we find that interference among different tasks and modalities is the main factor to this phenomenon. To mitigate such interference, we introduce the Conditional Mixture-of-Experts (Conditional MoEs) to generalist models. Routing strategies under different levels of conditions are proposed to take both the training/inference cost and generalization ability into account. By incorporating the proposed Conditional MoEs, the recently proposed generalist model Uni-Perceiver can effectively mitigate the interference across tasks and modalities, and achieves state-of-the-art results on a series of downstream tasks via prompt tuning on 1% of downstream data. Moreover, the introduction of Conditional MoEs still holds the generalization ability of generalist models to conduct zero-shot inference on new tasks, e.g., videotext retrieval and video caption. Code and pre-trained generalist models are publicly released at https://github.com/fundamentalvision/Uni-Perceiver.

title: Uni-Perceiver-MoE: Learning Sparse Generalist Models with Conditional MoEs

abstract: Self-supervised learning techniques are celebrating immense success in natural language processing (NLP) by enabling models to learn from broad language data at unprecedented scales. Here, we aim to leverage the success of these techniques for mental state decoding, where researchers aim to identify specific mental states (e.g., the experience of anger or joy) from brain activity. To this end, we devise a set of novel self-supervised learning frameworks for neuroimaging data inspired by prominent learning frameworks in NLP. At their core, these frameworks learn the dynamics of brain activity by modeling sequences of activity akin to how sequences of text are modeled in NLP. We evaluate the frameworks by pre-training models on a broad neuroimaging dataset spanning functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging data from 11,980 experimental runs of 1,726 individuals across 34 datasets, and subsequently adapting the pre-trained models to benchmark mental state decoding datasets. The pre-trained models transfer well, generally outperforming baseline models trained from scratch, while models trained in a learning framework based on causal language modeling clearly outperform the others.

The authors pretrain on functional magnetic resonance imaging data comprising 11,980 experimental runs from 1,726 individuals across 34 datasets. They then adapt the pretrained models to benchmark datasets for mental state decoding.

The pretrained models transfer well and generally outperform baseline models trained from scratch. Among the self-supervised frameworks studied, the one based on causal language modeling clearly performs best. These results support learning brain dynamics from broad data before specializing to a decoding task, while also showing that the choice of sequence-learning framework makes a meaningful difference in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: Self-supervised pretraining on broad fMRI data improves mental state decoding, with causal language modeling performing best among the tested frameworks.

title: Self-Supervised Learning of Brain Dynamics from Broad Neuroimaging Data

abstract: Kernel ridge regression (KRR) has recently attracted renewed interest due to its potential for explaining the transient effects, such as double descent, that emerge during neural network training. In this work, we study how the alignment between the target function and the kernel affects the performance of the KRR. We focus on the truncated KRR (TKRR) which utilizes an additional parameter that controls the spectral truncation of the kernel matrix. We show that for polynomial alignment, there is an over-aligned regime, in which TKRR can achieve a faster rate than what is achievable by full KRR. The rate of TKRR can improve all the way to the parametric rate, while that of full KRR is capped at a sub-optimal value. This shows that target alignemnt can be better leveraged by utilizing spectral truncation in kernel methods. We also consider the bandlimited alignment setting and show that the regularization surface of TKRR can exhibit transient effects including multiple descent and non-monotonic behavior. Our results show that there is a strong and quantifable relation between the shape of the alignment spectrum and the generalization performance of kernel methods, both in terms of rates and in finite samples.

paragraphs: Kernel ridge regression learns using a kernel that defines relationships among inputs. This paper studies how performance depends on alignment between that kernel and the target function being learned. It focuses on truncated kernel ridge regression, which adds a parameter controlling how much of the kernel matrix's spectrum is retained.

Under polynomial alignment, the authors identify an over-aligned regime where truncation can achieve a faster rate than full kernel ridge regression. The truncated method's rate can improve as far as the parametric rate, while the full method remains capped at a suboptimal rate. This is a conditional advantage tied to the alignment structure, showing how discarding spectral components can better exploit a favorable target.

The paper also studies bandlimited alignment. In this setting, the truncated method's regularization surface can display multiple descent and other non-monotonic behavior. These results connect the shape of the alignment spectrum to both convergence rates and finite-sample generalization. They help explain why changing regularization or truncation can produce more complicated performance patterns than a simple, steadily improving trend.
summary.tldr: Spectral truncation can outperform full kernel ridge regression under favorable target alignment and can produce multiple-descent behavior.

title: Target alignment in truncated kernel ridge regression

abstract: The problem of adversarial defenses for image classification, where the goal is to robustify a classifier against adversarial examples, is considered. Inspired by the hypothesis that these examples lie beyond the natural image manifold, a novel aDversarIal defenSe with local impliCit functiOns (DISCO) is proposed to remove adversarial perturbations by localized manifold projections. DISCO consumes an adversarial image and a query pixel location and outputs a clean RGB value at the location. It is implemented with an encoder and a local implicit module, where the former produces per-pixel deep features and the latter uses the features in the neighborhood of query pixel for predicting the clean RGB value. Extensive experiments demonstrate that both DISCO and its cascade version outperform prior defenses, regardless of whether the defense is known to the attacker. DISCO is also shown to be data and parameter efficient and to mount defenses that transfers across datasets, classifiers and attacks.

paragraphs: DISCO aims to protect image classifiers by removing adversarial perturbations from their inputs. Its starting point is the hypothesis that adversarial examples lie outside the manifold of natural images. The proposed defense uses localized projections toward that manifold, turning this hypothesis into a method for predicting clean image values from a perturbed image.

The model takes an image together with a queried pixel location and predicts a clean RGB value at that location. An encoder first produces deep features for individual pixels. A local implicit module then examines features around the queried location to estimate its output. This design makes local feature neighborhoods central to the reconstruction process.

The authors evaluate both DISCO and a cascaded version and report improvements over prior defenses in settings where attackers know the defense and settings where they do not. They also find efficiency in data and parameter use, along with transfer across datasets, classifiers, and attacks. These are empirical findings supporting the defense's usefulness; the natural-image-manifold premise remains the motivating hypothesis described by the paper.
summary.tldr: DISCO predicts clean pixel values from local image features and empirically improves defenses against adversarial image perturbations.

title: DISCO: Adversarial Defense with Local Implicit Functions

abstract: Sparse linear regression with ill-conditioned Gaussian random covariates is widely believed to exhibit a statistical/computational gap, but there is surprisingly little formal evidence for this belief. Recent work has shown that, for certain covariance matrices, the broad class of Preconditioned Lasso programs provably cannot succeed on polylogarithmically sparse signals with a sublinear number of samples. However, this lower bound only holds against deterministic preconditioners, and in many contexts randomization is crucial to the success of preconditioners. We prove a stronger lower bound that rules out randomized preconditioners. For an appropriate covariance matrix, we construct a single signal distribution on which any invertibly-preconditioned Lasso program fails with high probability, unless it receives a linear number of samples. Surprisingly, at the heart of our lower bound is a new robustness result in compressed sensing. In particular, we study recovering a sparse signal when a few measurements can be erased adversarially. To our knowledge, this natural question has not been studied before for sparse measurements. We surprisingly show that standard sparse Bernoulli measurements are almost-optimally robust to adversarial erasures: if $b$ measurements are erased, then all but $O(b)$ of the coordinates of the signal are identifiable.

Prior lower bounds for preconditioned Lasso applied only to deterministic preconditioners. This paper extends the limitation to randomized invertible preconditioning.

For a suitable covariance matrix, the authors construct one signal distribution on which any invertibly preconditioned Lasso fails with high probability unless it receives a linear number of samples. This strengthens evidence about the limits of that broad algorithmic family, rather than ruling out every possible regression algorithm.

The proof develops a robustness result for sparse compressed-sensing measurements under adversarial erasures. With standard sparse Bernoulli measurements, erasing b measurements leaves all but O(b) signal coordinates identifiable. The connection is notable because a positive robustness property in sparse recovery helps establish a negative sample-complexity result for preconditioned Lasso.
summary.tldr: Randomized invertible preconditioning cannot remove certain sample barriers for Lasso.

title: Lower Bounds on Randomly Preconditioned Lasso via Robust Sparse Designs

abstract: The ability to answer causal questions is crucial in many domains, as causal inference allows one to understand the impact of interventions. In many applications, only a single intervention is possible at a given time. However, in some important areas, multiple interventions are concurrently applied. Disentangling the effects of single interventions from jointly applied interventions is a challenging task---especially as simultaneously applied interventions can interact. This problem is made harder still by unobserved confounders, which influence both treatments and outcome. We address this challenge by aiming to learn the effect of a single-intervention from both observational data and sets of interventions. We prove that this is not generally possible, but provide identification proofs demonstrating that it can be achieved under non-linear continuous structural causal models with additive, multivariate Gaussian noise---even when unobserved confounders are present. Importantly, we show how to incorporate observed covariates and learn heterogeneous treatment effects. Based on the identifiability proofs, we provide an algorithm that learns the causal model parameters by pooling data from different regimes and jointly maximising the combined likelihood. The effectiveness of our method is empirically demonstrated on both synthetic and real-world data.

paragraphs: When several interventions happen together, separating the effect of each one is difficult because the interventions may interact. Hidden factors that influence both treatments and outcomes make this harder. This paper asks whether observational data and records of joint interventions can reveal what a single intervention would do on its own.

The authors first prove that this recovery is not possible in general. They then establish identification results for nonlinear continuous structural causal models with additive, multivariate Gaussian noise. Within this model class, individual intervention effects can be recovered even in the presence of unobserved confounders. The approach also incorporates observed covariates and allows treatment effects to vary across individuals or conditions.

The proofs motivate an algorithm that pools data from different observational and intervention regimes and fits causal model parameters by maximizing their combined likelihood. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate its effectiveness. The key result is a conditional route to separating intervention effects, with the stated structural and noise assumptions providing the basis for identification.
summary.tldr: Under a specified causal model with additive Gaussian noise, pooled observational and joint-intervention data can identify individual intervention effects despite hidden confounders.

title: Disentangling Causal Effects from Sets of Interventions in the Presence of Unobserved Confounders

abstract: Being able to discover diverse useful skills without external reward functions is beneficial in reinforcement learning research. Previous unsupervised skill discovery approaches mainly train different skills in parallel. Although impressive results have been provided, we found that parallel training procedure can sometimes block exploration when the state visited by different skills overlap, which leads to poor state coverage and restricts the diversity of learned skills. In this paper, we take a deeper look into this phenomenon and propose a novel framework to address this issue, which we call Recurrent Skill Training (ReST). Instead of training all the skills in parallel, ReST trains different skills one after another recurrently, along with a state coverage based intrinsic reward. We conduct experiments on a number of challenging 2D navigation environments and robotic locomotion environments. Evaluation results show that our proposed approach outperforms previous parallel training approaches in terms of state coverage and skill diversity. Videos of the discovered skills are available at https://sites.google.com/view/neurips22-rest.
