paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines labeled and unlabeled examples, but successful methods for classification do not transfer directly to regression. Classification predicts categories, whereas regression predicts numerical values. RankUp creates a connection between these settings by adding a ranking problem alongside the original numerical prediction task.

The auxiliary ranking classifier produces classification outputs about ordering, making it compatible with existing semi-supervised classification techniques. The model trains this task concurrently with the regression objective, so learning from rankings supports the original prediction problem. The paper also introduces regression distribution alignment, which improves pseudo-labels through distribution alignment. These pseudo-labels provide training targets where original labels are unavailable.

Across regression benchmarks in computer vision, audio, and natural language processing, RankUp achieves reported state-of-the-art results both with and without the additional alignment technique. Distribution alignment further improves its performance. The contribution is a simple way to reuse advances in semi-supervised classification for numerical prediction: supply a related categorical task that can benefit from those methods while continuing to optimize the regression output directly.
summary.tldr: RankUp trains an auxiliary ranking classifier alongside regression to bring semi-supervised classification methods to numerical prediction.

title: RankUp: Boosting Semi-Supervised Regression with an Auxiliary Ranking Classifier

abstract: Variance exploding (VE) based diffusion models, an important class of diffusion models, have shown state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance. However, only a few theoretical works analyze VE-based models, and those works suffer from a worse forward convergence rate $1/\text{poly}(T)$ than the $\exp{(-T)}$ of variance preserving (VP) based models, where $T$ is the forward diffusion time and the rate measures the distance between forward marginal distribution $q_T$ and pure Gaussian noise. The slow rate is due to the Brownian Motion without a drift term. In this work, we design a new drifted VESDE forward process, which allows a faster $\exp{(-T)}$ forward convergence rate. With this process, we achieve the first efficient polynomial sample complexity for a series of VE-based models with reverse SDE under the manifold hypothesis. Furthermore, unlike previous works, we allow the diffusion coefficient to be unbounded instead of a constant, which is closer to the SOTA models. Besides the reverse SDE, the other common reverse process is the probability flow ODE (PFODE) process, which is deterministic and enjoys faster sample speed. To deepen the understanding of VE-based models, we consider a more general setting considering reverse SDE and PFODE simultaneously, propose a unified tangent-based analysis framework, and prove the first quantitative convergence guarantee for SOTA VE-based models with reverse PFODE.We also show that the drifted VESDE can balance different error terms and improve generated samples without training through synthetic and real-world experiments.

The slow rate is due to the Brownian Motion without a drift term. In this work, we design a new drifted VESDE forward process, which allows a faster $\exp{(-T)}$ forward convergence rate. paragraphs: Diffusion models progressively transform data into noise before learning a reverse process for generation. Existing theoretical analyses of variance-exploding models have slower forward convergence guarantees than those for variance-preserving models. The paper attributes this gap to the absence of drift in the Brownian forward process and introduces a drifted variance-exploding stochastic differential equation.

The new process reaches an exponential forward convergence rate in diffusion time. Under the manifold hypothesis, the authors establish efficient polynomial sample complexity for a series of variance-exploding models using reverse stochastic differential equations. Their analysis also permits an unbounded diffusion coefficient, making the setting closer to the state-of-the-art models discussed in the paper.

A unified tangent-based framework covers both stochastic reverse processes and deterministic probability-flow ordinary differential equations. It yields a quantitative convergence guarantee for state-of-the-art variance-exploding models using the deterministic reverse process. Synthetic and real-world experiments additionally show that the drifted process can balance error terms and improve generated samples without training. The work combines conditional theoretical guarantees with empirical evidence for the practical value of modifying the forward dynamics.
summary.tldr: Adding drift to variance-exploding diffusion enables faster theoretical convergence, conditional sample-complexity guarantees, and empirical sample improvements without training.

title: Leveraging Drift to Improve Sample Complexity of Variance Exploding Diffusion Models

abstract: Although the neural radiance field (NeRF) exhibits high-fidelity visualization on the rendering task, it still suffers from rendering defects, especially in complex scenes. In this paper, we delve into the reason for the unsatisfactory performance and conjecture that it comes from interference in the training process. Due to occlusions in complex scenes, a 3D point may be invisible to some rays. On such a point, training with those rays that do not contain valid information about the point might interfere with the NeRF training. Based on the above intuition, we decouple the training process of NeRF in the ray dimension softly and propose a Ray-decoupled Training Framework for neural rendering (Rad-NeRF). Specifically, we construct an ensemble of sub-NeRFs and train a soft gate module to assign the gating scores to these sub-NeRFs based on specific rays. The gate module is jointly optimized with the sub-NeRF ensemble to learn the preference of sub-NeRFs for different rays automatically. Furthermore, we introduce depth-based mutual learning to enhance the rendering consistency among multiple sub-NeRFs and mitigate the depth ambiguity. Experiments on five datasets demonstrate that Rad-NeRF can enhance the rendering performance across a wide range of scene types compared with existing single-NeRF and multi-NeRF methods. With only 0.2% extra parameters, Rad-NeRF improves rendering performance by up to 1.5dB. Code is available at https://github.com/thu-nics/Rad-NeRF.

paragraphs: Neural radiance fields can render detailed scenes but still produce defects in complex environments. This paper proposes a possible cause: training interference from rays that provide no valid information about an occluded 3D point. The authors treat this as a motivating conjecture for changing how training information is distributed.

Rad-NeRF uses an ensemble of smaller radiance fields and a learned soft gate that assigns scores to them for each ray. The gate and ensemble train jointly, allowing different members to develop preferences for different rays. Depth-based mutual learning encourages rendering consistency between members and helps reduce ambiguity in their depth estimates.

Experiments on five datasets show rendering improvements across varied scene types compared with existing single-field and multi-field methods. The abstract reports gains of up to 1.5 dB with only 0.2% additional parameters. These findings support soft separation by ray as an effective design in the tested settings. The resulting performance evidence does not by itself turn the proposed explanation of interference into an established universal cause.
summary.tldr: Rad-NeRF softly routes rays across an ensemble of radiance fields and uses depth-based mutual learning to improve tested rendering quality.

title: Rad-NeRF: Ray-decoupled Training of Neural Radiance Field

abstract: We study the convergence behavior of a generalized Frank-Wolfe algorithm in constrained (stochastic) monotone variational inequality (MVI) problems. In recent years, there have been numerous efforts to design algorithms for solving constrained MVI problems due to their connections with optimization, machine learning, and equilibrium computation in games. Most work in this domain has focused on extensions of simultaneous gradient play, with particular emphasis on understanding the convergence properties of extragradient and optimistic gradient methods. In contrast, we examine the performance of an algorithm from another well-known class of optimization algorithms: Frank-Wolfe. We show that a generalized variant of this algorithm achieves a fast $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$ last-iterate convergence rate in constrained MVI problems. By drawing connections between our generalized Frank-Wolfe algorithm and the well-known smoothed fictitious play (FP) from game theory, we also derive a finite-sample convergence rate for smoothed FP in zero-sum matrix games. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a stochastic variant of the generalized Frank-Wolfe algorithm for MVI problems also converges in a last-iterate sense, albeit at a slower $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/6})$ convergence rate.

paragraphs: This paper studies constrained monotone variational inequalities, a mathematical setting connected to optimization, machine learning, and game equilibria. Much previous algorithmic work has examined extensions of simultaneous gradient play, including extragradient and optimistic methods. The authors instead analyze a generalized Frank-Wolfe algorithm and ask how its latest output approaches a solution.

They establish a last-iterate convergence rate of O(T^(-1/2)), where T is the number of iterations. The last-iterate distinction matters because the guarantee applies to the algorithm's current output, rather than only to an average over its past outputs. The result demonstrates that this generalized Frank-Wolfe approach has a quantitative convergence guarantee in the constrained monotone setting.

The analysis also connects the algorithm to smoothed fictitious play, yielding a finite-sample convergence rate for that procedure in zero-sum matrix games. A stochastic variant retains last-iterate convergence, but with the slower rate O(T^(-1/6)). These results distinguish the deterministic and stochastic guarantees while linking an optimization method to an established game-theoretic learning process.
summary.tldr: Generalized Frank-Wolfe achieves proven last-iterate convergence for constrained monotone variational inequalities, with a slower guarantee under stochastic updates.

title: Last-Iterate Convergence for Generalized Frank-Wolfe in Monotone Variational Inequalities

abstract: In bandit best-arm identification, an algorithm is tasked with finding the arm with highest mean reward with a specified accuracy as fast as possible. We study multi-fidelity best-arm identification, in which the algorithm can choose to sample an arm at a lower fidelity (less accurate mean estimate) for a lower cost. Several methods have been proposed for tackling this problem, but their optimality remain elusive, notably due to loose lower bounds on the total cost needed to identify the best arm. Our first contribution is a tight, instance-dependent lower bound on the cost complexity. The study of the optimization problem featured in the lower bound provides new insights to devise computationally efficient algorithms, and leads us to propose a gradient-based approach with asymptotically optimal cost complexity. We demonstrate the benefits of the new algorithm compared to existing methods in experiments. Our theoretical and empirical findings also shed light on an intriguing concept of optimal fidelity for each arm.

paragraphs: Best-arm identification asks an algorithm to find the option with the highest mean reward to a specified accuracy. In the multi-fidelity version, it can buy cheaper but less accurate observations instead of always paying for the highest fidelity. The challenge is to choose both which option to investigate and how much precision each observation should provide.

The paper derives a tight lower bound on the total cost required, with the bound depending on the particular problem instance. This sharpens earlier bounds that left algorithmic optimality unclear. Studying the optimization problem inside the bound then guides the design of a computationally efficient, gradient-based algorithm with asymptotically optimal cost complexity.

Experiments show benefits over existing methods, complementing the theoretical cost analysis. The work also provides insight into an optimal fidelity for each arm, linking the value of an observation's precision to the option being assessed. Its optimality claim is asymptotic: the algorithm's cost approaches the theoretical benchmark in the analyzed limiting regime.
summary.tldr: A tight cost lower bound leads to an asymptotically optimal algorithm for identifying the best option using observations of different costs and fidelities.

title: Optimal Multi-Fidelity Best-Arm Identification

abstract: Significant progress has been made in text-to-video generation through the use of powerful generative models and large-scale internet data. However, substantial challenges remain in precisely controlling individual elements within the generated video, such as the movement and appearance of specific characters and the manipulation of viewpoints. In this work, we propose a novel paradigm that generates each element in 3D representation separately and then composites them with priors from Large Language Models (LLMs) and 2D diffusion models. Specifically, given an input textual query, our scheme consists of four stages: 1) we leverage the LLMs as the director to first decompose the complex query into several sub-queries, where each sub-query describes each element of the generated video; 2) to generate each element, pre-trained models are invoked by the LLMs to obtain the corresponding 3D representation; 3) to composite the generated 3D representations, we prompt multi-modal LLMs to produce coarse guidance on the scale, location, and trajectory of different objects; 4) to make the results adhere to natural distribution, we further leverage 2D diffusion priors and use score distillation sampling to refine the composition. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method can generate high-fidelity videos from text with flexible control over each element.

paragraphs: Text-to-video systems can produce compelling scenes, but controlling individual characters, object movement, and viewpoints remains challenging. This paper approaches that problem by generating scene elements separately as three-dimensional representations and then composing them. A language model acts as a director, organizing the work described by the user's text.

The pipeline has four stages. First, the language model divides a complex request into descriptions of individual elements. It then invokes pretrained models to create their 3D representations. Next, multimodal language models provide rough guidance about object sizes, positions, and trajectories. Finally, information from 2D diffusion models refines the composition through score distillation sampling, helping the assembled scene better match natural-looking imagery.

Separating the elements gives the system explicit components whose placement and motion can be controlled during composition. The authors report that extensive experiments produce high-fidelity videos with flexible control over individual elements. The stated finding supports combining language-based scene planning, separate 3D generation, and diffusion-based refinement as a practical direction for controllable video generation.
summary.tldr: An LLM directs the creation and composition of separate 3D elements, with diffusion-based refinement enabling controllable text-to-video generation.

title: Compositional 3D-aware Video Generation with LLM Director

abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a promising machine learning paradigm that collaborates with client models to capture global knowledge. However, deploying FL models in real-world scenarios remains unreliable due to the coexistence of in-distribution data and unexpected out-of-distribution (OOD) data, such as covariate-shift and semantic-shift data. Current FL researches typically address either covariate-shift data through OOD generalization or semantic-shift data via OOD detection, overlooking the simultaneous occurrence of various OOD shifts. In this work, we propose FOOGD, a method that estimates the probability density of each client and obtains reliable global distribution as guidance for the subsequent FL process. Firstly, SM3D in FOOGD estimates score model for arbitrary distributions without prior constraints, and detects semantic-shift data powerfully. Then SAG in FOOGD provides invariant yet diverse knowledge for both local covariate-shift generalization and client performance generalization. In empirical validations, FOOGD significantly enjoys three main advantages: (1) reliably estimating non-normalized decentralized distributions, (2) detecting semantic shift data via score values, and (3) generalizing to covariate-shift data by regularizing feature extractor. The project is open in https://github.com/XeniaLLL/FOOGD-main.git.

paragraphs: Federated models can encounter several kinds of unfamiliar data simultaneously. Covariate shifts call for generalization across changed input distributions, while semantic shifts call for detecting unfamiliar content. The paper argues that addressing these separately leaves a gap when both occur in deployment, alongside data that matches the training distribution.

FOOGD estimates each client's probability density and uses a global distribution to guide subsequent federated learning. Its SM3D component estimates a score model for arbitrary distributions without prior constraints and uses score values to detect semantic shifts. Its SAG component supplies knowledge intended to be both invariant and diverse, supporting generalization within clients and across client performance.

Empirical evaluations report three benefits: reliable estimation of decentralized, non-normalized distributions; detection of semantic shifts through score values; and better covariate-shift generalization through feature-extractor regularization. The approach brings detection and generalization into one framework. Its stated findings suggest that distribution information shared through federated collaboration can help models both recognize unfamiliar data and handle changes they should generalize across.
summary.tldr: FOOGD combines distribution estimation, semantic-shift detection, and covariate-shift generalization within federated learning.

title: FOOGD: Federated Collaboration for Both Out-of-distribution Generalization and Detection

abstract: The ability of a brain or a neural network to efficiently learn depends crucially on both the task structure and the learning rule.Previous works have analyzed the dynamical equations describing learning in the relatively simplified context of the perceptron under assumptions of a student-teacher framework or a linearized output. While these assumptions have facilitated theoretical understanding, they have precluded a detailed understanding of the roles of the nonlinearity and input-data distribution in determining the learning dynamics, limiting the applicability of the theories to real biological or artificial neural networks.Here, we use a stochastic-process approach to derive flow equations describing learning, applying this framework to the case of a nonlinear perceptron performing binary classification. We characterize the effects of the learning rule (supervised or reinforcement learning, SL/RL) and input-data distribution on the perceptron's learning curve and the forgetting curve as subsequent tasks are learned.In particular, we find that the input-data noise differently affects the learning speed under SL vs. RL, as well as determines how quickly learning of a task is overwritten by subsequent learning. Additionally, we verify our approach with real data using the MNIST dataset.This approach points a way toward analyzing learning dynamics for more-complex circuit architectures.

paragraphs: How quickly a neural network learns depends on both its training rule and the structure of its data. Earlier perceptron theories often used student-teacher assumptions or simplified the output to a linear form. Those choices helped make analysis possible but restricted what the theories could explain about nonlinear responses and input distributions.

This paper uses a stochastic-process approach to derive equations describing how learning evolves in a nonlinear perceptron performing binary classification. The framework examines supervised and reinforcement learning, following both improvement on a task and the loss of that knowledge as subsequent tasks are learned. It therefore connects learning and forgetting within the same theoretical treatment.

The analysis finds that input noise affects learning speed differently under the two learning rules. It also influences how quickly later learning overwrites an earlier task. Verification using MNIST connects the approach to real data. The work provides a route toward analyzing more complex neural circuits, with its demonstrated analysis centered on the nonlinear perceptron.
summary.tldr: A stochastic-process theory explains how learning rules and input noise shape learning and forgetting in a nonlinear perceptron.

title: Dynamics of Supervised and Reinforcement Learning in the Non-Linear Perceptron

abstract: Sequence modeling faces challenges in capturing long-range dependencies across diverse tasks. Recent linear and transformer-based forecasters have shown superior performance in time series forecasting. However, they are constrained by their inherent inability to effectively address long-range dependencies in time series data, primarily due to using fixed-size inputs for prediction. Furthermore, they typically sacrifice essential temporal correlation among consecutive training samples by shuffling them into mini-batches. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a fast and effective Spectral Attention mechanism, which preserves temporal correlations among samples and facilitates the handling of long-range information while maintaining the base model structure. Spectral Attention preserves long-period trends through a low-pass filter and facilitates gradient to flow between samples. Spectral Attention can be seamlessly integrated into most sequence models, allowing models with fixed-sized look-back windows to capture long-range dependencies over thousands of steps. Through extensive experiments on 11 real-world time series datasets using 7 recent forecasting models, we consistently demonstrate the efficacy of our Spectral Attention mechanism, achieving state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasters often predict from a fixed window of past observations. That can restrict access to longer patterns, while shuffling consecutive training samples into batches can discard useful relationships between them. The paper introduces Spectral Attention to preserve those relationships and bring longer-range information into models that still use fixed-size input windows.

The mechanism uses a low-pass filter to retain long-period trends and allows gradients to flow between samples. This links the treatment of slowly changing patterns with learning across temporally related examples. Spectral Attention preserves the base model's structure and is designed to integrate into most sequence models, enabling fixed-window forecasters to capture dependencies spanning thousands of steps.

Experiments apply the mechanism to seven recent forecasting models across eleven real-world time-series datasets. The authors report consistent effectiveness and state-of-the-art results. These findings support supplementing the information available within each input window by preserving temporal connections across samples, providing a way to address long-range forecasting without redesigning the underlying forecasting model.
summary.tldr: Spectral Attention preserves long-period trends and links training samples so fixed-window forecasters can use longer-range information.

title: Introducing Spectral Attention for Long-Range Dependency in Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Animated QR codes present an exciting frontier for dynamic content delivery and digital interaction. However, despite their potential, there has been no prior work focusing on the generation of animated QR codes that are both visually appealing and universally scannable. In this paper, we introduce AnimateQR, **the first generative framework** for creating **animated QR codes** that balance aesthetic flexibility with scannability. Unlike previous methods that focus on static QR codes, AnimateQR leverages **hierarchical luminance guidance** and **progressive spatiotemporal control** to produce high-quality dynamic QR codes. Our first innovation is a multi-scale hierarchical control signal that adjusts luminance across different spatial scales, ensuring that the QR code remains decodable while allowing for artistic expression. The second innovation is a progressive control mechanism that dynamically adjusts spatiotemporal guidance throughout the diffusion denoising steps, enabling fine-grained balance between visual quality and scannability. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that AnimateQR achieves state-of-the-art performance in both decoding success rates (96\% vs. 56\% baseline) and visual quality (user preference: 7.2 vs. 2.3 on a 10-point scale). Codes are availble at https://github.com/mulns/AnimateQR.

paragraphs: An animated QR code has two jobs: it should look appealing as moving imagery, and it should preserve the visual structure needed for decoding. These goals can compete as appearance changes over time. AnimateQR introduces a generative framework that manages this balance during the creation of animated codes, extending beyond the static QR images addressed by earlier methods.

The framework controls brightness at several spatial scales. This hierarchical luminance guidance helps maintain decodable patterns while leaving room for artistic variation. A second mechanism progressively adjusts guidance over both space and time throughout diffusion denoising. Together, the controls influence how the animation develops, with the aim of coordinating visual quality and scan reliability rather than optimizing either in isolation.

The reported experiments achieve a 96% decoding success rate, compared with 56% for the baseline. Visual preference scores also improve, from 2.3 to 7.2 on a ten-point scale. These findings support the framework’s ability to improve both objectives in the evaluated settings; the reported decoding rate does not amount to universal scanning success.
summary.tldr: AnimateQR coordinates brightness and motion guidance to generate animated QR codes with improved visual appeal and decoding success.

title: AnimateQR: Bridging Aesthetics and Functionality in Dynamic QR Code Generation

abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) have emerged as efficient alternatives to Vision Transformers (ViTs), with VMamba standing out as a pioneering architecture designed for vision tasks. However, their generalization performance degrades significantly under distribution shifts. To address this limitation, we propose TRUST (Test-Time Refinement using Uncertainty-Guided SSM Traverses), a novel test-time adaptation (TTA) method that leverages diverse traversal permutations to generate multiple causal perspectives of the input image. Model predictions serve as pseudo-labels to guide updates of the Mamba-specific parameters, and the adapted weights are averaged to integrate the learned information across traversal scans. Altogether, TRUST is the first approach that explicitly leverages the unique architectural properties of SSMs for adaptation. Experiments on seven benchmarks show that TRUST consistently improves robustness and outperforms existing TTA methods.

paragraphs: TRUST addresses the loss of robustness that vision state space models can experience when test inputs differ from their training distribution. Although architectures such as VMamba offer efficient alternatives to Vision Transformers, efficiency alone does not resolve this generalization problem. The paper proposes adapting the model during testing using its own architectural structure.

The method processes an image through different traversal permutations, creating multiple ordered perspectives on the same input. Predictions act as pseudo-labels that guide updates to Mamba-specific parameters. The resulting adapted weights are averaged to combine information learned across the different traversal scans.

Experiments on seven benchmarks show consistent robustness improvements and better performance than existing test-time adaptation methods. The authors present TRUST as the first adaptation approach explicitly built around the distinctive properties of state space models. Its significance lies in treating traversal order as a source of complementary adaptation information, then integrating the resulting parameter updates into a shared model for handling shifted inputs.
summary.tldr: TRUST adapts vision state space models at test time using varied image traversals, pseudo-labels, and averaged parameter updates.

title: TRUST: Test-Time Refinement using Uncertainty-Guided SSM Traverses

abstract: Pruning is a widely used technique to reduce the size and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), but it often causes performance degradation. To mitigate this, existing restoration methods typically employ parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), such as LoRA, to recover the pruned model's performance. However, most PEFT methods are designed for dense models and overlook the distinct properties of pruned models, often resulting in suboptimal recovery. In this work, we propose a targeted restoration strategy for pruned models that restores performance while preserving their low cost and high efficiency. We observe that pruning-induced information loss is reflected in attention activations, and selectively reintroducing components of this information can significantly recover model performance. Based on this insight, we introduce RestoreLCC (Restoring Pruned LLMs via Lost Component Compensation), a plug-and-play method that contrastively probes critical attention heads via activation editing, extracts lost components from activation differences, and finally injects them back into the corresponding pruned heads for compensation and recovery. RestoreLCC is compatible with structured, semi-structured, and unstructured pruning schemes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RestoreLCC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both general and task-specific performance recovery, without compromising the sparsity or inference efficiency of pruned models.

Restoration often uses parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods originally designed for dense models. This paper develops a restoration strategy around the specific information lost through pruning, using changes in attention activations to locate what needs compensation.

The findings suggest that targeted compensation in attention activations can recover useful behavior without giving up the computational benefits that motivated pruning.
summary.tldr: RestoreLCC compensates for pruning-related losses in attention activations, recovering model performance while preserving sparsity and inference efficiency.

title: Restoring Pruned Large Language Models via Lost Component Compensation

abstract: The performance of an algorithm often critically depends on its hyperparameter configuration. Dynamic algorithm configuration (DAC) is a recent trend in automated machine learning, which can dynamically adjust the algorithm’s configuration during the execution process and relieve users from tedious trial-and-error tuning tasks. Recently, multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approaches have improved the configuration of multiple heterogeneous hyperparameters, making various parameter configurations for complex algorithms possible. However, many complex algorithms have inherent inter-dependencies among multiple parameters (e.g., determining the operator type first and then the operator's parameter), which are, however, not considered in previous approaches, thus leading to sub-optimal results. In this paper, we propose the sequential multi-agent DAC (Seq-MADAC) framework to address this issue by considering the inherent inter-dependencies of multiple parameters. Specifically, we propose a sequential advantage decomposition network, which can leverage action-order information through sequential advantage decomposition. Experiments from synthetic functions to the configuration of multi-objective optimization algorithms demonstrate Seq-MADAC's superior performance over state-of-the-art MARL methods and show strong generalization across problem classes. Seq-MADAC establishes a new paradigm for the widespread dependency-aware automated algorithm configuration. Our code is available at https://github.com/lamda-bbo/seq-madac.

paragraphs: Dynamic algorithm configuration adjusts hyperparameters while an algorithm runs, reducing the need for manual trial and error. Multi-agent reinforcement learning can coordinate several different hyperparameters, but their decisions may depend on one another. For example, selecting an operator can determine which setting for that operator makes sense.

Seq-MADAC builds these dependencies into the configuration process. Its sequential advantage decomposition network uses action-order information when decomposing the advantage associated with decisions. This gives the learning framework an explicit way to account for the sequence in which related parameter choices are made, addressing a dependency that earlier approaches did not consider.

Experiments range from synthetic functions to configuring multi-objective optimization algorithms. The authors report better performance than state-of-the-art multi-agent reinforcement-learning methods and strong generalization across problem classes. These results support treating parameter dependencies as part of the configuration problem itself. The broader contribution is a framework for automated tuning that uses the structure among configuration choices during execution.
summary.tldr: Seq-MADAC improves dynamic algorithm configuration by using sequential multi-agent learning to account for dependencies among hyperparameter choices.

title: Sequential Multi-Agent Dynamic Algorithm Configuration

abstract: In the natural sciences, a common challenge is to disentangle distinct, unknown sources from observations. Examples of this source separation task include deblending galaxies in a crowded field, distinguishing the activity of individual neurons from overlapping signals, and separating seismic events from the ambient background. Traditional analyses often rely on simplified source models that fail to accurately reproduce the data. Recent advances have shown that diffusion models can directly learn complex prior distributions from noisy, incomplete data. In this work, we show that diffusion models can solve the source separation problem without explicit assumptions about the source. Our method relies only on multiple views, or the property that different sets of observations contain different linear transformations of the unknown sources. We show that our method succeeds even when no source is individually observed and the observations are noisy, incomplete, and vary in resolution. The learned diffusion models enable us to sample from the source priors, evaluate the probability of candidate sources, and draw from the joint posterior of our sources given an observation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a range of synthetic problems as well as real-world galaxy observations.

paragraphs: Scientific observations often combine several sources that researchers want to study separately. Overlapping galaxies are one example: the recorded image contains blended contributions rather than a clean picture of each galaxy. This paper develops a diffusion-model approach to separating such sources without explicitly specifying a simplified model of what each source should look like.

The central requirement is access to multiple views, where different observations contain different linear transformations of the unknown sources. These views provide complementary information about the mixture. The method learns source distributions even when no source is observed alone, and the observations contain noise, missing information, or different resolutions.

The learned models support more than a single proposed separation. They can generate samples from source distributions, assess candidate sources, and sample joint source explanations conditioned on an observation. This makes uncertainty part of the reconstruction process. Demonstrations on synthetic problems and real galaxy observations support the approach, showing how multiple views can replace explicit source assumptions with distributions learned from data.
summary.tldr: Diffusion models learn to separate mixed sources from multiple observation views, including noisy and incomplete data.

title: A Data-Driven Prism: Multi-View Source Separation with Diffusion Model Priors

abstract: Conformal prediction methods are statistical tools designed to quantify uncertainty and generate predictive sets with guaranteed coverage probabilities. This work introduces an innovative refinement to these methods for classification tasks, specifically tailored for scenarios where multiple observations (multi-inputs) of a single instance are available at prediction time. Our approach is particularly motivated by applications in citizen science, where multiple images of the same plant or animal are captured by individuals. Our method integrates the information from each observation into conformal prediction, enabling a reduction in the size of the predicted label set while preserving the required class-conditional coverage guarantee. The approach is based on the aggregation of conformal p-values computed from each observation of a multi-input. By exploiting the exact distribution of these p-values, we propose a general aggregation framework using an abstract scoring function, encompassing many classical statistical tools. Knowledge of this distribution also enables refined versions of standard strategies, such as majority voting. We evaluate our method on simulated and real data, with a particular focus on Pl@ntNet, a prominent citizen science platform that facilitates the collection and identification of plant species through user-submitted images.

paragraphs: A classification system may receive several observations of the same instance, such as multiple photographs of one plant. Those images provide complementary evidence, but combining them should also preserve reliable uncertainty estimates. This paper adapts conformal prediction to that setting, producing a set of plausible labels while maintaining the required coverage guarantee separately for each class.

The method computes conformal p-values from each observation and then aggregates them. Its central ingredient is the exact distribution of those p-values, which supports a general framework for combining evidence through a scoring function. The framework accommodates many classical statistical tools and also enables refined versions of familiar approaches such as majority voting.

Using the extra observations can reduce the number of labels returned without sacrificing the stated class-conditional coverage. The authors evaluate the method on simulated and real data, with particular attention to plant identification through Pl@ntNet. The contribution connects a practical prediction setting with a statistical guarantee: multiple images can sharpen the answer while retaining uncertainty protection at the class level.
summary.tldr: Aggregating conformal p-values from multiple observations can produce smaller prediction sets while preserving class-conditional coverage.

title: Class conditional conformal prediction for multiple inputs by p-value aggregation

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is critical for ensuring the reliability of deep learning models in open-world applications. While post-hoc methods are favored for their efficiency and ease of deployment, existing approaches often underexploit the rich information embedded in the model’s logits space. In this paper, we propose LogitGap, a novel post-hoc OOD detection method that explicitly exploits the relationship between the maximum logit and the remaining logits to enhance the separability between in-distribution (ID) and OOD samples. To further improve its effectiveness, we refine LogitGap by focusing on a more compact and informative subset of the logit space. Specifically, we introduce a training-free strategy that automatically identifies the most informative logits for scoring. We provide both theoretical analysis and empirical evidence to validate the effectiveness of our approach. Extensive experiments on both vision-language and vision-only models demonstrate that LogitGap consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse OOD detection scenarios and benchmarks.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the data a model is intended to handle. LogitGap approaches this after model training by examining logits, the model’s output scores. The paper argues that existing post-hoc detectors leave useful information in the relationships among those scores underused.

The method explicitly compares the maximum logit with the remaining logits to improve separation between familiar and unfamiliar inputs. It then refines this idea by identifying a smaller, more informative subset of scores. An automatic training-free selection strategy determines which logits contribute to detection, concentrating the scoring process on information that is useful for distinguishing the two input types.

The authors support the approach with theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations on both vision-only and vision-language models. They report consistent state-of-the-art performance across diverse detection benchmarks and scenarios. The contribution is a way to obtain a stronger detection signal from a trained model’s existing score relationships, together with a selection mechanism that avoids requiring additional training for that refinement.
summary.tldr: LogitGap detects unfamiliar inputs by comparing the largest output score with an automatically selected set of other informative scores.

title: Revisiting Logit Distributions for Reliable Out-of-Distribution Detection

abstract: Bilevel optimization has garnered significant attention in the machine learning community recently, particularly regarding the development of efficient numerical methods. While substantial progress has been made in developing efficient algorithms for optimistic bilevel optimization, the study of methods for solving Pessimistic Bilevel Optimization (PBO) remains relatively less explored, especially the design of fully first-order, single-loop gradient-based algorithms. This paper aims to bridge this research gap. We first propose a novel smooth approximation to the PBO problem, using penalization and regularization techniques. Building upon this approximation, we then propose SiPBA (Single-loop Pessimistic Bilevel Algorithm), a new gradient-based method specifically designed for PBO which avoids second-order derivative information or inner-loop iterations for subproblem solving. We provide theoretical validation for the proposed smooth approximation scheme and establish theoretical convergence for the algorithm SiPBA. Numerical experiments on synthetic examples and practical applications demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of SiPBA.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization links two optimization problems, so decisions at one level depend on the solution of another. This paper addresses the pessimistic version, an area where efficient numerical methods are less developed than for optimistic formulations. Its specific goal is a gradient algorithm that avoids expensive derivative calculations and repeated inner optimization.

The authors first construct a smooth approximation using penalties and regularization. This approximation supplies the foundation for SiPBA, their Single-loop Pessimistic Bilevel Algorithm. SiPBA uses first-order gradient information and does not require an inner loop to solve subproblems. These design choices directly address two computational complications that can make bilevel algorithms cumbersome.

The paper provides theoretical support for the approximation and establishes convergence of SiPBA. Experiments on synthetic examples and practical applications also demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency. Together, these contributions connect a mathematically justified reformulation with a simpler computational procedure, giving pessimistic bilevel optimization a method specifically designed around a single loop of gradient updates.
summary.tldr: SiPBA uses a theoretically supported smooth approximation to solve pessimistic bilevel problems with a single-loop, first-order gradient algorithm.

title: A Single-Loop Gradient Algorithm for Pessimistic Bilevel Optimization via Smooth Approximation

abstract: We propose a new calibration method for survival models based on the Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) metric. Existing approaches—including conformal prediction, D-calibration, and Kaplan–Meier (KM)-based methods—often rely on heuristic binning or additional nonparametric estimators, which undermine their adaptability to continuous-time settings and complex model outputs. To address these limitations, we introduce a streamlined $\textit{KS metric-based post-processing}$ framework (KSP) that calibrates survival predictions without relying on discretization or KM estimation. This design enhances flexibility and broad applicability. We conduct extensive experiments on diverse real-world datasets using a variety of survival models. Empirical results demonstrate that our method consistently improves calibration performance over existing methods while maintaining high predictive accuracy. We also provide a theoretical analysis of the KS metric and discuss extensions to in-processing settings.

paragraphs: KSP addresses calibration in survival models: how well their predicted probabilities agree with observed outcomes over time. The paper focuses on adjusting predictions after a model has been trained. Its motivation is that existing calibration approaches often depend on heuristic bins or additional nonparametric estimates, making continuous-time predictions and complex model outputs harder to handle flexibly.

The proposed post-processing framework uses the Kolmogorov–Smirnov metric as its basis. It avoids both discretizing predictions and estimating a Kaplan–Meier curve. Removing those dependencies gives the method a streamlined design intended to work across different survival models. The authors also analyze the metric theoretically and discuss extending the approach to calibration performed during model training.

Experiments span diverse real-world datasets and multiple survival models. Within these evaluations, KSP consistently improves calibration over existing methods while maintaining high predictive accuracy. The findings indicate that adjusting probability reliability need not come with a loss of strong predictive performance in the tested settings, and that the framework can be used across varied model choices.
summary.tldr: KSP improves survival-model calibration through KS-based post-processing without discretization or Kaplan–Meier estimation.

title: KSP: Kolmogorov-Smirnov metric-based Post-Hoc Calibration for Survival Analysis

abstract: After pre-training, large language models are aligned with human preferences based on pairwise comparisons. State-of-the-art alignment methods (such as PPO-based RLHF and DPO) are built on the assumption of aligning with a single preference model, despite being deployed in settings where users have diverse preferences. As a result, it is not even clear that these alignment methods produce models that satisfy users \emph{on average} --- a minimal requirement for pluralistic alignment. Drawing on social choice theory and modeling users' comparisons through individual Bradley-Terry (BT) models, we introduce an alignment method's \emph{distortion}: the worst-case ratio between the optimal achievable average utility, and the average utility of the learned policy. The notion of distortion helps draw sharp distinctions between alignment methods: \emph{Nash Learning from Human Feedback} achieves the minimax optimal distortion of $(\frac{1}{2} + o(1)) \cdot \beta$ (for the BT temperature $\beta$), robustly across utility distributions, distributions of comparison pairs, and permissible KL divergences from the reference policy. RLHF and DPO, by contrast, suffer $\geq (1 - o(1)) \cdot \beta$ distortion already without a KL constraint, and $e^{\Omega(\beta)}$ or even unbounded distortion in the full setting, depending on how comparison pairs are sampled.

paragraphs: Preference alignment commonly trains language models from comparisons between pairs of responses. This paper asks whether methods built around a single preference model serve users well on average when different users have different preferences. It studies that question through social choice theory, representing each user's comparisons with an individual Bradley–Terry model.

The authors define distortion as the worst-case ratio of the best achievable average utility to the average utility of the learned policy. A large ratio means substantial average benefit can be lost. This criterion distinguishes methods that might otherwise appear similar when evaluated as ways to fit comparison data.

Within this formulation, Nash Learning from Human Feedback achieves minimax-optimal distortion of approximately half the Bradley–Terry temperature parameter beta. That guarantee holds across the specified utility distributions, comparison-pair distributions, and permitted KL constraints. RLHF and DPO have worst-case distortion at least approximately beta even without a KL constraint; in the full setting it can be exponential in beta or unbounded, depending on pair sampling. These are theoretical worst-case distinctions, showing that fitting preferences and protecting average utility can diverge.
summary.tldr: A social-choice analysis shows that preference-alignment methods can differ sharply in their worst-case protection of average user utility.

title: Distortion of AI Alignment: Does Preference Optimization Optimize for Preferences?

abstract: The selection of hyperparameters, such as prompt templates in large language models (LLMs), must often strike a balance between reliability and cost. In many cases, structural relationships between the expected reliability levels of the hyperparameters can be inferred from prior information and held-out data -- e.g., longer prompt templates may be more detailed and thus more reliable. However, existing hyperparameter selection methods either do not provide formal reliability guarantees or are unable to incorporate structured knowledge in the hyperparameter space. This paper introduces reliability graph-based Pareto testing (RG-PT), a novel multi-objective hyperparameter selection framework that maintains formal reliability guarantees in terms of false discovery rate (FDR), while accounting for known relationships among hyperparameters via a directed acyclic graph. Edges in the graph reflect expected reliability and cost trade-offs among hyperparameters, which are inferred via the Bradley-Terry (BT) ranking model from prior information and held-out data. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that RG-PT significantly outperforms existing methods such as learn-then-test (LTT) and Pareto testing (PT) through a more efficient exploration of the hyperparameter space.

paragraphs: Choosing a model configuration often involves balancing reliability against cost. Prior knowledge can suggest relationships among candidates: a longer prompt, for example, may provide more detail and therefore be more reliable. Existing selection methods do not always combine such structured information with formal statistical guarantees about the configurations they accept.

Reliability graph-based Pareto testing represents expected reliability and cost relationships as a directed acyclic graph. The graph is inferred from prior information and held-out data using a Bradley-Terry ranking model. These relationships guide exploration of the configuration space, allowing the selection procedure to use evidence about how candidates compare rather than considering their structure irrelevant.

The framework maintains reliability guarantees expressed through false discovery rate control. This is a statistical guarantee about erroneous discoveries in the selection process, rather than certainty that every accepted configuration is reliable. Experiments show significant improvements over learn-then-test and Pareto testing, attributed to more efficient exploration. The contribution combines structured comparisons, multiple objectives, and formal testing within one selection framework.
summary.tldr: RG-PT uses graphs of expected reliability–cost relationships to improve hyperparameter selection while controlling false discoveries.

title: Multi-Objective Hyperparameter Selection via Hypothesis Testing on Reliability Graphs

abstract: Model editing enables targeted updates to the knowledge of large language models (LLMs) with minimal retraining. Among existing approaches, locate-then-edit methods constitute a prominent paradigm: they first identify critical layers, then compute residuals at the final critical layer based on the target edit, and finally apply least-squares-based multi-layer updates via $\textbf{residual distribution}$. While empirically effective, we identify a counterintuitive failure mode: residual distribution, a core mechanism in these methods, introduces weight shift errors that undermine editing precision. Through theoretical and empirical analysis, we show that such errors increase with the distribution distance, batch size, and edit sequence length, ultimately leading to inaccurate or suboptimal edits. To address this, we propose the $\textbf{B}$oundary $\textbf{L}$ayer $\textbf{U}$pdat$\textbf{E (BLUE)}$ strategy to enhance locate-then-edit methods. Sequential batch editing experiments on three LLMs and two datasets demonstrate that BLUE not only delivers an average performance improvement of 35.59\%, significantly advancing the state of the art in model editing, but also enhances the preservation of LLMs' general capabilities. Our code is available at https://github.com/xpq-tech/BLUE.

paragraphs: Locate-then-edit methods update specific knowledge in a language model by identifying important layers and changing their weights. A common procedure computes the desired correction at the final selected layer, then distributes that residual across several layers through least-squares updates. This paper finds that the distribution step can itself reduce editing precision.

The authors analyze the problem both theoretically and empirically. They show that residual distribution introduces weight-shift errors, and that these errors grow with distribution distance, batch size, and the length of an edit sequence. This identifies a mechanism through which a seemingly useful multi-layer update can lead to inaccurate or suboptimal changes, especially as editing accumulates.

To address the failure mode, they propose Boundary Layer Update, or BLUE, as a strategy for improving locate-then-edit methods. Sequential batch-editing experiments on three language models and two datasets report an average performance improvement of 35.59%, alongside better preservation of general capabilities. The contribution links a specific source of editing error to a corrective strategy, with evidence covering both successful updates and retention of broader model ability.
summary.tldr: BLUE improves targeted language-model editing by addressing weight-shift errors caused by distributing residual corrections across layers.

title: Rethinking Residual Distribution in Locate-then-Edit Model Editing

abstract: *Precision* and *Recall* are fundamental metrics in machine learning tasks where both accurate predictions and comprehensive coverage are essential, such as in multi-label learning, language generation, medical studies, and recommender systems. A key challenge in these settings is the prevalence of one-sided feedback, where only positive examples are observed during training—e.g., in multi-label tasks like tagging people in Facebook photos, we may observe only a few tagged individuals, without knowing who else appears in the image. To address learning under such partial feedback, we introduce a Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) framework in which hypotheses are set functions that map each input to a set of labels, extending beyond single-label predictions and generalizing classical binary, multi-class, and multi-label models. Our results reveal sharp statistical and algorithmic separations from standard settings: classical methods such as Empirical Risk Minimization provably fail, even for simple hypothesis classes. We develop new algorithms that learn from positive data alone, achieving optimal sample complexity in the realizable case, and establishing multiplicative—rather than additive—approximation guarantees in the agnostic case, where achieving additive regret is impossible.

paragraphs: Many learning problems provide only a partial list of correct answers. A photograph may have some people tagged without revealing everyone present, for example. In such settings, an unobserved label is not necessarily incorrect. This paper studies how to learn predictions that balance precision and recall when training supplies positive examples alone.

The authors introduce a Probably Approximately Correct framework in which each hypothesis maps an input to a set of labels. This accommodates richer outputs than a single predicted class and generalizes classical binary, multiclass, and multilabel formulations. Their analysis shows that familiar tools can behave very differently here: empirical risk minimization provably fails even for simple hypothesis classes.

New algorithms achieve optimal sample complexity in the realizable case, where the hypothesis class can represent the target. In the agnostic case, they provide multiplicative approximation guarantees, while additive regret guarantees are impossible in the studied framework. The results clarify both what positive-only feedback allows and why precision-and-recall learning requires methods and guarantees tailored to incomplete observations.
summary.tldr: A new learning framework establishes algorithms and limits for predicting label sets with good precision and recall from positive-only feedback.

title: Probably Approximately Precision and Recall Learning

abstract: Enabling virtual humans to dynamically and realistically respond to diverse auditory stimuli remains a key challenge in character animation, demanding the integration of perceptual modeling and motion synthesis. Despite its significance, this task remains largely unexplored. Most previous works have primarily focused on mapping modalities like speech, audio, and music to generate human motion. As of yet, these models typically overlook the impact of spatial features encoded in spatial audio signals on human motion. To bridge this gap and enable high-quality modeling of human movements in response to spatial audio, we introduce the first comprehensive "Spatial Audio-Driven Human Motion" (SAM) dataset, which contains diverse and high-quality spatial audio and motion data. For benchmarking, we develop a simple yet effective diffusion-based generative framework for human "MOtion generation driven by SPatial Audio," termed MOSPA, which faithfully captures the relationship between body motion and spatial audio through an effective fusion mechanism. Once trained, MOSPA can generate diverse realistic human motions conditioned on varying spatial audio inputs. We perform a thorough investigation of the proposed dataset and conduct extensive experiments for benchmarking, where our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on this task. Our code and model are publicly available at https://github.com/xsy27/Mospa-Acoustic-driven-Motion-Generation.git

paragraphs: MOSPA studies how virtual humans can move in response to spatial audio. Previous audio-to-motion work has largely focused on speech, music, or other sound content while overlooking spatial features in the audio signal. The paper treats those features as meaningful inputs for generating body motion responsive to the surrounding auditory environment.

The authors introduce SAM, a dataset containing diverse spatial audio paired with human motion. They also develop MOSPA, a diffusion-based generative framework that combines audio and motion information through a fusion mechanism. Its purpose is to learn the relationship between spatial sound and body movement, allowing different audio inputs to condition different generated motions.

Once trained, the model produces diverse, realistic motion sequences. The paper investigates the dataset and benchmarks the method through extensive experiments, reporting leading performance on the spatial-audio-driven motion task. The dataset and model together establish both training material and a reference approach for studying this relationship. The contribution broadens audio-conditioned animation toward movements informed by spatial auditory information, beyond the speech and music mappings emphasized in earlier work.
summary.tldr: MOSPA pairs a spatial-audio-and-motion dataset with a diffusion model that generates realistic body movements conditioned on spatial sound.

title: 🎧MOSPA: Human Motion Generation Driven by Spatial Audio

abstract: Diffusion models have achieved impressive performance in generating high-quality and diverse synthetic data. However, their success typically assumes a class-balanced training distribution. In real-world settings, multi-class data often follow a long-tailed distribution, where standard diffusion models struggle—producing low-diversity and lower-quality samples for underrepresented (tail) classes. While this degradation is well-documented, its underlying cause remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate the behavior of diffusion models trained on long-tailed datasets and identify a key issue: the latent representations (from the bottleneck layer of the U-Net) for tail class subspaces exhibit significant overlap with those of head classes, leading to feature borrowing and poor generation quality. Importantly, we show that this is not merely due to limited data per class, but that the relative class imbalance significantly contributes to this phenomenon. To address this, we propose **CO**ntrastive **R**egularization for **A**ligning **L**atents (CORAL), a contrastive latent alignment framework that leverages supervised contrastive losses to encourage well-separated latent class representations. Experiments demonstrate that CORAL significantly improves both the diversity and visual quality of samples generated for tail classes relative to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Diffusion models trained on imbalanced datasets often generate less varied and lower-quality examples for rare classes. This paper investigates what happens inside the model when some classes dominate training. It focuses on latent representations at the bottleneck of the U-Net, where information used during generation is represented internally.

The authors identify substantial overlap between the latent subspaces of rare classes and those of common classes. They connect this overlap to feature borrowing, in which rare-class generation draws on features associated with dominant classes. Their analysis indicates that relative class imbalance contributes to the problem beyond the effect of having few examples of a particular class.

CORAL addresses this overlap through supervised contrastive losses that encourage class representations to separate. The intervention therefore targets the organization of the latent space during learning. Experiments report significant improvements in both diversity and visual quality for rare-class samples compared with state-of-the-art methods. The findings connect an internal representational problem to a training objective designed to reduce it.
summary.tldr: CORAL separates overlapping class representations in diffusion models to improve the diversity and quality of samples from underrepresented classes.

title: CORAL: Disentangling Latent Representations in Long-Tailed Diffusion

abstract: Open-world perception aims to develop a model adaptable to novel domains and various sensor configurations and can understand uncommon objects and corner cases. However, current research lacks sufficiently comprehensive open-world 3D perception benchmarks and robust generalizable methodologies. This paper introduces OpenAD, the first real open-world autonomous driving benchmark for 3D object detection. OpenAD is built upon a corner case discovery and annotation pipeline that integrates with a multimodal large language model (MLLM). The proposed pipeline annotates corner case objects in a unified format for five autonomous driving perception datasets with 2000 scenarios. In addition, we devise evaluation methodologies and evaluate various open-world and specialized 2D and 3D models. Moreover, we propose a vision-centric 3D open-world object detection baseline and further introduce an ensemble method by fusing general and specialized models to address the issue of lower precision in existing open-world methods for the OpenAD benchmark. We host an online challenge on EvalAI. Data, toolkit codes, and evaluation codes are available at https://github.com/VDIGPKU/OpenAD.

paragraphs: Open-world driving perception must handle unfamiliar objects, unusual situations, and changes in sensing conditions. The authors argue that existing 3D perception benchmarks do not comprehensively evaluate this combination. OpenAD addresses that gap by bringing corner-case objects from multiple autonomous-driving datasets into a common benchmark for three-dimensional detection.

The benchmark uses a discovery and annotation pipeline incorporating a multimodal large language model. It produces annotations in a unified format across five driving-perception datasets and 2,000 scenarios. The authors also develop evaluation methods and assess a range of open-world and specialized models operating in two and three dimensions.

Beyond the benchmark, the paper introduces a vision-centric baseline for open-world 3D detection. It also proposes an ensemble combining general and specialized models to address the low precision of existing open-world methods on OpenAD. The contribution therefore includes both a way to measure difficult perception cases and an approach intended to improve handling of them. An online challenge and released evaluation tools support continued comparison of methods under this shared evaluation setting.
summary.tldr: OpenAD unifies unusual driving scenarios for evaluating open-world 3D detection and introduces baseline and ensemble approaches.

title: OpenAD: Open-World Autonomous Driving Benchmark for 3D Object Detection

abstract: Securing software supply chains is a growing challenge due to the inadequacy of existing datasets in capturing the complexity of next-gen attacks, such as multiphase malware execution, remote access activation, and dynamic payload generation. Existing datasets, which rely on metadata inspection and static code analysis, are inadequate for detecting such attacks. This creates a critical gap because these datasets do not capture what happens during and after a package is installed. To address this gap, we present QUT-DV25, a dynamic analysis dataset specifically designed to support and advance research on detecting and mitigating supply chain attacks within the Python Package Index (PyPI) ecosystem. This dataset captures install and post-install-time traces from 14,271 Python packages, of which 7,127 are malicious. The packages are executed in an isolated sandbox environment using an extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) kernel and user-level probes. It captures 36 real-time features, that includes system calls, network traffic, resource usages, directory access patterns, dependency logs, and installation behaviors, enabling the study of next-gen attack vectors. abstract: Super-resolution (SR) advances astronomical imaging by enabling cost-effective high-resolution capture, crucial for detecting faraway celestial objects and precise structural analysis. However, existing datasets for astronomical SR (ASR) exhibit three critical limitations: flux inconsistency, object-crop setting, and insufficient data diversity, significantly impeding ASR development. We propose STAR, a large-scale astronomical SR dataset containing 54,738 flux-consistent star field image pairs covering wide celestial regions. These pairs combine Hubble Space Telescope high-resolution observations with physically faithful low-resolution counterparts generated through a flux-preserving data generation pipeline, enabling systematic development of field-level ASR models. To further empower the ASR community, STAR provides a novel Flux Error (FE) to evaluate SR models in physical view. Leveraging this benchmark, we propose a Flux-Invariant Super Resolution (FISR) model that could accurately infer the flux-consistent high-resolution images from input photometry, suppressing several SR state-of-the-art methods by 24.84% on a novel designed flux consistency metric, showing the priority of our method for astrophysics. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method and the value of our dataset. Code and models are available at https://github.com/GuoCheng12/STAR.

paragraphs: STAR focuses on improving astronomical image resolution while preserving flux, the light information needed for physically meaningful analysis. The paper identifies problems in existing datasets: inconsistent flux, an emphasis on cropped objects, and limited diversity. Its benchmark instead covers broad star fields, supporting models that reconstruct larger celestial regions.

The dataset contains 54,738 image pairs. High-resolution images come from Hubble Space Telescope observations, and their lower-resolution counterparts are generated with a physically faithful, flux-preserving pipeline. The authors also introduce Flux Error as a measure for evaluating the physical consistency of super-resolution results. This makes preservation of light measurements an explicit part of both data construction and evaluation.

Using STAR, the authors develop Flux-Invariant Super Resolution, or FISR, to infer high-resolution images consistent with input photometry. They report a 24.84% improvement over several state-of-the-art super-resolution methods on their flux-consistency metric. The contribution combines a dataset, an evaluation criterion, and a model around the same scientific requirement: increased image detail should remain consistent with the measured light.
summary.tldr: STAR pairs a flux-preserving astronomical dataset with a physical evaluation metric and a model that improves reported flux consistency.

title: STAR: A Benchmark for Astronomical Star Fields Super-Resolution

abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models has been successfully incentivized through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, leading to improved one-shot precision. In this work, we turn our focus to the coding domain. Beyond one-shot precision, we highlight unit test generation as another key factor for enhancing coding ability, since accurate unit tests are essential for enabling self-checking and self-correction during inference. Traditional approaches for fine-tuning LLMs on unit test generation rely heavily on ground-truth code solutions in the training data. We propose CURE, a novel reinforcement learning framework with a dedicated reward design that co-evolves coding and unit test generation capabilities based on their interaction outcomes—without any ground-truth code as supervision. This approach enables flexible and scalable training and allows the unit tester to learn directly from the coder’s mistakes. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that our CURE models, derived from base models of varying sizes, excel in both code generation and unit test generation. They naturally extend to downstream tasks such as test-time scaling—achieving a 6.2\% improvement over the base model—and agentic unit test generation, with a 25.1\% improvement. Our 4B model consistently outperforms Qwen3-4B while achieving 64.8\% inference efficiency in unit test generation. Notably, we also find that the CURE model can serve as an effective reward model for reinforcement learning on base models, even in the absence of any labeled supervision.

paragraphs: Improving a coding model involves more than getting its first answer right. Useful unit tests also let the model check and revise code during inference. This paper develops CURE, a reinforcement learning framework that jointly improves code generation and test generation without using ground-truth code solutions as supervision.

CURE trains through interactions between a coder and a unit tester, using a dedicated reward design based on their outcomes. The tester can learn from mistakes made by the coder, making those mistakes part of the training signal. This matters because conventional unit-test fine-tuning depends heavily on reference implementations, whereas CURE builds supervision from the interaction itself.

Evaluations across model sizes report strong results in both coding and test generation. The abstract gives improvements of 6.2% for test-time scaling and 25.1% for agentic unit-test generation. Its 4B model also consistently outperforms Qwen3-4B. Beyond these tasks, the authors find that a CURE model can provide effective rewards for reinforcement learning on base models without labeled supervision, extending the usefulness of the learned testing capability.
summary.tldr: CURE jointly trains coding and unit-testing abilities through reinforcement learning interactions without ground-truth code supervision.

title: Co-Evolving LLM Coder and Unit Tester via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The modern connectivist framing of neural computation emphasizes the primacy of synaptic communication at the risk of neglecting the influence of the surrounding neuromodulatory environment --- a neuron's 'biophysical context.' Decades of experimental work has established two views of neuromodulatory (NMs) influence: 1) NMs significantly alter circuit dynamics and 2) NMs gate synaptic plasticity, acting as a 'third factor' in learning. Here, we unify these perspectives, proposing that neuromodulation via volume transmission implements a powerful computational principle: context factorization. We derive an endogenously neuromodulated Recurrent Neural Network (e-nmRNN) from a rate reduction of NM release, showing how NM concentrations dynamically factorize network connectivity. This framework reveals how multiplicative NM gating distinctly influences dynamical regimes compared to additive input. Crucially, this context factorization enables targeted online credit assignment: learning rules derived for the e-nmRNN are naturally gated by NM concentrations, localizing updates to relevant contexts. We demonstrate that e-nmRNN dynamics can learn to approximate gradient descent, facilitating rapid in-context adaptation akin to meta-learning. Empirically, e-nmRNNs achieve strong compositional generalization in sequence-to-sequence tasks, outperforming baselines and exhibiting greater hyperparameter robustness. Furthermore, when trained on complex multitasking benchmarks, e-nmRNNs develop emergent properties mirroring biological observations, including modularity, cell-type specialization based on NM release, and distinct neuromodulatory timescales encoding task context. The model's interpretability allows us to reverse engineer these emergent structures. Notably, in reinforcement learning tasks, the e-nmRNN learns to encode context and signals like Reward Prediction Error (RPE) within its neuromodulator dynamics, demonstrating a mechanism for RPE-gated online credit assignment essential for learning how to learn. By bridging biophysical mechanisms with computational principles and empirical validation, our work presents e-nmRNNs as a performant, interpretable model for understanding the computational role of neuromodulation in flexible and compositional learning.

title: Volume Transmission Implements Context Factorization to Target Online Credit Assignment and Enable Compositional Generalization

abstract: In recent years, many studies proposed to generate solutions for Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) scheduling problem in one shot by combining reinforcement learning and list scheduling heuristic. However, these existing methods suffer from biased estimation of sampling probabilities and inefficient guidance in training, due to redundant comparisons among node priorities and the sparse reward challenge. To address these issues, we analyze of the limitations of these existing methods, and propose a novel one-shot DAG scheduling method with comparability identification and dense reward signal, based on the policy gradient framework. In our method, a comparable antichain identification mechanism is proposed to eliminate the problem of redundant nodewise priority comparison. We also propose a dense reward signal for node level decision-making optimization in training, effectively addressing the sparse reward challenge. The experimental results show that the proposed method can yield superior results of scheduling objectives compared to other learning-based DAG scheduling methods.
