paragraphs: Scheduling a directed acyclic graph involves arranging tasks whose dependencies restrict their execution order. Existing learning methods combine reinforcement learning with list scheduling to produce a solution in one shot. This paper identifies two training problems in those methods: redundant comparisons between node priorities can bias sampling-probability estimates, and sparse rewards provide inefficient guidance.

The proposed method works within a policy-gradient framework. A comparable antichain identification mechanism removes redundant nodewise priority comparisons. Alongside it, a dense reward signal supplies guidance for individual node decisions during training. These components address different parts of the learning process: which comparisons are needed and how much useful feedback the learner receives.

Experiments show better scheduling objectives than other learning-based DAG scheduling methods. The contribution is a targeted revision of how a one-shot scheduling policy is trained, rather than merely adding a different scoring model. By reducing unnecessary priority comparisons and making decision-level feedback denser, the method aims to improve both probability estimation and the effectiveness of training guidance.
summary.tldr: Removing redundant priority comparisons and providing dense node-level rewards improves learned one-shot DAG scheduling in experiments.

title: Reinforcement learning for one-shot DAG scheduling with comparability identification and dense reward

abstract: Data fusion techniques integrate information from heterogeneous data sources to improve learning, generalization, and decision-making across data sciences. In causal inference, these methods leverage rich observational data to improve causal effect estimation, while maintaining the trustworthiness of randomized controlled trials. Existing approaches often relax the strong "no unobserved confounding" assumption by instead assuming exchangeability of counterfactual outcomes across data sources. However, when both assumptions simultaneously fail—a common scenario in practice—current methods cannot identify or estimate causal effects. We address this limitation by proposing a novel partial identification framework that enables researchers to answer key questions such as: *Is the causal effect positive/negative?* and *How severe must assumption violations be to overturn this conclusion?* Our approach introduces interpretable sensitivity parameters that quantify assumption violations and derives corresponding causal effect bounds. We develop doubly robust estimators for these bounds and operationalize breakdown frontier analysis to understand how causal conclusions change as assumption violations increase. We apply our framework to the Project STAR study, which investigates the effect of classroom size on students’ third-grade standardized test performance. Our analysis reveals that the Project STAR results are robust to simultaneous violations of key assumptions, both on average and across various subgroups of interest. This strengthens confidence in the study's conclusions despite potential unmeasured biases in the data.

title: Data Fusion for Partial Identification of Causal Effects

abstract: Inspired by the success of large language models, there is a trend toward developing graph foundation models to conduct diverse downstream tasks in various domains. However, current models often require extra fine-tuning to apply their learned structural and semantic representations to new graphs, which limits their versatility. Recent breakthroughs in zero-shot inductive reasoning on knowledge graphs (KGs), offer us a new perspective on extending KG reasoning to general graph applications. In this paper, we introduce SCR, a unified graph reasoning framework designed to train on knowledge graphs and effectively generalize across a wide range of graph tasks and domains. We begin by designing the task-specific KG structures to establish a unified topology for different task formats. Then we propose semantic-conditioned message passing, a novel mechanism addressing the inherent semantic isolation in traditional KG reasoning, by jointly modeling structural and semantic invariance patterns in graph representations. Evaluated on 38 diverse datasets spanning node-, link-, and graph-level tasks, SCR achieves substantial performance gains over existing foundation models and supervised baselines, demonstrating its remarkable efficacy and adaptability.

paragraphs: SCR investigates whether training on knowledge graphs can produce a model useful across many other graph tasks. Existing graph foundation models often need additional fine-tuning to apply what they have learned to new graphs. The paper takes inspiration from zero-shot inductive knowledge-graph reasoning and develops a unified framework for broader transfer.

The framework first constructs task-specific knowledge-graph structures that give different task formats a shared topology. It then uses semantic-conditioned message passing to combine structural and semantic patterns in graph representations. This mechanism addresses semantic isolation in traditional knowledge-graph reasoning, allowing meaning and connectivity to contribute jointly to transferable representations.

The evaluation covers 38 datasets with tasks involving individual nodes, links, and entire graphs. SCR achieves substantial gains over the existing foundation models and supervised baselines considered in those experiments. The findings support knowledge-graph training as a route toward reusable graph reasoning. They also connect that transfer to two design choices: expressing tasks through compatible structures and incorporating semantics directly into message passing.
summary.tldr: SCR combines unified task structures with semantic-conditioned message passing to transfer knowledge-graph training across diverse graph tasks.

title: Towards Graph Foundation Models: Training on Knowledge Graphs Enables Transferability to General Graphs

abstract: Rectilinear Steiner Minimum Tree (RSMT) is widely used in Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) and aims at connecting a set of pins using rectilinear edges while minimizing wirelength. Recently, learning-based methods have been explored to tackle this problem effectively. However, existing methods either suffer from excessive exploration of the search space or rely on heuristic combinations that compromise effectiveness and efficiency, and this limitation becomes notably exacerbated when extended to the obstacle-avoiding RSMT (OARSMT). To address this, we propose OAREST, a reinforcement learning-based framework for constructing an Obstacle-Avoiding Rectilinear Edge Sequence (RES) Tree. We theoretically establish the optimality of RES in obstacle-avoiding scenarios, which forms the foundation of our approach. Leveraging this theoretical insight, we introduce a dynamic masking strategy that supports parallel training across varying numbers of pins and extends to obstacles during inference. Empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks show superior effectiveness and efficiency for RSMT and OARSMT problems, particularly in handling obstacles without training on them. Code available: https://github.com/Thinklab-SJTU/EDA-AI/.

paragraphs: This paper tackles a chip-routing problem: connecting a collection of pins with horizontal and vertical edges while minimizing total wire length. Adding obstacles makes the task harder because routes must also avoid blocked regions. The authors identify excessive search and reliance on heuristic combinations as obstacles to effective and efficient learning-based solutions.

Their framework, OAREST, uses reinforcement learning to construct an obstacle-avoiding Rectilinear Edge Sequence tree. They first establish the optimality of this representation in obstacle-avoiding settings, providing a theoretical foundation for the construction method. A dynamic masking strategy then supports parallel training with different numbers of pins and extends to handling obstacles at inference time.

The central practical result is that the model can handle obstacles without being trained on them. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world benchmarks report superior effectiveness and efficiency for both the ordinary and obstacle-avoiding problems. The work links a theoretically supported tree representation with a training procedure that transfers to the additional routing constraints introduced at test time.
summary.tldr: OAREST combines a theoretically supported routing representation with reinforcement learning to handle obstacles at inference without obstacle-based training.

title: Train on Pins and Test on Obstacles for Rectilinear Steiner Minimum Tree

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have attained human-level fluency in text generation, which complicates the distinguishing between human-written and LLM generated texts. This increases the risk of misuse and highlights the need for reliable detectors. Yet, existing detectors exhibit poor robustness on out-of-distribution (OOD) data and attacked data, which is critical for real-world scenarios. Also, they struggle to provide interpretable evidence to support their decisions, thus undermining reliability. In light of these challenges, we propose IPAD (Inverse Prompt for AI Detection), a novel framework consisting of a Prompt Inverter that identifies predicted prompts that could have generated the input text, and two Distinguishers that examine the probability that the input texts align with the predicted prompts. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that IPAD outperforms the strongest baselines by 9.05% (Average Recall) on in-distribution data, 12.93% (AUROC) on out-of-distribution (OOD) data, and 5.48% (AUROC) on attacked data. IPAD also performs robust on structured datasets. Furthermore, an interpretability assessment is conducted to illustrate that IPAD enhances the AI detection trustworthiness by allowing users to directly examine the decision-making evidence, which provides interpretable support for its state-of-the-art detection results.

paragraphs: IPAD tackles the difficulty of distinguishing fluent model-generated text from human writing. The paper focuses on two weaknesses of existing detectors: reduced robustness when data differs from the training distribution or has been attacked, and limited evidence that people can inspect to understand a detection decision.

The framework begins with a Prompt Inverter that predicts prompts capable of producing the input text. Two Distinguishers then examine how likely the text is to align with those predicted prompts. This makes the inferred relationship between a possible instruction and its response part of the detection process, providing material that users can examine alongside the resulting decision.

It also performs robustly on structured datasets. An interpretability assessment supports the value of exposing decision evidence. The reported contribution therefore combines stronger empirical detection with a mechanism for making the basis of a classification more inspectable.
summary.tldr: IPAD detects generated text by reconstructing plausible prompts and evaluating text–prompt alignment, improving reported robustness while exposing decision evidence.

title: IPAD: Inverse Prompt for AI Detection - A Robust and Interpretable LLM-Generated Text Detector

abstract: Tests of conditional independence (CI) underpin a number of important problems in machine learning and statistics, from causal discovery to evaluation of predictor fairness and out-of-distribution robustness. Shah and Peters (2020) showed that, contrary to the unconditional case, no universally finite-sample valid test can ever achieve nontrivial power. While informative, this result (based on “hiding” dependence) does not seem to explain the frequent practical failures observed with popular CI tests. We investigate the Kernel-based Conditional Independence (KCI) test – of which we show the Generalized Covariance Measure underlying many recent tests is _nearly_ a special case – and identify the major factors underlying its practical behavior. We highlight the key role of errors in the conditional mean embedding estimate for the Type I error, while pointing out the importance of selecting an appropriate conditioning kernel (not recognized in previous work) as being necessary for good test power but also tending to inflate Type I error.

We highlight the key role of errors in the conditional mean embedding estimate for the Type I error, while pointing out the importance of selecting an appropriate conditioning kernel (not recognized in previous work) as being necessary for good test power but also tending to inflate Type I error.

paragraphs: Conditional independence testing asks whether two quantities remain related after accounting for other information. Such tests support causal discovery and assessments of fairness and robustness. A known impossibility result rules out universally valid finite-sample tests with nontrivial detection power, but the authors argue that this result does not adequately explain the failures often seen in practical tests.

They investigate the Kernel-based Conditional Independence test, or KCI, to identify more concrete causes of its behavior. Their analysis also shows that the Generalized Covariance Measure, which underlies many recent tests, is nearly a special case of KCI. This connection makes the investigation relevant to a broader family of testing methods.

The paper highlights errors in estimating conditional mean embeddings as a key influence on false positives, also called Type I errors. It further identifies the conditioning kernel as an important choice: an appropriate kernel is necessary for good detection power, but also tends to inflate false positives. The analysis therefore exposes a practical tension between finding dependence and maintaining error control.
summary.tldr: The paper links practical conditional independence testing failures to conditional estimation errors and a kernel-choice tension between detection power and false positives.

title: On the Hardness of Conditional Independence Testing In Practice

abstract: In many machine learning applications the quality of the data is limited by resource constraints (may it be power, bandwidth, memory, ...). In such cases, the constraints are on the average resources allocated, therefore there is some control over each sample’s quality. In most cases this option remains unused and the data’s quality is uniform over the samples. In this paper we propose to actively allocate resources to each sample such that resources are used optimally overall. We propose a method to compute the optimal resource allocation. We further derive generalization bounds for the case where the problem’s model is unknown. We demonstrate the potential benefit of this approach on both simulated and real-life problems.

paragraphs: The quality of observations used by a classifier can depend on limited resources such as power, bandwidth, or memory. When the constraint applies to average resource use, individual samples need not all receive the same allocation. This creates an opportunity to choose how much to spend on acquiring each sample while respecting the overall budget.

The paper proposes actively allocating resources across samples to improve overall classification. It develops a method for computing the optimal allocation, making acquisition quality a decision variable within the learning problem. The approach matters because uniformly acquired data leave this flexibility unused even when the resource constraint permits different treatment of different samples.

The authors also derive generalization bounds for the case where the problem's model is unknown. This addresses the need to learn about the problem while deciding how to allocate acquisition resources. Simulated and real-life examples demonstrate the potential benefit of the approach. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support considering data acquisition and prediction jointly when quality can be controlled under an average budget.
summary.tldr: Dynamic sensing optimizes how acquisition resources are distributed across samples under an average budget, with generalization bounds when the model is unknown.

title: Dynamic Sensing: Better Classification under Acquisition Constraints

abstract: Automatic forecasting of time series data is a challenging problem in many industries. Current forecast models adopted by businesses do not provide adequate means for including data representing external factors that may have a significant impact on the time series, such as weather, national events, local events, social media trends, promotions, etc. This paper introduces a novel neural network attention mechanism that naturally incorporates data from multiple external sources without the feature engineering needed to get other techniques to work. We demonstrate empirically that the proposed model achieves superior performance for predicting the demand of 20 commodities across 107 stores of one of America’s largest retailers when compared to other baseline models, including neural networks, linear models, certain kernel methods, Bayesian regression, and decision trees. Our method ultimately accounts for a 23.9% relative improvement as a result of the incorporation of external data sources, and provides an unprecedented level of descriptive ability for a neural network forecasting model.

paragraphs: A time series can change because of influences outside its own history. Weather, events, promotions, and social media trends can all matter for business forecasts, yet the forecasting systems discussed in this paper lack adequate ways to incorporate such information. The authors focus on making multiple external data sources usable within a neural forecasting model.

Their contribution is an attention mechanism that incorporates these sources without the feature engineering needed by other techniques. The approach makes external information part of the forecasting process and also gives the model a greater descriptive ability. This matters because the external factors are useful not only for improving predictions but also for describing what the model takes into account.

The empirical evaluation covers demand for 20 commodities across 107 stores of a large American retailer. The model outperforms the tested neural, linear, kernel, Bayesian regression, and decision-tree baselines. The authors report a 23.9% relative improvement from incorporating external sources, supporting the practical value of this information in the evaluated forecasting setting.
summary.tldr: Multifactor neural attention incorporates external data into retail forecasts and delivers a reported 23.9% relative improvement.

title: Correcting Forecasts with Multifactor Neural Attention

abstract: We introduce topological mixture estimation, a completely nonparametric and computationally efficient solution to the problem of estimating a one-dimensional mixture with generic unimodal components. We repeatedly perturb the unimodal decomposition of Baryshnikov and Ghrist to produce a topologically and information-theoretically optimal unimodal mixture. We also detail a smoothing process that optimally exploits topological persistence of the unimodal category in a natural way when working directly with sample data. Finally, we illustrate these techniques through examples.

We also detail a smoothing process that optimally exploits topological persistence of the unimodal category in a natural way when working directly with sample data. Finally, we illustrate these techniques through examples.

paragraphs: A mixture model represents a distribution through a combination of component distributions. This paper considers one-dimensional mixtures whose components are unimodal, meaning each component has a single mode. It introduces a fully nonparametric and computationally efficient method, allowing generic unimodal components rather than requiring a specified parametric family for their shapes.

The method repeatedly perturbs an existing unimodal decomposition due to Baryshnikov and Ghrist. Through those perturbations, it produces a mixture described as optimal in topological and information-theoretic terms. The central idea is to use properties of unimodal decomposition to guide estimation, making the structure of the mixture part of the method itself.

The authors also address the case where the input consists directly of samples by developing a smoothing procedure. This procedure uses topological persistence of the unimodal category, connecting smoothing to how that structural quantity persists. Examples illustrate both the mixture-estimation method and the smoothing technique. The stated scope is one-dimensional mixtures with unimodal components.
summary.tldr: Topological mixture estimation uses unimodal decompositions and persistence-guided smoothing to estimate one-dimensional mixtures nonparametrically.

title: Topological mixture estimation

abstract: Despite significant recent advances in deep neural networks, training them remains a challenge due to the highly non-convex nature of the objective function. State-of-the-art methods rely on error backpropagation, which suffers from several well-known issues, such as vanishing and exploding gradients, inability to handle non-differentiable nonlinearities and to parallelize weight-updates across layers, and biological implausibility. These limitations continue to motivate exploration of alternative training algorithms, including several recently proposed auxiliary-variable methods which break the complex nested objective function into local subproblems. However, those techniques are mainly offline (batch), which limits their applicability to extremely large datasets, as well as to online, continual or reinforcement learning. The main contribution of our work is a novel online (stochastic/mini-batch) alternating minimization (AM) approach for training deep neural networks, together with the first theoretical convergence guarantees for AM in stochastic settings and promising empirical results on a variety of architectures and datasets.

paragraphs: Training a deep network involves optimizing a highly nonconvex function built from nested layers. Backpropagation is the usual approach, but the paper motivates alternatives through issues including vanishing or exploding gradients, nondifferentiable nonlinearities, and difficulties updating layers in parallel. Auxiliary-variable methods offer another formulation by breaking the nested training objective into local subproblems.

The obstacle addressed here is that existing auxiliary-variable approaches mainly operate in batch settings. That limits their usefulness when datasets are extremely large or learning must proceed through incoming observations. The authors introduce an online alternating minimization approach that can train using stochastic updates or minibatches, bringing this alternative formulation into a more incremental learning setting.

The paper contributes what it describes as the first theoretical convergence guarantees for alternating minimization in stochastic settings. It also reports promising results across multiple architectures and datasets. Together, these contributions give theoretical and empirical support for an online alternative to backpropagation, without establishing that it universally resolves every difficulty motivating the work.
summary.tldr: An online alternating minimization method extends auxiliary-variable neural-network training to stochastic and minibatch settings with convergence guarantees.

title: Beyond Backprop: Online Alternating Minimization with Auxiliary Variables

abstract: It is well-known that the expressivity of a neural network depends on its architecture, with deeper networks expressing more complex functions. In the case of networks that compute piecewise linear functions, such as those with ReLU activation, the number of distinct linear regions is a natural measure of expressivity. It is possible to construct networks with merely a single region, or for which the number of linear regions grows exponentially with depth; it is not clear where within this range most networks fall in practice, either before or after training. In this paper, we provide a mathematical framework to count the number of linear regions of a piecewise linear network and measure the volume of the boundaries between these regions. In particular, we prove that for networks at initialization, the average number of regions along any one-dimensional subspace grows linearly in the total number of neurons, far below the exponential upper bound. We also find that the average distance to the nearest region boundary at initialization scales like the inverse of the number of neurons. Our theory suggests that, even after training, the number of linear regions is far below exponential, an intuition that matches our empirical observations. We conclude that the practical expressivity of neural networks is likely far below that of the theoretical maximum, and that this gap can be quantified.

paragraphs: A network with piecewise linear activations divides its input space into regions, each governed by a linear function. Counting these regions measures one aspect of its expressive capacity. Although specially constructed networks can have exponentially many regions as depth increases, that possibility does not establish how much complexity ordinary networks actually exhibit.

The paper develops a mathematical framework for counting regions and measuring the boundaries between them. At initialization, it proves that the average number of regions encountered along any one-dimensional subspace grows linearly with the total neuron count. It also finds that the average distance to the nearest boundary scales inversely with the number of neurons.

These results distinguish achievable architectural complexity from typical behavior at initialization. For trained networks, the conclusion is more qualified: the theory suggests region counts remain far below exponential, and the authors’ empirical observations agree with that suggestion. The work therefore provides a way to quantify a likely gap between maximum theoretical expressivity and the expressivity realized in practice.
summary.tldr: Typical initialized networks have far fewer linear regions along one-dimensional subspaces than exponential expressivity bounds permit, with evidence suggesting a similar gap after training.

title: Complexity of Linear Regions in Deep Networks

abstract: We provide a new approach to training neural models to exhibit transparency in a well-defined, functional manner. Our approach naturally operates over structured data and tailors the predictor, functionally, towards a chosen family of (local) witnesses. The estimation problem is setup as a co-operative game between an unrestricted predictor such as a neural network, and a set of witnesses chosen from the desired transparent family. The goal of the witnesses is to highlight, locally, how well the predictor conforms to the chosen family of functions, while the predictor is trained to minimize the highlighted discrepancy. We emphasize that the predictor remains globally powerful as it is only encouraged to agree locally with locally adapted witnesses. We analyze the effect of the proposed approach, provide example formulations in the context of deep graph and sequence models, and empirically illustrate the idea in chemical property prediction, temporal modeling, and molecule representation learning.

The goal of the witnesses is to highlight, locally, how well the predictor conforms to the chosen family of functions, while the predictor is trained to minimize the highlighted discrepancy. paragraphs: This paper makes transparency part of neural model training by encouraging the predictor to behave locally like functions from a chosen transparent family. The approach applies naturally to structured data. Its goal is a functional form of transparency: nearby behavior should be describable through the selected family, while the overall predictor can remain expressive.

Training is formulated as a cooperative game between an unrestricted predictor and a collection of local witnesses. Each witness highlights how closely the predictor matches the desired function family in its local region. The predictor is trained to reduce the discrepancies those witnesses identify. Because witnesses adapt locally, different parts of the prediction function can receive different explanations.

The authors analyze the approach and give formulations for deep graph and sequence models. They illustrate it empirically through chemical property prediction, temporal modeling, and molecule representation learning. The central contribution is a mechanism for shaping model behavior toward local transparency during learning, while preserving the capacity for a more complex global function.
summary.tldr: A cooperative training game encourages powerful neural predictors to agree locally with interpretable witness functions.

title: Functional Transparency for Structured Data: a Game-Theoretic Approach

abstract: We devise a distributional variant of gradient temporal-difference (TD) learning. Distributional reinforcement learning has been demonstrated to outperform the regular one in the recent study \citep{bellemare2017distributional}. In the policy evaluation setting, we design two new algorithms called distributional GTD2 and distributional TDC using the Cram{é}r distance on the distributional version of the Bellman error objective function, which inherits advantages of both the nonlinear gradient TD algorithms and the distributional RL approach. In the control setting, we propose the distributional Greedy-GQ using similar derivation. We prove the asymptotic almost-sure convergence of distributional GTD2 and TDC to a local optimal solution for general smooth function approximators, which includes neural networks that have been widely used in recent study to solve the real-life RL problems. In each step, the computational complexity of above three algorithms is linear w.r.t. the number of the parameters of the function approximator, thus can be implemented efficiently for neural networks.

In the control setting, we propose the distributional Greedy-GQ using similar derivation. paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning models a distribution of returns rather than only an expected return. This paper brings that approach into gradient temporal-difference learning, developing algorithms that can use nonlinear function approximators. The objective is to combine distributional modeling with the convergence properties and computational structure of gradient TD methods.

For policy evaluation, the authors introduce distributional GTD2 and distributional TDC. Both use the Cramér distance in a distributional version of the Bellman-error objective, measuring disagreement between return distributions. For control, where the agent also seeks a better decision policy, they derive a related algorithm called distributional Greedy-GQ.

The authors prove asymptotic almost-sure convergence to a local optimal solution for the two policy-evaluation algorithms with general smooth function approximators, including neural networks. The stated guarantee is local and applies to GTD2 and TDC, rather than establishing the same result for all three methods. Each algorithm requires computation per step that grows linearly with the number of approximator parameters, supporting efficient implementation with neural networks.
summary.tldr: The paper develops efficient distributional gradient TD algorithms and proves local convergence for two policy-evaluation methods with smooth nonlinear approximators.

title: Nonlinear Distributional Gradient Temporal-Difference Learning

abstract: We introduce the Metropolis-Hastings generative adversarial network (MH-GAN), which combines aspects of Markov chain Monte Carlo and GANs. The MH-GAN draws samples from the distribution implicitly defined by a GAN’s discriminator-generator pair, as opposed to standard GANs which draw samples from the distribution defined only by the generator. It uses the discriminator from GAN training to build a wrapper around the generator for improved sampling. With a perfect discriminator, this wrapped generator samples from the true distribution on the data exactly even when the generator is imperfect. We demonstrate the benefits of the improved generator on multiple benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10 and CelebA, using the DCGAN, WGAN, and progressive GAN.

It uses the discriminator from GAN training to build a wrapper around the generator for improved sampling. With a perfect discriminator, this wrapped generator samples from the true distribution on the data exactly even when the generator is imperfect. We demonstrate the benefits of the improved generator on multiple benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-10 and CelebA, using the DCGAN, WGAN, and progressive GAN.

paragraphs: A standard generative adversarial network produces samples using its generator, even though training also creates a discriminator. This paper proposes using both components during sampling. The Metropolis-Hastings GAN combines ideas from Markov chain Monte Carlo with GANs to improve the samples obtained from an already trained generator.

The method builds a wrapper around the generator using the discriminator from training. As a result, samples come from a distribution implicitly defined by the pair, rather than only the generator's distribution. The paper gives a strong conditional result: with a perfect discriminator, the wrapped generator samples exactly from the true data distribution even if the generator is imperfect. The perfect discriminator condition is essential to the stated exactness claim.

Experiments demonstrate sampling benefits on multiple benchmarks, including CIFAR-10 and CelebA, using DCGAN, WGAN, and progressive GAN models. These results support the practical value of retaining the discriminator for sample generation. The broader contribution is to make the learned discriminator part of the sampling procedure itself.
summary.tldr: MH-GAN uses a trained discriminator to improve generator sampling, with exact recovery of the data distribution conditional on a perfect discriminator.

title: Metropolis-Hastings Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: We propose a class of variance-reduced stochastic conditional gradient methods. By adopting the recent stochastic path-integrated differential estimator technique (SPIDER) of Fang et. al. (2018) for the classical Frank-Wolfe (FW) method, we introduce SPIDER-FW for finite-sum minimization as well as the more general expectation minimization problems. SPIDER-FW enjoys superior complexity guarantees in the non-convex setting, while matching the best known FW variants in the convex case. We also extend our framework a la conditional gradient sliding (CGS) of Lan & Zhou. (2016), and propose SPIDER-CGS.

By adopting the recent stochastic path-integrated differential estimator technique (SPIDER) of Fang et. al. (2018) for the classical Frank-Wolfe (FW) method, we introduce SPIDER-FW for finite-sum minimization as well as the more general expectation minimization problems. paragraphs: This paper develops stochastic conditional gradient methods that use variance reduction to improve optimization efficiency. Its central construction combines the classical Frank–Wolfe method with SPIDER, a stochastic path-integrated differential estimator. The resulting method, SPIDER-FW, connects the choice of gradient estimator to the complexity guarantees of a conditional gradient algorithm.

The framework covers two objective types: finite sums and more general expectations. A finite-sum objective aggregates a collection of terms, while an expectation objective expresses an average over a distribution. Addressing both settings broadens the scope of the proposed method beyond problems described by a fixed collection of terms. The paper also extends the framework using conditional gradient sliding, producing a second method called SPIDER-CGS.

The main stated findings concern theoretical complexity. In nonconvex optimization, SPIDER-FW has stronger complexity guarantees, while in the convex setting it matches the best known Frank–Wolfe variants. The distinction matters: the contribution claims an improvement for the nonconvex case and competitive guarantees for the convex case.
summary.tldr: SPIDER-based variance reduction strengthens nonconvex conditional gradient complexity guarantees while matching leading Frank–Wolfe variants in the convex setting.

title: Conditional Gradient Methods via Stochastic Path-Integrated Differential Estimator

abstract: The structural design process for buildings is time-consuming and laborious. To automate this process, structural engineers combine optimization methods with simulation tools to find an optimal design with minimal building mass subject to building regulations. However, structural engineers in practice often avoid optimization and compromise on a suboptimal design for the majority of buildings, due to the large size of the design space, the iterative nature of the optimization methods, and the slow simulation tools. In this work, we formulate the building structures as graphs and create an end-to-end pipeline that can learn to propose the optimal cross-sections of columns and beams by training together with a pre-trained differentiable structural simulator. The performance of the proposed structural designs is comparable to the ones optimized by genetic algorithm (GA), with all the constraints satisfied. The optimal structural design with the reduced the building mass can not only lower the material cost, but also decrease the carbon footprint.

paragraphs: Designing a building structure involves choosing components that satisfy regulations while keeping building mass low. Conventional optimization repeatedly evaluates candidate designs with simulation tools, making the process costly when the design space is large and simulations are slow. This paper develops a learned pipeline for proposing the cross-sections of columns and beams.

The authors represent building structures as graphs and train the design system together with a pretrained differentiable structural simulator. Differentiability allows the simulator to participate directly in the learning pipeline. This connects the proposed structural choices with their simulated performance during training, supporting an end-to-end approach to learning how to produce designs.

The reported designs perform comparably to those optimized by a genetic algorithm, while satisfying all constraints in the evaluation. This supports the feasibility of learning design proposals for the structural problem studied. The motivation also extends beyond the optimization process itself: reducing building mass can lower material costs and carbon footprint. The stated comparison establishes competitive design performance, rather than a proof that every generated design is a global optimum.
summary.tldr: A graph-based design pipeline trained with a differentiable simulator proposes building components with performance comparable to genetic-algorithm designs.

title: Learning to Simulate and Design for Structural Engineering

abstract: At the heart of machine learning lies the question of generalizability of learned rules over previously unseen data. While over-parameterized models based on neural networks are now ubiquitous in machine learning applications, our understanding of their generalization capabilities is incomplete and this task is made harder by the non-convexity of the underlying learning problems. We provide a general framework to characterize the asymptotic generalization error for single-layer neural networks (i.e., generalized linear models) with arbitrary non-linearities, making it applicable to regression as well as classification problems. This framework enables analyzing the effect of (i) over-parameterization and non-linearity during modeling; (ii) choices of loss function, initialization, and regularizer during learning; and (iii) mismatch between training and test distributions. As examples, we analyze a few special cases, namely linear regression and logistic regression. We are also able to rigorously and analytically explain the \emph{double descent} phenomenon in generalized linear models.

We provide a general framework to characterize the asymptotic generalization error for single-layer neural networks (i.e., generalized linear models) with arbitrary non-linearities, making it applicable to regression as well as classification problems. We are also able to rigorously and analytically explain the \emph{double descent} phenomenon in generalized linear models.

paragraphs: Understanding performance on unseen data becomes difficult when models have many parameters and learning involves nonconvex optimization. This paper develops a framework for studying that question in generalized linear models, described here as single-layer neural networks. It characterizes asymptotic generalization error and accommodates arbitrary nonlinearities, covering both regression and classification problems.

The framework connects generalization to several choices that are often studied separately. These include the degree of overparameterization, the model's nonlinearity, the loss function, initialization, and regularization. It also permits analysis when training and test distributions differ. This makes it possible to examine how modeling choices, learning choices, and distribution mismatch affect prediction within a common analytical setting.

The authors work through linear and logistic regression as examples. They also give a rigorous analytical explanation of double descent in generalized linear models, addressing how generalization can behave nonmonotonically as model size changes. The scope is an asymptotic theory for these single-layer models; its stated results do not establish a corresponding characterization for arbitrary deep networks.
summary.tldr: An asymptotic framework characterizes generalization in generalized linear models and rigorously explains their double-descent behavior.

title: Generalization Error of Generalized Linear Models in High Dimensions

abstract: In the paper, we propose a class of efficient momentum-based policy gradient methods for the model-free reinforcement learning, which use adaptive learning rates and do not require any large batches. Specifically, we propose a fast important-sampling momentum-based policy gradient (IS-MBPG) method based on a new momentum-based variance reduced technique and the importance sampling technique. We also propose a fast Hessian-aided momentum-based policy gradient (HA-MBPG) method based on the momentum-based variance reduced technique and the Hessian-aided technique. Moreover, we prove that both the IS-MBPG and HA-MBPG methods reach the best known sample complexity of $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary point of the nonconcave performance function, which only require one trajectory at each iteration. In particular, we present a non-adaptive version of IS-MBPG method, i.e., IS-MBPG*, which also reaches the best known sample complexity of $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ without any large batches. In the experiments, we apply four benchmark tasks to demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms.

Specifically, we propose a fast important-sampling momentum-based policy gradient (IS-MBPG) method based on a new momentum-based variance reduced technique and the importance sampling technique. We also propose a fast Hessian-aided momentum-based policy gradient (HA-MBPG) method based on the momentum-based variance reduced technique and the Hessian-aided technique. Moreover, we prove that both the IS-MBPG and HA-MBPG methods reach the best known sample complexity of $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary point of the nonconcave performance function, which only require one trajectory at each iteration. In the experiments, we apply four benchmark tasks to demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper proposes policy-gradient methods for model-free reinforcement learning that combine momentum with variance reduction. The aim is to make learning efficient without requiring large batches of trajectories. The main methods use adaptive learning rates and reuse information through a new momentum-based variance-reduction technique.

Two versions combine that technique with different ingredients. IS-MBPG uses importance sampling, while HA-MBPG uses Hessian information. The authors prove that both reach the stated best-known sample complexity of O(ε⁻³) for finding an ε-stationary point of the nonconcave performance objective, using only one trajectory per iteration. The guarantee targets approximate stationarity, rather than a globally optimal policy.

A further method, IS-MBPG*, removes adaptive learning rates while retaining the same sample-complexity order and avoiding large batches. Experiments on four benchmark tasks demonstrate the algorithms’ effectiveness. Together, the results show that the stated sample-efficiency bound can be achieved with small per-iteration data requirements through several related momentum-based designs, including a non-adaptive variant.
summary.tldr: Momentum-based policy-gradient methods achieve the stated best-known stationarity sample complexity without large trajectory batches.

title: Momentum-Based Policy Gradient Methods

abstract: Finite-horizon sequential experimental design (SED) arises naturally in many contexts, including hyperparameter tuning in machine learning among more traditional settings. Computing the optimal policy for such problems requires solving Bellman equations, which are generally intractable. Most existing work resorts to severely myopic approximations by limiting the decision horizon to only a single time-step, which can underweight exploration in favor of exploitation. We present BINOCULARS: Batch-Informed NOnmyopic Choices, Using Long-horizons for Adaptive, Rapid SED, a general framework for deriving efficient, nonmyopic approximations to the optimal experimental policy. Our key idea is simple and surprisingly effective: we first compute a one-step optimal batch of experiments, then select a single point from this batch to evaluate. We realize BINOCULARS for Bayesian optimization and Bayesian quadrature – two notable example problems with radically different objectives – and demonstrate that BINOCULARS significantly outperforms significantly outperforms myopic alternatives in real-world scenarios.

It first computes a batch of experiments that is optimal for a one-step batch objective, then chooses a single member of that batch to evaluate. This lets information about a collection of experiments influence the next sequential choice without directly solving the full optimal-policy problem.

They report significant improvements over myopic alternatives in real-world scenarios. summary.tldr: BINOCULARS uses an optimized batch of experiments to choose one next experiment with a broader planning perspective.

title: BINOCULARS for efficient, nonmyopic sequential experimental design

abstract: We provide an exact analysis of a class of randomized algorithms for solving overdetermined least-squares problems. We consider first-order methods, where the gradients are pre-conditioned by an approximation of the Hessian, based on a subspace embedding of the data matrix. This class of algorithms encompasses several randomized methods among the fastest solvers for least-squares problems. We focus on two classical embeddings, namely, Gaussian projections and subsampled randomized Hadamard transforms (SRHT). Our key technical innovation is the derivation of the limiting spectral density of SRHT embeddings. Leveraging this novel result, we derive the family of normalized orthogonal polynomials of the SRHT density and we find the optimal pre-conditioned first-order method along with its rate of convergence. Our analysis of Gaussian embeddings proceeds similarly, and leverages classical random matrix theory results. In particular, we show that for a given sketch size, SRHT embeddings exhibits a faster rate of convergence than Gaussian embeddings. Then, we propose a new algorithm by optimizing the computational complexity over the choice of the sketching dimension. To our knowledge, our resulting algorithm yields the best known complexity for solving least-squares problems with no condition number dependence.

title: Optimal Randomized First-Order Methods for Least-Squares Problems

abstract: Self-supervised learning, which learns by constructing artificial labels given only the input signals, has recently gained considerable attention for learning representations with unlabeled datasets, i.e., learning without any human-annotated supervision. In this paper, we show that such a technique can be used to significantly improve the model accuracy even under fully-labeled datasets. Our scheme trains the model to learn both original and self-supervised tasks, but is different from conventional multi-task learning frameworks that optimize the summation of their corresponding losses. Our main idea is to learn a single unified task with respect to the joint distribution of the original and self-supervised labels, i.e., we augment original labels via self-supervision. This simple, yet effective approach allows to train models easier by relaxing a certain invariant constraint during learning the original and self-supervised tasks simultaneously. It also enables an aggregated inference which combines the predictions from different augmentations to improve the prediction accuracy. Furthermore, we propose a novel knowledge transfer technique, which we refer to as self-distillation, that has the effect of the aggregated inference in a single (faster) inference. We demonstrate the large accuracy improvement and wide applicability of our framework on various fully-supervised settings, e.g., the few-shot and imbalanced classification scenarios.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning creates training labels from the inputs themselves. This paper shows how that idea can improve accuracy even when human-provided labels are already available for the full dataset. The method combines the original prediction task with a self-supervised task through an augmented label space.

Instead of adding separate task losses, the model learns one unified task defined over the joint distribution of original and self-supervised labels. The authors explain that this relaxes an invariance constraint that arises when learning the two tasks simultaneously, making training easier. At inference time, predictions from different input augmentations can also be aggregated to improve accuracy.

The paper then introduces self-distillation to transfer the effect of that aggregated inference into a single, faster inference. This addresses the prediction-time cost of combining multiple augmentations. Experiments report large accuracy improvements across fully supervised settings, including few-shot and imbalanced classification. The contribution combines a different way to formulate training labels with techniques for improving predictions and retaining those benefits more efficiently.
summary.tldr: Joint original and self-supervised labels improve supervised learning, while aggregated predictions and self-distillation extend the accuracy benefits to inference.

title: Self-supervised Label Augmentation via Input Transformations

abstract: Although state-of-the-art (SOTA) CNNs achieve outstanding performance on various tasks, their high computation demand and massive number of parameters make it difficult to deploy these SOTA CNNs onto resource-constrained devices. Previous works on CNN acceleration utilize low-rank approximation of the original convolution layers to reduce computation cost. However, these methods are very difficult to conduct upon sparse models, which limits execution speedup since redundancies within the CNN model are not fully exploited. We argue that kernel granularity decomposition can be conducted with low-rank assumption while exploiting the redundancy within the remaining compact coefficients. Based on this observation, we propose PENNI, a CNN model compression framework that is able to achieve model compactness and hardware efficiency simultaneously by (1) implementing kernel sharing in convolution layers via a small number of basis kernels and (2) alternately adjusting bases and coefficients with sparse constraints. Experiments show that we can prune 97% parameters and 92% FLOPs on ResNet18 CIFAR10 with no accuracy loss, and achieve a 44% reduction in run-time memory consumption and a 53% reduction in inference latency.

These findings connect compression to measured execution benefits, demonstrating that the framework can improve both model compactness and hardware efficiency in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: PENNI combines shared basis kernels and sparse coefficients to compress CNNs while reducing measured memory use and inference latency.

title: PENNI: Pruned Kernel Sharing for Efficient CNN Inference

abstract: The problem of finding an ancestral acyclic directed mixed graph (ADMG) that represents the causal relationships between a set of variables is an important area of research on causal inference. Most existing score-based structure learning methods focus on learning directed acyclic graph (DAG) models without latent variables. A number of score-based methods have recently been proposed for the ADMG learning, yet they are heuristic in nature and do not guarantee an optimal solution. We propose a novel exact score-based method that solves an integer programming (IP) formulation and returns a score-maximizing ancestral ADMG for a set of continuous variables that follow a multivariate Gaussian distribution. We generalize the state-of-the-art IP model for DAG learning problems and derive new classes of valid inequalities to formulate an IP model for ADMG learning. Empirically, our model can be solved efficiently for medium-sized problems and achieves better accuracy than state-of-the-art score-based methods as well as benchmark constraint-based methods.

paragraphs: Learning a causal graph becomes more complicated when some relevant variables are unobserved. This paper focuses on ancestral acyclic directed mixed graphs, a model class used to represent causal relationships in that setting. Existing score-based approaches for these graphs are described as heuristic, leaving open whether the best-scoring graph has actually been found.

The authors formulate structure learning as an integer programming problem that returns a score-maximizing ancestral graph. Their method applies to continuous variables following a multivariate Gaussian distribution. It extends an integer programming formulation for directed acyclic graphs and introduces new valid inequalities to express the additional requirements of mixed-graph learning.

Experiments show that the formulation can be solved efficiently for medium-sized problems and achieves better accuracy than the compared score-based and constraint-based methods. The exactness claim concerns maximizing the chosen score within the specified graph class and distributional setting. This provides an optimization guarantee alongside empirical accuracy results, rather than treating a heuristic search result as necessarily optimal.
summary.tldr: An integer programming formulation exactly maximizes a causal-graph score for Gaussian continuous variables with latent-variable structure.

title: Integer Programming for Causal Structure Learning in the Presence of Latent Variables

abstract: Methods that sparsify a network at initialization are important in practice because they greatly improve the efficiency of both learning and inference. Our work is based on a recently proposed decomposition of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) that has decoupled the dynamics of the training process into a data-dependent component and an architecture-dependent kernel {–} the latter referred to as Path Kernel. That work has shown how to design sparse neural networks for faster convergence, without any training data, using the Synflow-L2 algorithm. We first show that even though Synflow-L2 is optimal in terms of convergence, for a given network density, it results in sub-networks with “bottleneck” (narrow) layers {–} leading to poor performance as compared to other data-agnostic methods that use the same number of parameters. Then we propose a new method to construct sparse networks, without any training data, referred to as Paths with Higher-Edge Weights (PHEW). PHEW is a probabilistic network formation method based on biased random walks that only depends on the initial weights. It has similar path kernel properties as Synflow-L2 but it generates much wider layers, resulting in better generalization and performance. PHEW achieves significant improvements over the data-independent SynFlow and SynFlow-L2 methods at a wide range of network densities.

paragraphs: Choosing a sparse network before training can improve the efficiency of learning and inference. This paper builds on a decomposition of the Neural Tangent Kernel that separates a data-dependent component from an architecture-dependent Path Kernel. That framework had motivated Synflow-L2, a method for constructing networks with favorable convergence properties without training data.

The authors identify a tradeoff: although Synflow-L2 is optimal in terms of convergence at a given density, it creates narrow bottleneck layers. These subnetworks perform poorly compared with other data-independent methods using the same number of parameters. Favorable convergence properties alone therefore do not settle how a sparse network should distribute its connections.

It retains similar Path Kernel properties while producing wider layers, resulting in better generalization and performance. The reported evaluations show significant gains over SynFlow and SynFlow-L2 across a wide range of network densities. The contribution combines a data-free construction procedure with attention to layer width as well as convergence.
summary.tldr: PHEW uses initial-weight-based random walks to construct sparse networks with wider layers and improved generalization without training data.

title: PHEW : Constructing Sparse Networks that Learn Fast and Generalize Well without Training Data

abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a successful approach for deep neural network acceleration, with which a compact network (student) is trained by mimicking the softmax output of a pre-trained high-capacity network (teacher). In tradition, KD usually relies on access to the training samples and the parameters of the white-box teacher to acquire the transferred knowledge. However, these prerequisites are not always realistic due to storage costs or privacy issues in real-world applications. Here we propose the concept of decision-based black-box (DB3) knowledge distillation, with which the student is trained by distilling the knowledge from a black-box teacher (parameters are not accessible) that only returns classes rather than softmax outputs. We start with the scenario when the training set is accessible. We represent a sample’s robustness against other classes by computing its distances to the teacher’s decision boundaries and use it to construct the soft label for each training sample. After that, the student can be trained via standard KD. We then extend this approach to a more challenging scenario in which even accessing the training data is not feasible. We propose to generate pseudo samples that are distinguished by the decision boundaries of the DB3 teacher to the largest extent and construct soft labels for these samples, which are used as the transfer set. We evaluate our approaches on various benchmark networks and datasets and experiment results demonstrate their effectiveness.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a compact student to imitate a larger teacher, commonly using the teacher's softmax outputs. This paper studies a more restricted setting: the teacher's parameters are inaccessible, and it returns only predicted classes. The challenge is to recover useful training guidance from those decisions without access to the teacher's probability outputs.

When training examples are available, the method computes their distances to the teacher's decision boundaries. Those distances represent how robust an example is against assignment to other classes and are used to construct soft labels. The student can then be trained with standard distillation using these reconstructed targets.

The authors also handle the case where the original training data are unavailable. They generate pseudo examples designed to be distinguished as much as possible by the teacher's decision boundaries, then construct soft labels to form a transfer set. Evaluations across benchmark networks and datasets demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution is a boundary-based route to distillation under both restricted teacher access and, in the extended setting, missing training data.
summary.tldr: The method distills class-only black-box teachers by constructing soft labels from decision boundaries, including when original training data are unavailable.

title: Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation from a Decision-Based Black-Box Model

abstract: Contrastive learning is a popular form of self-supervised learning that encourages augmentations (views) of the same input to have more similar representations compared to augmentations of different inputs. Recent attempts to theoretically explain the success of contrastive learning on downstream classification tasks prove guarantees depending on properties of augmentations and the value of contrastive loss of representations. We demonstrate that such analyses, that ignore inductive biases of the function class and training algorithm, cannot adequately explain the success of contrastive learning, even provably leading to vacuous guarantees in some settings. Extensive experiments on image and text domains highlight the ubiquity of this problem – different function classes and algorithms behave very differently on downstream tasks, despite having the same augmentations and contrastive losses. Theoretical analysis is presented for the class of linear representations, where incorporating inductive biases of the function class allows contrastive learning to work with less stringent conditions compared to prior analyses.

Recent attempts to theoretically explain the success of contrastive learning on downstream classification tasks prove guarantees depending on properties of augmentations and the value of contrastive loss of representations. We demonstrate that such analyses, that ignore inductive biases of the function class and training algorithm, cannot adequately explain the success of contrastive learning, even provably leading to vacuous guarantees in some settings. Extensive experiments on image and text domains highlight the ubiquity of this problem – different function classes and algorithms behave very differently on downstream tasks, despite having the same augmentations and contrastive losses. Theoretical analysis is presented for the class of linear representations, where incorporating inductive biases of the function class allows contrastive learning to work with less stringent conditions compared to prior analyses.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning encourages different views of the same input to have similar representations, relative to views of different inputs. Some theoretical explanations connect downstream classification performance to the augmentations used and the achieved contrastive loss. This paper argues that those quantities alone cannot adequately explain success because the function class and training algorithm also shape what is learned.

The authors show that analyses ignoring these inductive biases can produce vacuous guarantees in some settings. Experiments on images and text reinforce the issue: different function classes and algorithms can have the same augmentations and contrastive losses yet behave very differently on downstream tasks. Matching the training objective’s value therefore need not imply matching the usefulness of the resulting representation.

For linear representations, the paper provides a theoretical analysis that explicitly incorporates the function class’s inductive biases. Doing so allows guarantees under less stringent conditions than earlier analyses. The combined theoretical and experimental findings identify architectural and algorithmic preferences as essential ingredients in a fuller explanation of contrastive learning, beyond the augmentation scheme and loss value.
summary.tldr: Contrastive loss and augmentations alone can miss downstream behavior; incorporating inductive biases yields a more informative theory.

title: Understanding Contrastive Learning Requires Incorporating Inductive Biases

abstract: The Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) optimization algorithm has been shown to control large eigenvalues of the loss Hessian and provide generalization benefits in a variety of settings. The original motivation for SAM was a modified loss function which penalized sharp minima; subsequent analyses have also focused on the behavior near minima. However, our work reveals that SAM provides a strong regularization of the eigenvalues throughout the learning trajectory. We show that in a simplified setting, SAM dynamically induces a stabilization related to the edge of stability (EOS) phenomenon observed in large learning rate gradient descent. Our theory predicts the largest eigenvalue as a function of the learning rate and SAM radius parameters. Finally, we show that practical models can also exhibit this EOS stabilization, and that understanding SAM must account for these dynamics far away from any minima.

However, our work reveals that SAM provides a strong regularization of the eigenvalues throughout the learning trajectory. paragraphs: Sharpness Aware Minimization, or SAM, was motivated by penalizing sharp minima, and much of its analysis has focused on behavior near those minima. This paper argues that an important part of SAM's operation occurs throughout training. It finds strong regulation of Hessian eigenvalues, quantities that describe curvature of the loss, along the learning trajectory.

In a simplified setting, the authors show that SAM dynamically induces a stabilization related to the edge-of-stability phenomenon seen in gradient descent with large learning rates. Their theory predicts the largest eigenvalue as a function of the learning rate and SAM radius. This connects curvature control to the optimizer's evolving dynamics and its parameters.

The authors also show that practical models can exhibit this stabilization. The result changes how SAM's behavior should be interpreted: analyzing only the geometry of a final minimum misses effects that occur far from any minimum. The simplified theory and practical observations support a dynamical account of eigenvalue regularization, while the practical finding is that this behavior can occur, rather than that every model must display it.
summary.tldr: SAM controls loss curvature throughout training through dynamics linked to edge-of-stability behavior, not just through behavior near minima.

title: SAM operates far from home: eigenvalue regularization as a dynamical phenomenon

abstract: We consider the stochastic linear contextual bandit problem with high-dimensional features. We analyze the Thompson sampling algorithm using special classes of sparsity-inducing priors (e.g., spike-and-slab) to model the unknown parameter and provide a nearly optimal upper bound on the expected cumulative regret. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that provides theoretical guarantees of Thompson sampling in high-dimensional and sparse contextual bandits. For faster computation, we use variational inference instead of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to approximate the posterior distribution. Extensive simulations demonstrate the improved performance of our proposed algorithm over existing ones.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that provides theoretical guarantees of Thompson sampling in high-dimensional and sparse contextual bandits. paragraphs: This paper studies contextual bandits with many features but a sparse underlying reward parameter. In that setting, only a limited subset of features contributes through the unknown linear parameter. The authors analyze Thompson sampling with priors designed to favor sparsity, including spike-and-slab priors, so the statistical model reflects that structure.

The main theoretical result is a nearly optimal upper bound on expected cumulative regret, which measures the reward lost while learning compared with optimal decisions. The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first theoretical guarantee for Thompson sampling in high-dimensional sparse contextual bandits. The result ties the algorithm's performance to a setting where the ambient feature dimension is large but the parameter is sparse.

For computation, the proposed implementation approximates the posterior through variational inference instead of Markov chain Monte Carlo. This choice is intended to make posterior approximation faster. Extensive simulations report improved performance over existing algorithms. The contribution combines a theoretical analysis of sparse Thompson sampling with a computational approach evaluated empirically.
summary.tldr: Sparsity-inducing priors give Thompson sampling nearly optimal regret guarantees for high-dimensional sparse contextual bandits.

title: Thompson Sampling for High-Dimensional Sparse Linear Contextual Bandits

abstract: We analyze Newton’s method with lazy Hessian updates for solving general possibly non-convex optimization problems. We propose to reuse a previously seen Hessian for several iterations while computing new gradients at each step of the method. This significantly reduces the overall arithmetic complexity of second-order optimization schemes. By using the cubic regularization technique, we establish fast global convergence of our method to a second-order stationary point, while the Hessian does not need to be updated each iteration. For convex problems, we justify global and local superlinear rates for lazy Newton steps with quadratic regularization, which is easier to compute. The optimal frequency for updating the Hessian is once every $d$ iterations, where $d$ is the dimension of the problem. This provably improves the total arithmetic complexity of second-order algorithms by a factor $\sqrt{d}$.

This paper asks how often that second-order information must be refreshed. Its method reuses a previously computed Hessian across several iterations while computing a new gradient at every step, reducing the arithmetic work associated with second-order optimization.

For convex problems, the authors justify global convergence and local superlinear rates using quadratic regularization, which is easier to compute.

The analysis identifies updating the Hessian once every d iterations as the optimal frequency, where d is the problem dimension. This yields a provable square-root-of-d improvement in total arithmetic complexity. The result shows that carefully controlled reuse of curvature information can preserve strong convergence properties while reducing the overall computational cost of the method.
summary.tldr: Reusing Hessians for multiple Newton steps preserves stated convergence guarantees and improves arithmetic complexity by a square-root-of-dimension factor.

title: Second-Order Optimization with Lazy Hessians

abstract: In private federated learning (FL), a server aggregates differentially private updates from a large number of clients in order to train a machine learning model. The main challenge in this setting is balancing privacy with both classification accuracy of the learnt model as well as the number of bits communicated between the clients and server. Prior work has achieved a good trade-off by designing a privacy-aware compression mechanism, called the minimum variance unbiased (MVU) mechanism, that numerically solves an optimization problem to determine the parameters of the mechanism. This paper builds upon it by introducing a new interpolation procedure in the numerical design process that allows for a far more efficient privacy analysis. The result is the new Interpolated MVU mechanism that is more scalable, has a better privacy-utility trade-off, and provides SOTA results on communication-efficient private FL on a variety of datasets.

paragraphs: Private federated learning combines updates from many clients while protecting those updates through differential privacy. Designing the communication mechanism requires balancing three objectives: privacy, predictive accuracy, and the number of transmitted bits. A mechanism that handles privacy and compression together can address these competing demands within a single design.

This paper builds on the minimum variance unbiased, or MVU, mechanism, whose parameters are found by numerically solving an optimization problem. The new method introduces interpolation into that numerical design process. Its central benefit is a much more efficient privacy analysis, addressing a computational obstacle in designing the mechanism.

The resulting Interpolated MVU mechanism is reported to scale better and offer an improved privacy-utility trade-off. Across a variety of datasets, it achieves state-of-the-art results for communication-efficient private federated learning. The contribution shows how changing the numerical design procedure can improve both the practicality of privacy analysis and the quality of the resulting training mechanism, while keeping communication cost part of the optimization problem.
summary.tldr: Interpolated MVU makes privacy-aware compression more scalable and improves the reported privacy-utility trade-off in federated learning.

title: Privacy-Aware Compression for Federated Learning Through Numerical Mechanism Design

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks are effective at predicting links, but their dependence on neighborhood information can make inference slow. Multilayer perceptrons are efficient, yet typically lack the relational knowledge that gives graph models their advantage. This paper investigates how to transfer that knowledge into a faster student model.

The authors first examine direct distillation through matching predicted link logits or node representations and find that these approaches perform poorly for link prediction. Their proposed LLP framework instead transfers relational knowledge organized around each anchor node. It combines rank-based and distribution-based matching, which provide complementary ways to teach the student how relationships are structured.

Experiments show substantial improvements in the student perceptrons' link-prediction performance. LLP even exceeds its teacher graph neural networks on seven of eight benchmarks and reports a 70.68-fold inference speedup over graph neural networks on the large-scale OGB dataset. These results support distilling relationships around nodes as a way to retain predictive effectiveness while gaining the inference efficiency of the student architecture.
summary.tldr: LLP transfers relational knowledge from graph networks into fast perceptrons, improving link prediction and reporting a substantial inference speedup.

title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation

abstract: Given a pre-trained in-distribution (ID) model, the inference-time out-of-distribution (OOD) detection aims to recognize OOD data during the inference stage. However, some representative methods share an unproven assumption that the probability that OOD data belong to every ID class should be the same, i.e., these OOD-to-ID probabilities actually form a uniform distribution. In this paper, we show that this assumption makes the above methods incapable when the ID model is trained with class-imbalanced data.Fortunately, by analyzing the causal relations between ID/OOD classes and features, we identify several common scenarios where the OOD-to-ID probabilities should be the ID-class-prior distribution and propose two strategies to modify existing inference-time detection methods: 1) replace the uniform distribution with the ID-class-prior distribution if they explicitly use the uniform distribution; 2) otherwise, reweight their scores according to the similarity between the ID-class-prior distribution and the softmax outputs of the pre-trained model. Extensive experiments show that both strategies can improve the OOD detection performance when the ID model is pre-trained with imbalanced data, reflecting the importance of ID-class prior in OOD detection.
