paragraphs: An out-of-distribution detector tries to recognize inputs outside the classes represented in a pretrained model’s training data. Some inference-time methods assume that such inputs should receive equal probabilities across all known classes. The paper shows that this assumption causes those methods to fail when the model was trained on unequal numbers of examples per class.

By analyzing causal relationships between classes and features, the authors identify several common scenarios in which unfamiliar inputs should instead follow the known classes’ prior distribution. That distribution reflects their relative prevalence. They propose replacing an explicitly used uniform distribution with this class prior, or reweighting detection scores using similarity between the prior and the model’s softmax output.

Experiments show that both modifications can improve detection when the pretrained model learned from imbalanced data. The finding gives class prevalence a concrete role in interpreting a model’s response to unfamiliar inputs. Its scope is qualified: the causal analysis identifies scenarios supporting the prior-based distribution, rather than asserting that every out-of-distribution input must follow it.
summary.tldr: Accounting for training-class prevalence can improve inference-time detection of unfamiliar inputs when the pretrained model learned from imbalanced data.

title: Detecting Out-of-distribution Data through In-distribution Class Prior

abstract: Causal structure learning can reveal the causal mechanism behind natural systems. It is well studied that the multiple domain data consisting of observational and interventional samples benefit causal identifiability. However, for non-stationary time series data, domain indexes are often unavailable, making it difficult to distinguish observational samples from interventional samples. To address these issues, we propose a novel Latent Intervened Non-stationary learning (LIN) method to make the domain indexes recovery process and the causal structure learning process mutually promote each other. We characterize and justify a possible faithfulness condition to guarantee the identifiability of the proposed LIN method. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms the baselines on causal structure learning for latent intervened non-stationary data.

To address these issues, we propose a novel Latent Intervened Non-stationary learning (LIN) method to make the domain indexes recovery process and the causal structure learning process mutually promote each other. paragraphs: Learning causal structure can benefit from data collected under different conditions, including both ordinary observations and interventions. In changing time series, however, the labels identifying those conditions may be missing. Without them, a method has difficulty distinguishing changes caused by interventions from observations generated under other conditions.

The proposed Latent Intervened Non-stationary learning method, LIN, couples recovery of these hidden domain labels with causal structure learning. Rather than treating the recovered labels as a completely separate input, the approach lets the two learning processes support each other. Information about the causal structure helps recover domains, while the recovered domains help reveal causal structure.

The authors formulate and justify a possible faithfulness condition under which LIN is identifiable. The guarantee therefore depends on that condition; it does not establish unrestricted causal recovery from any changing time series. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show better causal structure learning than the tested baselines in the latent-intervention setting.
summary.tldr: LIN jointly recovers hidden domain labels and causal structure from changing time series, with identifiability guaranteed under a stated faithfulness condition.

title: Causal Structure Learning for Latent Intervened Non-stationary Data

abstract: Exploration remains a key challenge in deep reinforcement learning (RL). Optimism in the face of uncertainty is a well-known heuristic with theoretical guarantees in the tabular setting, but how best to translate the principle to deep reinforcement learning, which involves online stochastic gradients and deep network function approximators, is not fully understood. In this paper we propose a new, differentiable optimistic objective that when optimized yields a policy that provably explores efficiently, with guarantees even under function approximation. Our new objective is a zero-sum two-player game derived from endowing the agent with an epistemic-risk-seeking utility function, which converts uncertainty into value and encourages the agent to explore uncertain states. We show that the solution to this game minimizes an upper bound on the regret, with the ’players’ each attempting to minimize one component of a particular regret decomposition. We derive a new model-free algorithm which we call ’epistemic-risk-seeking actor-critic’ (ERSAC), which is simply an application of simultaneous stochastic gradient ascent-descent to the game. Finally, we discuss a recipe for incorporating off-policy data and show that combining the risk-seeking objective with replay data yields a double benefit in terms of statistical efficiency. We conclude with some results showing good performance of a deep RL agent using the technique on the challenging ’DeepSea’ environment, showing significant performance improvements even over other efficient exploration techniques, as well as improved performance on the Atari benchmark.

paragraphs: An agent can explore by treating uncertainty as a reason to investigate potentially valuable states. Translating this optimistic principle into deep reinforcement learning is difficult because policies are learned with neural approximators and stochastic updates. This paper introduces a differentiable objective designed to make optimism directly compatible with that learning process.

The objective takes the form of a two-player zero-sum game derived from an epistemic-risk-seeking utility. It assigns value to uncertainty about the environment, encouraging exploration. The authors show that solving the game minimizes an upper bound on regret, with the two players addressing different terms in its decomposition. They also establish efficient-exploration guarantees that accommodate function approximation.

Their model-free algorithm, ERSAC, applies simultaneous stochastic gradient ascent and descent to this game. The paper additionally describes incorporating off-policy replay data and reports a combined statistical-efficiency benefit from replay and the risk-seeking objective. Experiments show substantial improvements on DeepSea, including over other efficient exploration techniques, and improved Atari performance. These results connect an exploration objective grounded in theory with a practical actor-critic learning procedure.
summary.tldr: ERSAC turns uncertainty-seeking exploration into a differentiable game with theoretical guarantees and reported gains on DeepSea and Atari.

title: Efficient Exploration via Epistemic-Risk-Seeking Policy Optimization

abstract: In this work, we focus on safe policy improvement in multi-agent domains where current state-of-the-art methods cannot be effectively applied because of large state and action spaces. We consider recent results using Monte Carlo Tree Search for Safe Policy Improvement with Baseline Bootstrapping and propose a novel algorithm that scales this approach to multi-agent domains, exploiting the factorization of the transition model and value function. Given a centralized behavior policy and a dataset of trajectories, our algorithm generates an improved policy by selecting joint actions using a novel extension of Max-Plus (or Variable Elimination) that constrains local actions to guarantee safety criteria. An empirical evaluation on multi-agent SysAdmin and multi-UAV Delivery shows that the approach scales to very large domains where state-of-the-art methods cannot work.

Given a centralized behavior policy and a dataset of trajectories, our algorithm generates an improved policy by selecting joint actions using a novel extension of Max-Plus (or Variable Elimination) that constrains local actions to guarantee safety criteria. paragraphs: Safe policy improvement becomes difficult in multi-agent systems because the combined state and action spaces can be too large for existing methods. This paper develops an algorithm for that setting, starting from a centralized behavior policy and a dataset of trajectories. Its goal is to improve the policy while satisfying safety criteria.

The method extends work combining Monte Carlo Tree Search with Safe Policy Improvement through Baseline Bootstrapping. To scale to multiple agents, it exploits factorization in the transition model and value function. A new extension of Max-Plus, or Variable Elimination, selects joint actions while constraining local actions so that the safety criteria hold.

This connects the computational structure of the multi-agent problem with the constraints needed for policy improvement. Empirical evaluation on multi-agent SysAdmin and multi-UAV Delivery shows that the approach reaches very large domains where the compared state-of-the-art methods cannot operate. The result supports using factored structure to make safety-constrained policy improvement computationally feasible in the evaluated multi-agent settings.
summary.tldr: A factored multi-agent planning algorithm constrains local actions to support safe policy improvement in domains too large for existing methods.

title: Scalable Safe Policy Improvement for Factored Multi-Agent MDPs

abstract: In recent years, interest in gradient-based optimization over Riemannian manifolds has surged. However, a significant challenge lies in the reliance on hyperparameters, especially the learning rate, which requires meticulous tuning by practitioners to ensure convergence at a suitable rate. In this work, we introduce innovative learning-rate-free algorithms for stochastic optimization over Riemannian manifolds, eliminating the need for hand-tuning and providing a more robust and user-friendly approach. We establish high probability convergence guarantees that are optimal, up to logarithmic factors, compared to the best-known optimally tuned rate in the deterministic setting. Our approach is validated through numerical experiments, demonstrating competitive performance against learning-rate-dependent algorithms.

In this work, we introduce innovative learning-rate-free algorithms for stochastic optimization over Riemannian manifolds, eliminating the need for hand-tuning and providing a more robust and user-friendly approach. We establish high probability convergence guarantees that are optimal, up to logarithmic factors, compared to the best-known optimally tuned rate in the deterministic setting. Our approach is validated through numerical experiments, demonstrating competitive performance against learning-rate-dependent algorithms.

paragraphs: Optimization over Riemannian manifolds uses gradient methods in spaces with geometric structure. As in more familiar optimization settings, the learning rate strongly affects how quickly an algorithm converges. Choosing it can require careful manual tuning. This paper develops stochastic optimization algorithms for these spaces that remove the need to hand-tune the learning rate.

The theoretical contribution is a set of high-probability convergence guarantees. The authors compare these guarantees with the best-known optimally tuned rate in the deterministic setting and show optimality up to logarithmic factors. This comparison gives a precise sense in which removing manual learning-rate selection can coexist with a strong convergence guarantee, rather than relying solely on practical convenience.

Numerical experiments show competitive performance against algorithms that depend on a learning rate. The findings combine a reduction in tuning burden with theoretical support and empirical validation. The stated empirical outcome is competitive performance, while the theoretical comparison is specifically to the optimally tuned deterministic rate and allows logarithmic differences.
summary.tldr: Learning-rate-free algorithms for Riemannian stochastic optimization provide high-probability convergence guarantees and competitive empirical performance without manual learning-rate tuning.

title: Learning-Rate-Free Stochastic Optimization over Riemannian Manifolds

abstract: Causal inference on networks faces challenges posed in part by violations of standard identification assumptions due to dependencies between treatment units. Although graph geometry fundamentally influences such dependencies, the potential of geometric tools for causal inference on networked treatment units is yet to be unlocked. Moreover, despite significant progress utilizing graph neural networks (GNNs) for causal inference on networks, methods for evaluating their achievable reliability without ground truth are lacking. In this work we establish for the first time a theoretical link between network geometry, the graph Ricci curvature in particular, and causal inference, formalizing the intrinsic challenges that negative curvature poses to estimating causal parameters. The Ricci curvature can then be used to assess the reliability of causal estimates in structured data, as we empirically demonstrate. Informed by this finding, we propose a method using the geometric Ricci flow to reduce causal effect estimation error in networked data, showcasing how this newfound connection between graph geometry and causal inference could improve GNN-based causal inference. Bridging graph geometry and causal inference, this paper opens the door to geometric techniques for improving causal estimation on networks.

paragraphs: Causal inference becomes harder when treatment units are connected in a network. Dependencies between units can violate assumptions used to identify causal effects. Although network structure shapes these dependencies, the paper argues that its geometry has been underused, particularly when assessing the reliability of graph neural network estimates without known ground-truth effects.

The authors establish a theoretical connection between causal inference and graph Ricci curvature, a geometric property of the network. Their analysis formalizes difficulties that negative curvature creates for estimating causal parameters. They then demonstrate empirically that curvature can help assess the reliability of causal estimates in structured data.

The connection also motivates an intervention in the estimation method: the authors use geometric Ricci flow to reduce causal effect estimation error on networked data. Their results indicate how geometry could improve GNN-based causal inference. The broader contribution is to make network geometry useful both for understanding estimation difficulty and for designing methods that address it, without treating connectivity as merely an input feature.
summary.tldr: The paper links graph Ricci curvature to causal-estimation difficulty and uses that connection to assess reliability and improve network-based estimates.

title: From Geometry to Causality- Ricci Curvature and the Reliability of Causal Inference on Networks

abstract: We introduce an optimization-based reconstruction attack capable of completely or near-completely reconstructing a dataset utilized for training a random forest. Notably, our approach relies solely on information readily available in commonly used libraries such as scikit-learn. To achieve this, we formulate the reconstruction problem as a combinatorial problem under a maximum likelihood objective. We demonstrate that this problem is NP-hard, though solvable at scale using constraint programming - an approach rooted in constraint propagation and solution-domain reduction. Through an extensive computational investigation, we demonstrate that random forests trained without bootstrap aggregation but with feature randomization are susceptible to a complete reconstruction. This holds true even with a small number of trees. Even with bootstrap aggregation, the majority of the data can also be reconstructed. These findings underscore a critical vulnerability inherent in widely adopted ensemble methods, warranting attention and mitigation. Although the potential for such reconstruction attacks has been discussed in privacy research, our study provides clear empirical evidence of their practicability.

paragraphs: This paper demonstrates that information exposed by a trained random forest can be enough to reconstruct its training data completely or almost completely. The attack uses information readily available in common libraries such as scikit-learn. Its significance is practical: the reconstruction does not depend on an unusual model representation unavailable in ordinary software.

The authors formulate reconstruction as a combinatorial optimization problem with a maximum-likelihood objective. They prove that the problem is NP-hard, but show that constraint programming can solve it at scale in their investigation. Constraint propagation and reductions in possible solution values make the attack computationally workable despite that worst-case complexity.

The reported outcomes depend on how the forest was trained. Forests using feature randomization without bootstrap aggregation were susceptible to complete reconstruction, even with few trees. With bootstrap aggregation, most of the data could still be recovered. These empirical findings turn a previously discussed privacy possibility into a demonstrated attack and show that bootstrap aggregation did not prevent substantial leakage in the studied cases.
summary.tldr: An optimization-based attack reconstructs all or most training data from random forests in the studied settings using routinely available model information.

title: Trained Random Forests Completely Reveal your Dataset

abstract: Neural collapse provides an elegant mathematical characterization of learned last layer representations (a.k.a. features) and classifier weights in deep classification models. Such results not only provide insights but also motivate new techniques for improving practical deep models. However, most of the existing empirical and theoretical studies in neural collapse focus on the case that the number of classes is small relative to the dimension of the feature space. This paper extends neural collapse to cases where the number of classes are much larger than the dimension of feature space, which broadly occur for language models, retrieval systems, and face recognition applications. We show that the features and classifier exhibit a generalized neural collapse phenomenon, where the minimum one-vs-rest margins is maximized. We provide empirical study to verify the occurrence of generalized neural collapse in practical deep neural networks. Moreover, we provide theoretical study to show that the generalized neural collapse provably occurs under unconstrained feature model with spherical constraint, under certain technical conditions on feature dimension and number of classes.

paragraphs: Neural collapse describes geometric structure in the final features and classifier weights learned by deep classification models. Much existing work considers settings with relatively few classes compared with the number of feature dimensions. This paper investigates the opposite regime, where many classes must be represented in a lower-dimensional feature space.

The authors characterize a generalized collapse phenomenon in which the smallest one-versus-rest margin is maximized. In plain terms, the geometry emphasizes the weakest separation between a class and its alternatives. This extends the study of learned feature structure to settings relevant to language models, retrieval systems, and face recognition.

The paper provides empirical evidence that this generalized structure appears in practical neural networks. It also proves occurrence within an unconstrained feature model subject to a spherical constraint and technical conditions relating feature dimension to class count. The empirical observations and conditional theoretical result serve different roles: one establishes practical occurrence in the studied networks, while the other explains it within a specified mathematical setting.
summary.tldr: The paper extends neural collapse to many-class settings, finding margin-maximizing geometry empirically and proving it under specified model conditions.

title: Generalized Neural Collapse for a Large Number of Classes

abstract: Recent works show that reducing the number of layers in a convolutional neural network can enhance efficiency while maintaining the performance of the network. Existing depth compression methods remove redundant non-linear activation functions and merge the consecutive convolution layers into a single layer. However, these methods suffer from a critical drawback; the kernel size of the merged layers becomes larger, significantly undermining the latency reduction gained from reducing the depth of the network. We show that this problem can be addressed by jointly pruning convolution layers and activation functions. To this end, we propose LayerMerge, a novel depth compression method that selects which activation layers and convolution layers to remove, to achieve a desired inference speed-up while minimizing performance loss. Since the corresponding selection problem involves an exponential search space, we formulate a novel surrogate optimization problem and efficiently solve it via dynamic programming. Empirical results demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing depth compression and layer pruning methods on various network architectures, both on image classification and generation tasks. We release the code at https://github.com/snu-mllab/LayerMerge.

paragraphs: Reducing a convolutional network’s depth can improve inference speed while preserving predictive performance. A common strategy removes activation functions so that consecutive convolution layers can be merged. However, merging enlarges convolution kernels, which can consume much of the latency benefit obtained from having fewer layers.

LayerMerge addresses this tradeoff by choosing convolution layers and activation layers for removal together. Its objective is to reach a desired inference speedup while minimizing performance loss. Coordinating these choices allows the method to account for the cost of the resulting merged layers, rather than treating depth reduction alone as the goal.

The possible removal combinations form an exponentially large search space. The authors therefore construct a surrogate optimization problem and solve it efficiently with dynamic programming. Across the tested architectures, LayerMerge consistently outperforms existing depth-compression and layer-pruning approaches on image classification and generation tasks. The results support making pruning and merging decisions jointly when the practical objective is faster inference with limited loss of model performance.
summary.tldr: LayerMerge jointly prunes convolution and activation layers to reduce network depth without losing speed gains to oversized merged kernels.

title: LayerMerge: Neural Network Depth Compression through Layer Pruning and Merging

abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) are pivotal methodologies in reward learning, which involve inferring and shaping the underlying reward function of sequential decision-making problems based on observed human demonstrations and feedback. Most prior work in reward learning has relied on prior knowledge or assumptions about decision or preference models, potentially leading to robustness issues. In response, this paper introduces a novel linear programming (LP) framework tailored for offline reward learning. Utilizing pre-collected trajectories without online exploration, this framework estimates a feasible reward set from the primal-dual optimality conditions of a suitably designed LP, and offers an optimality guarantee with provable sample efficiency. Our LP framework also enables aligning the reward functions with human feedback, such as pairwise trajectory comparison data, while maintaining computational tractability and sample efficiency. We demonstrate that our framework potentially achieves better performance compared to the conventional maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) approach through analytical examples and numerical experiments.

title: A Unified Linear Programming Framework for Offline Reward Learning from Human Demonstrations and Feedback

abstract: Information theoretic quantities play a central role in machine learning. The recent surge in the complexity of data and models has increased the demand for accurate estimation of these quantities. However, as the dimension grows the estimation presents significant challenges, with existing methods struggling already in relatively low dimensions. To address this issue, in this work, we introduce REMEDI for efficient and accurate estimation of differential entropy, a fundamental information theoretic quantity. The approach combines the minimization of the cross-entropy for simple, adaptive base models and the estimation of their deviation, in terms of the relative entropy, from the data density. Our approach demonstrates improvement across a broad spectrum of estimation tasks, encompassing entropy estimation on both synthetic and natural data. Further, we extend important theoretical consistency results to a more generalized setting required by our approach. We illustrate how the framework can be naturally extended to information theoretic supervised learning models, with a specific focus on the Information Bottleneck approach. It is demonstrated that the method delivers better accuracy compared to the existing methods in Information Bottleneck. In addition, we explore a natural connection between REMEDI and generative modeling using rejection sampling and Langevin dynamics.

summary.tldr: REMEDI improves entropy estimation by fitting a simple base model and estimating a correction for its mismatch with the data distribution.

title: REMEDI: Corrective Transformations for Improved Neural Entropy Estimation

abstract: The temperature parameter plays a profound role during training and/or inference with large foundation models (LFMs) such as large language models (LLMs) and CLIP models. Particularly, it adjusts the logits in the softmax function in LLMs, which is crucial for next token generation, and it scales the similarities in the contrastive loss for training CLIP models. A significant question remains: “ Is it viable to learn a neural network to predict a personalized temperature of any input data for enhancing LFMs?" In this paper, we present a principled framework for learning a small yet generalizable temperature prediction network (TempNet) to improve LFMs. Our solution is composed of a novel learning framework with robust losses underpinned by constrained distributionally robust optimization (DRO), and a properly designed TempNet with theoretical inspiration. TempNet can be trained together with a large foundation model from scratch or learned separately given a pretrained foundation model. It is not only useful for predicting personalized temperature to promote the training of LFMs but also generalizable and transferable to new tasks. Our experiments on LLMs and CLIP models demonstrate that TempNet greatly improves the performance of existing solutions or models.

That framework supplies robust losses, while theoretical considerations inform the network design. TempNet can be trained jointly with a foundation model from scratch or learned separately for an already pretrained model, giving it two routes into existing modeling workflows.

The authors report that the learned temperature predictor generalizes and transfers to new tasks. These findings support input-specific temperature prediction as a useful learned component across the evaluated settings, linking a small auxiliary network to consequential choices in foundation-model training and inference.
summary.tldr: TempNet learns input-specific temperatures through a distributionally robust framework, improving the evaluated language and CLIP models.

title: To Cool or not to Cool? Temperature Network Meets Large Foundation Models via DRO

abstract: We present a new approach for input optimization of ReLU networks that explicitly takes into account the effect of changes in activation patterns. We analyze local optimization steps in both the input space and the space of activation patterns to propose methods with superior local descent properties. To accomplish this, we convert the discrete space of activation patterns into differentiable representations and propose regularization terms that improve each descent step. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed input-optimization methods for improving the state-of-the-art in various areas, such as adversarial learning, generative modeling, and reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to optimize the input of a ReLU network while explicitly accounting for changes in its activation pattern. Changing an input can change which units are active, so evaluating a local update requires considering both the input movement and its effect on those activations. The authors make that interaction central to their optimization approach.

They analyze local steps in two connected spaces: the space of inputs and the space of activation patterns. Because activation patterns are discrete, the method converts them into differentiable representations that can participate in gradient-based optimization. It then adds regularization terms designed to improve the descent achieved by each step.

The resulting methods have improved local descent properties according to the paper’s analysis. Experiments also report improvements over the state of the art in applications spanning adversarial learning, generative modeling, and reinforcement learning. The contribution connects those application results to a specific optimization mechanism: explicitly representing activation changes provides additional guidance for choosing useful input updates.
summary.tldr: Differentiable representations of ReLU activation patterns help guide input updates with improved local descent properties.

title: Activation-Descent Regularization for Input Optimization of ReLU Networks

abstract: Control tasks with safety requirements under high levels of model uncertainty are increasingly common. Machine learning techniques are frequently used to address such tasks, typically by leveraging model error bounds to specify robust constraint-based safety filters. However, if the learned model uncertainty is very high, the corresponding filters are potentially invalid, meaning no control input satisfies the constraints imposed by the safety filter. While most works address this issue by assuming some form of safe backup controller, ours tackles it by collecting additional data on the fly using a Gaussian process bandit-type algorithm. We combine a control barrier function with a learned model to specify a robust certificate that ensures safety if feasible. Whenever infeasibility occurs, we leverage the control barrier function to guide exploration, ensuring the collected data contributes toward the closed-loop system safety. By combining a safety filter with exploration in this manner, our method provably achieves safety in a general setting that does not require any prior model or backup controller, provided that the true system lies in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first safe learning-based control method that achieves this.

paragraphs: Safety filters use uncertainty estimates to restrict a controller’s available actions. When uncertainty is very large, those restrictions can become infeasible: no input satisfies the filter’s constraints. This paper addresses that situation by collecting additional data during operation, rather than assuming that a safe backup controller is available.

The method combines a learned model with a control barrier function to construct a robust safety certificate. When feasible, that certificate ensures safety. When infeasibility occurs, a Gaussian-process bandit-type algorithm explores, guided by the barrier function so that the additional data contributes toward the safety of the closed-loop system.

This integration makes exploration part of the response to uncertainty that prevents the filter from operating. That function-space assumption is part of the guarantee: the result supports safe learning under the specified setting, rather than unconditional safety for arbitrary unknown systems.
summary.tldr: Barrier-guided bandit exploration restores useful safety information when uncertainty makes a control filter infeasible, with guarantees under an RKHS assumption.

title: Learning Safe Control via On-the-Fly Bandit Exploration

abstract: Text-to-image synthesis has witnessed remarkable advancements in recent years. Many attempts have been made to adopt text-to-image models to support multiple tasks. However, existing approaches typically require resource-intensive re-training or additional parameters to accommodate for the new tasks, which makes the model inefficient for on-device deployment. We propose Multi-Task Upcycling (MTU), a simple yet effective recipe that extends the capabilities of a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model to support a variety of image-to-image generation tasks. MTU replaces Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layers in the diffusion model with smaller FFNs, referred to as experts, and combines them with a dynamic routing mechanism. To the best of our knowledge, MTU is the first multi-task diffusion modeling approach that seamlessly blends multi-tasking with on-device compatibility, by mitigating the issue of parameter inflation. We show that the performance of MTU is on par with the single-task fine-tuned diffusion models across several tasks including image editing, super-resolution, and inpainting, while maintaining similar latency and computational load (GFLOPs) as the single-task fine-tuned models.

The contribution is a recipe that combines multi-task diffusion with the parameter and runtime considerations relevant to on-device use.
summary.tldr: Multi-Task Upcycling uses smaller routed experts to add image-generation tasks while maintaining performance and computational costs comparable to single-task models.

title: Upcycling Text-to-Image Diffusion Models for Multi-Task Capabilities

abstract: Grokking refers to a delayed generalization following overfitting when optimizing artificial neural networks with gradient-based methods. In this work, we demonstrate that grokking can be induced by regularization, either explicit or implicit. More precisely, we show that when there exists a model with a property $P$ (e.g., sparse or low-rank weights) that generalizes on the problem of interest, gradient descent with a small but non-zero regularization of $P$ (e.g., $\ell_1$ or nuclear norm regularization) results in grokking. This extends previous work showing that small non-zero weight decay induces grokking. Moreover, our analysis shows that over-parameterization by adding depth makes it possible to grok or ungrok without explicitly using regularization, which is impossible in shallow cases. We further show that the $\ell_2$ norm is not a reliable proxy for generalization when the model is regularized toward a different property $P$, as the $\ell_2$ norm grows in many cases where no weight decay is used, but the model generalizes anyway. We also show that grokking can be amplified solely through data selection, with any other hyperparameter fixed.

paragraphs: Grokking is the delayed emergence of generalization after a neural network has already overfit its training data. This paper investigates how regularization can produce that pattern. It extends the discussion beyond weight decay to properties such as sparse or low-rank weights, which can favor different kinds of solutions.

The key result is conditional: when a model with a property P generalizes on the problem, gradient descent with small but nonzero regularization toward P results in grokking. The analysis also finds that adding depth can make grokking appear or disappear through implicit regularization, without an explicit regularization term. The authors distinguish this possibility from the shallow cases they analyze.

These findings challenge the use of the Euclidean weight norm as a general indicator of learning quality. When training favors another property, that norm can grow while the model still generalizes. The paper additionally shows that data selection alone can amplify grokking while other hyperparameters remain fixed. Together, the results connect delayed generalization to the property favored by training, model depth, and the selected data.
summary.tldr: Grokking can arise from regularization toward generalizing properties beyond small weight norms, including sparsity and low rank.

title: Grokking Beyond the Euclidean Norm of Model Parameters

abstract: Hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) improves the efficiency of long-horizon reinforcement-learning tasks with sparse rewards by decomposing the task into a hierarchy of subgoals. The main challenge of HRL is efficient discovery of the hierarchical structure among subgoals and utilizing this structure to achieve the final goal. We address this challenge by modeling the subgoal structure as a causal graph and propose a causal discovery algorithm to learn it. Additionally, rather than intervening on the subgoals at random during exploration, we harness the discovered causal model to prioritize subgoal interventions based on their importance in attaining the final goal. These targeted interventions result in a significantly more efficient policy in terms of the training cost. Unlike previous work on causal HRL, which lacked theoretical analysis, we provide a formal analysis of the problem. Specifically, for tree structures and, for a variant of Erdős-Rényi random graphs, our approach results in remarkable improvements. Our experimental results on HRL tasks also illustrate that our proposed framework outperforms existing work in terms of training cost.

summary.tldr: Learning causal relationships between subgoals helps hierarchical reinforcement learning target useful interventions and reduce training cost.

title: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Targeted Causal Interventions

abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing Large Language Model (LLM) activations into interpretable latents, however they have a substantial training cost and SAEs learned on different models are not directly comparable. Motivated by relative representation similarity measures, we introduce Inference-Time Decomposition of Activation models (ITDAs). ITDAs are constructed by greedily sampling activations into a dictionary based on an error threshold on their matching pursuit reconstruction. ITDAs can be trained in 1% of the time of SAEs, allowing us to cheaply train them on Llama-3.1 70B and 405B. ITDA dictionaries also enable cross-model comparisons, and outperform existing methods like CKA, SVCCA, and a relative representation method on a benchmark of representation similarity. Code available at https://github.com/pleask/itda.

This paper introduces Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations, or ITDA, as a way to address both the construction cost and the cross-model comparison problem.

ITDA builds a dictionary by greedily selecting activations. Selection depends on whether a matching-pursuit reconstruction meets an error threshold, tying dictionary construction to how well existing entries represent the activations. The approach is motivated by relative representation similarity, connecting the decomposition method with the broader goal of comparing internal representations.

The authors report construction in 1% of the training time needed by sparse autoencoders, enabling inexpensive application to Llama-3.1 models with 70 billion and 405 billion parameters. ITDA dictionaries also outperform CKA, SVCCA, and a relative representation method on a representation-similarity benchmark. The findings support a cheaper approach to activation decomposition whose dictionaries can additionally serve as a basis for comparing different models.
summary.tldr: ITDA constructs activation dictionaries at a small fraction of sparse-autoencoder training time and improves benchmarked cross-model representation comparisons.

title: Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA): A Scalable Approach to Interpreting Large Language Models

abstract: We introduce a framework for designing efficient diffusion models for $d$-dimensional symmetric-space Riemannian manifolds, including the torus, sphere, special orthogonal group and unitary group. Existing manifold diffusion models often depend on heat kernels, which lack closed-form expressions and require either $d$ gradient evaluations or exponential-in-$d$ arithmetic operations per training step. We introduce a new diffusion model for symmetric manifolds with a spatially-varying covariance, allowing us to leverage a projection of Euclidean Brownian motion to bypass heat kernel computations. Our training algorithm minimizes a novel efficient objective derived via Ito’s Lemma, allowing each step to run in $O(1)$ gradient evaluations and nearly-linear-in-$d$ ($O(d^{1.19})$) arithmetic operations, reducing the gap between diffusions on symmetric manifolds and Euclidean space. Manifold symmetries ensure the diffusion satisfies an "average-case" Lipschitz condition, enabling accurate and efficient sample generation. Empirically, our model outperforms prior methods in training speed and improves sample quality on synthetic datasets on the torus, special orthogonal group, and unitary group.

For symmetric manifolds such as spheres, tori, and certain matrix groups, existing approaches often rely on heat kernels that lack closed-form expressions. Computing with these kernels can require many gradient evaluations or arithmetic costs that grow exponentially with dimension.

The stated framework covers symmetric manifolds, and the empirical results concern the listed geometric settings.
summary.tldr: A geometry-aware diffusion framework avoids expensive heat-kernel calculations and improves training efficiency on symmetric manifolds.

title: Efficient Diffusion Models for Symmetric Manifolds

abstract: Machine learning relies heavily on data, yet the continuous growth of real-world data poses challenges for efficient dataset construction and training. A fundamental yet unsolved question is: given our current model and data, does a new data (sample/batch) need annotation/learning? Conventional approaches retain all available data, leading to non-optimal data and training efficiency. Active learning aims to reduce data redundancy by selecting a subset of samples to annotate, while it increases pipeline complexity and introduces bias. In this work, we propose Info-Coevolution, a novel framework that efficiently enables models and data to coevolve through online selective annotation with no bias. Leveraging task-specific models (and open-source models), it selectively annotates and integrates online and web data to improve datasets efficiently. For real-world datasets like ImageNet-1K, Info-Coevolution reduces annotation and training costs by 32% without performance loss. It is able to automatically give the saving ratio without tuning the ratio. It can further reduce the annotation ratio to 50% with semi-supervised learning. We also explore retrieval-based dataset enhancement using unlabeled open-source data. Code is available at https://github.com/NUS-HPC-AI-Lab/Info-Coevolution/.

paragraphs: As new data arrives, a learning system must decide whether each sample or batch is worth annotating and learning from. Keeping everything can waste labeling and training effort. Info-Coevolution addresses this decision online, allowing dataset construction and model improvement to proceed together instead of automatically absorbing all available data.

The framework uses task-specific models, along with open-source models, to select and annotate incoming or web data. The authors describe the selection process as avoiding bias. summary.tldr: Info-Coevolution selectively annotates incoming data, reducing reported annotation and training costs by 32% without performance loss.

title: Info-Coevolution: An Efficient Framework for Data Model Coevolution

abstract: Fine-tuning significantly improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This paper aims to provide an in-depth interpretation of the fine-tuning process through circuit analysis, a popular tool in Mechanistic Interpretability (MI). Unlike previous studies (Prakash et al. 2024, Chhabra et al. 2024) that focus on tasks where pre-trained models already perform well, we develop a set of mathematical tasks where fine-tuning yields substantial performance gains, bringing the setup closer to real-world scenarios. In our experiments, we identify circuits at various checkpoints during fine-tuning and examine the interplay between circuit analysis, fine-tuning methods, and task complexities. First, we find that while circuits maintain high node similarity before and after fine-tuning, their edges undergo significant changes, contrasting with previous work (Prakash et al. 2024, Chhabra et al. 2024) that reported only small circuit additions after fine-tuning. Based on these observations, we develop a circuit-aware Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) method that assigns ranks to layers according to edge changes in the circuits. Experimental results demonstrate that our circuit-based LoRA achieves an average improvement of 2.46% over standard LoRA with comparable parameter sizes. Furthermore, we explore how combining circuits from subtasks can enhance fine-tuning in compositional tasks, offering new insights into task design and deepening our understanding of circuit dynamics and fine-tuning mechanisms.

paragraphs: This paper investigates what changes inside a language model when fine-tuning substantially improves its performance. It constructs mathematical tasks where the pretrained model has meaningful room to improve, then identifies internal circuits at multiple training checkpoints. This setup examines learning beyond tasks the starting model already handles well.

The experiments find that circuit nodes remain highly similar before and after fine-tuning, while connections between those nodes change substantially. This contrasts with earlier findings of only small circuit additions. The result points to changes in internal connectivity as an important part of adaptation in these experiments, even when many participating components remain similar.

The authors use this observation to design circuit-aware LoRA, assigning adaptation ranks to layers according to changes in circuit edges. It achieves a reported average improvement of 2.46% over standard LoRA at comparable parameter sizes. The paper also explores combining subtask circuits to improve fine-tuning on compositional tasks. Together, these investigations connect circuit analysis to both an explanation of adaptation and a practical method for allocating adaptation capacity.
summary.tldr: Circuit analysis reveals substantial connection changes during fine-tuning and guides a LoRA variant that improves reported performance.

title: Towards Understanding Fine-Tuning Mechanisms of LLMs via Circuit Analysis

abstract: In recent years, SignSGD has garnered interest as both a practical optimizer as well as a simple model to understand adaptive optimizers like Adam. Though there is a general consensus that SignSGD acts to precondition optimization and reshapes noise, quantitatively understanding these effects in theoretically solvable settings remains difficult. We present an analysis of SignSGD in a high dimensional limit, and derive a limiting SDE and ODE to describe the risk. Using this framework we quantify four effects of SignSGD: effective learning rate, noise compression, diagonal preconditioning, and gradient noise reshaping. Our analysis is consistent with experimental observations but moves beyond that by quantifying the dependence of these effects on the data and noise distributions. We conclude with a conjecture on how these results might be extended to Adam.

paragraphs: SignSGD is useful both as an optimizer and as a simplified setting for studying adaptive methods such as Adam. Researchers broadly understand that it changes the geometry of optimization and reshapes gradient noise, but those descriptions do not by themselves quantify what happens. This paper develops a solvable high-dimensional analysis to make those effects precise.

The authors derive a limiting stochastic differential equation and an ordinary differential equation describing risk. Their framework separates four effects: the effective learning rate, noise compression, diagonal preconditioning, and gradient-noise reshaping. It also quantifies how these effects depend on the distributions of the data and noise.

The resulting analysis agrees with experimental observations while explaining their distributional dependence more explicitly. Its theoretical conclusions are established in a high-dimensional limit, which is central to the framework. The paper closes with a conjecture about extending the results to Adam; that proposed extension is a direction for further work rather than an established result of the analysis.
summary.tldr: A high-dimensional analysis quantifies how SignSGD changes learning rates, preconditioning, and gradient noise as data and noise distributions vary.

title: Exact risk curves of signSGD in High-Dimensions: quantifying preconditioning and noise-compression effects

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated the ability to solve a wide range of practical tasks within multi-agent systems. However, existing human-designed multi-agent frameworks are typically limited to a small set of pre-defined scenarios, while current automated design methods suffer from several limitations, such as the lack of tool integration, dependence on external training data, and rigid communication structures. In this paper, we propose MetaAgent, a finite state machine based framework that can automatically generate a multi-agent system. Given a task description, MetaAgent will design a multi-agent system and polish it through an optimization algorithm. When the multi-agent system is deployed, the finite state machine will control the agent’s actions and the state transitions. To evaluate our framework, we conduct experiments on both text-based tasks and practical tasks. The results indicate that the generated multi-agent system surpasses other auto-designed methods and can achieve a comparable performance with the human-designed multi-agent system, which is optimized for those specific tasks.

paragraphs: Building a useful multi-agent language-model system usually requires decisions about how agents act and coordinate. Human-designed frameworks often target a narrow set of scenarios, while automated alternatives can have rigid communication structures or depend on external training data. MetaAgent studies how to generate a coordinated system directly from a task description.

The framework represents the resulting system using a finite state machine. It first designs the multi-agent system and then refines it through an optimization algorithm. At deployment, the state machine governs agent actions and transitions between states. This supplies an explicit structure for controlling execution as the agents work through the task.

The authors evaluate MetaAgent on both text-based and practical tasks. Its generated systems outperform other automatically designed methods and achieve performance comparable to human-designed systems optimized for those tasks. These findings suggest that automated construction can approach specialized manual designs in the evaluated settings. The contribution combines system generation, optimization, and deployment control within a common state-machine framework.
summary.tldr: MetaAgent generates and optimizes multi-agent systems from task descriptions, using finite state machines to control their execution.

title: MetaAgent: Automatically Constructing Multi-Agent Systems Based on Finite State Machines

abstract: We introduce GraphGPT, a novel self-supervised generative pre-trained model for graph learning based on the Graph Eulerian Transformer (GET). First, we propose GET, which combines a standard transformer encoder or decoder architecture with an innovative graph-to-sequence transformation method. This method converts graphs or sampled subgraphs into sequences of tokens representing nodes, edges, and attributes in a reversible manner using Eulerian paths. We pre-train GET using either of the two self-supervised tasks: next-token prediction (NTP) and scheduled masked-token prediction (SMTP). The pre-trained model is then fine-tuned for downstream tasks such as graph-, edge-, and node-level prediction. Despite its simplicity, GraphGPT achieves performance comparable to or surpassing state-of-the-art methods on multiple large-scale Open Graph Benchmark (OGB) datasets. It demonstrates exceptional results on the molecular property prediction dataset PCQM4Mv2 and the protein-protein interaction dataset ogbl-ppa. Notably, generative pre-training enables scaling GraphGPT to 2 billion parameters while maintaining performance gains — a breakthrough that overcomes the scalability limitations of traditional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and prior graph transformers (GTs). To advance research in graph foundation models and facilitate scientific discovery in chemistry, materials science, and related fields, we have released the source code (https://github.com/alibaba/graph-gpt) and model checkpoints (https://www.modelscope.cn/organization/Alibaba-DT).

paragraphs: GraphGPT applies generative pretraining to graph learning by first making graphs usable as token sequences. Its Graph Eulerian Transformer converts a graph or sampled subgraph into tokens describing nodes, edges, and attributes. The conversion uses Eulerian paths and is reversible, preserving the graph information represented by the sequence.

This representation lets the method use a standard transformer encoder or decoder. Pretraining uses either next-token prediction or scheduled masked-token prediction, learning from the graph sequences without requiring task-specific labels at that stage. The pretrained model is then fine-tuned for predictions about entire graphs, individual edges, or individual nodes.

On multiple large-scale Open Graph Benchmark datasets, GraphGPT matches or exceeds state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong reported results for molecular property prediction on PCQM4Mv2 and protein interactions on ogbl-ppa. The authors also scale it to two billion parameters while continuing to obtain performance gains. This is the main scaling result: their graph representation and generative training approach support a substantially larger model with continued empirical benefit.
summary.tldr: GraphGPT reversibly converts graphs into token sequences, enabling generative transformer pretraining and continued performance gains at two billion parameters.

title: GraphGPT: Generative Pre-trained Graph Eulerian Transformer

abstract: With the widespread adoption of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, there is a growing demand for efficient inference on memory-constrained devices. While offloading expert parameters to CPU memory and loading activated experts on demand has emerged as a potential solution, the large size of activated experts overburdens the limited PCIe bandwidth, hindering the effectiveness in latency-sensitive scenarios. To mitigate this, we propose FloE, an on-the-fly MoE inference system on memory-constrained GPUs. FloE is built on the insight that there exists substantial untapped redundancy within sparsely activated experts. It employs various compression techniques on the expert’s internal parameter matrices to reduce the data movement load, combined with low-cost sparse prediction, achieving perceptible inference acceleration in wall-clock time on resource-constrained devices. Empirically, FloE achieves a 9.3$\times$ compression of parameters per expert in Mixtral-8$\times$7B; enables deployment on a GPU with only 11GB VRAM, reducing the memory footprint by up to 8.5$\times$; and delivers a 48.7$\times$ inference speedup compared to DeepSpeed-MII on a single GeForce RTX 3090—all with only a 4.4% $\sim$ 7.6% average performance degradation.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts models can exceed the memory available on a GPU. Keeping expert parameters in CPU memory and loading activated experts as needed helps with capacity, but transferring those parameters through PCIe can create a latency bottleneck. FloE addresses this data-movement problem by exploiting redundancy inside the experts that are activated during inference.

The system compresses experts' internal parameter matrices and combines these techniques with low-cost sparse prediction. Reducing the amount of expert data that must move makes on-demand loading more practical on memory-constrained devices. The approach targets actual wall-clock acceleration, linking parameter compression to the transfer bottleneck that limits offloaded inference.

For Mixtral-8×7B, the reported experiments achieve 9.3× parameter compression per expert and deployment with 11GB of GPU memory, with memory-footprint reductions of up to 8.5×. On a single GeForce RTX 3090, FloE reports a 48.7× inference speedup over DeepSpeed-MII. These benefits come with average performance degradation of 4.4%–7.6%, making the result an explicit efficiency-performance tradeoff in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: FloE compresses MoE experts to reduce CPU–GPU transfers, enabling substantial reported memory and speed gains with 4.4%–7.6% average performance degradation.

title: FloE: On-the-Fly MoE Inference on Memory-constrained GPU

abstract: To detect distribution shifts and improve model safety, many out-of-distribution (OOD) detection methods rely on the predictive uncertainty or features of supervised models trained on in-distribution data. In this position paper, we critically re-examine this popular family of OOD detection procedures, and we argue that these methods are fundamentally answering the wrong questions for OOD detection. There is no simple fix to this misalignment, since a classifier trained only on in-distribution classes cannot be expected to identify OOD points; for instance, a cat-dog classifier may confidently misclassify an airplane if it contains features that distinguish cats from dogs, despite generally appearing nothing alike. We find that uncertainty-based methods incorrectly conflate high uncertainty with being OOD, while feature-based methods incorrectly conflate far feature-space distance with being OOD. We show how these pathologies manifest as irreducible errors in OOD detection and identify common settings where these methods are ineffective. Additionally, interventions to improve OOD detection such as feature-logit hybrid methods, scaling of model and data size, epistemic uncertainty representation, and outlier exposure also fail to address this fundamental misalignment in objectives.

paragraphs: This position paper examines methods that detect unfamiliar inputs using the uncertainty or internal features of supervised classifiers. The authors argue that classifying known categories and identifying out-of-distribution inputs are fundamentally misaligned objectives. A classifier trained only to distinguish cats from dogs, for example, can confidently assign an airplane to one of those categories.

The paper identifies a different mistaken equivalence in each major approach. Uncertainty-based methods treat uncertainty as evidence that an input is outside the distribution. Feature-based methods treat distance in the learned representation as evidence of the same thing. The authors show how these mismatches produce irreducible detection errors and identify common settings where the methods are ineffective.

They further argue that combining features and classifier outputs, increasing scale, representing epistemic uncertainty, or exposing models to outliers does not resolve the underlying objective mismatch. The implication concerns the basis for detection: signals learned to separate known classes cannot simply be assumed to answer whether an input belongs to the expected distribution. The paper challenges that assumption rather than offering a simple adjustment.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that classifier uncertainty and feature distance are fundamentally misaligned with detecting out-of-distribution inputs.

title: Position: Supervised Classifiers Answer the Wrong Questions for OOD Detection

abstract: Transformer-based tabular foundation models (TFMs) dominate small to medium tabular predictive benchmark tasks, yet their inference mechanisms remain largely unexplored. We present the first large-scale mechanistic study of layerwise dynamics in 6 state-of-the-art tabular in-context learning models. We explore how predictions emerge across depth, identify distinct stages of inference and reveal latent-space dynamics that differ from those of language models. Our findings indicate substantial depthwise redundancy across multiple models, suggesting iterative refinement with overlapping computations during inference stages. Guided by these insights, we design a proof-of-concept, looped single-layer model that uses only 20% of the original model’s parameters while achieving comparable performance. The code is available at https://github.com/amirbalef/is_one_layer_enough.

paragraphs: Tabular foundation models make predictions for structured tables using information supplied in context, but how those predictions develop inside their transformer layers remains poorly understood. This paper investigates inference across depth in six state-of-the-art models. The goal is to connect their internal computations to the architectural capacity they actually appear to use.

The study tracks how predictions emerge, identifies distinct stages of inference, and examines changes in latent representations. It finds dynamics that differ from those observed in language models. Across multiple tabular models, substantial computations overlap across depth, suggesting that successive layers partly perform iterative refinement rather than wholly distinct operations. This is evidence of redundancy in the studied systems, not a claim that depth never contributes.

Motivated by these observations, the authors build a proof-of-concept model that repeatedly applies a single layer. It uses only 20% of the original model’s parameters while achieving comparable performance. The result links mechanistic analysis to a concrete parameter-saving design and shows why repeated computation can be worth exploring for tabular inference.
summary.tldr: Layerwise analysis reveals redundant computation in tabular foundation models and motivates a looped single-layer prototype with 20% of the original parameters.

title: Is One Layer Enough? Understanding Inference Dynamics in Tabular Foundation Models

abstract: Existing Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods are fundamentally constrained by a static allocation paradigm, which overlooks the model’s evolving optimization priorities during training. To address this, we introduce Dynamic Adaptive Fine-tuning (DAF), a novel framework that periodically evaluates and reconfigures the trainable structure based on a context-aware decoupled sensitivity analysis. DAF employs a Rebuild-and-Refocus strategy to preserve learned knowledge by freezing outdated modules while decisively reallocating the parameter budget to newly identified critical regions. Extensive experiments on challenging vision benchmarks demonstrate that DAF significantly outperforms mainstream static PEFT methods and achieves superior performance and efficiency, particularly under extreme parameter budgets. Our work fundamentally challenges the static nature of the field, offering a more intelligent and efficient paradigm for adapting large pretrained models. The code is available at https://github.com/E-green11/DAF.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model by training only a limited set of parameters. This paper questions the usual choice to keep that allocation fixed throughout training. Its premise is that the regions most useful to optimize can change as adaptation progresses, so an initially sensible allocation may stop matching the model’s current needs.

Dynamic Adaptive Fine-tuning, or DAF, periodically reassesses the model using a context-aware sensitivity analysis and then changes which structures remain trainable. Its Rebuild-and-Refocus strategy freezes modules that are no longer the current priority, preserving what they have learned. It redirects the available parameter budget toward regions newly identified as important.

Experiments on challenging vision benchmarks report significant improvements over mainstream methods with static allocations, including better performance and efficiency under especially restrictive parameter budgets. These findings support treating parameter allocation as part of the optimization process itself. The contribution is a mechanism for repeatedly deciding where adaptation effort is most valuable while retaining knowledge from earlier training stages.
summary.tldr: DAF periodically reallocates trainable parameters toward newly important model regions, improving vision adaptation under tight parameter budgets.

title: Beyond Static Allocation: Dynamic Sensitivity-Aware Fine-Tuning for Vision Transformers

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) demonstrate impressive cross-modal capabilities, yet their substantial size poses significant deployment challenges. Knowledge distillation (KD) is a promising solution for compressing these models, but existing methods primarily rely on static next-token alignment, neglecting the dynamic token interactions, which embed essential capabilities for multimodal understanding and generation. To this end, we introduce Align-TI, a novel KD framework designed from the perspective of Token Interactions. Our approach is motivated by the insight that MLLMs rely on two primary interactions: vision-instruction token interactions to extract relevant visual information, and intra-response token interactions for coherent generation. Accordingly, Align-TI introduces two components: IVA enables the student model to imitate the teacher’s instruction-relevant visual information extract capability by aligning on salient visual regions. TPA captures the teacher’s dynamic generative logic by aligning the sequential token-to-token transition probabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate Align-TI’s superiority. Notably, our approach achieves 2.6% relative improvement over Vanilla KD, and our distilled Align-TI-2B even outperforms LLaVA-1.5-7B (a much larger MLLM) by 7.0%, establishing a new state-of-the-art distillation framework for training parameter-efficient MLLMs.

paragraphs: Compressing a multimodal language model requires transferring both visual understanding and coherent generation to a smaller model. The paper argues that matching a teacher’s next-token predictions alone overlooks important relationships between tokens. Align-TI therefore organizes distillation around how instructions interact with visual information and how response tokens interact during generation.

Its first component, IVA, trains the student to match the teacher’s attention to salient visual regions relevant to the instruction. The aim is to transfer the ability to extract the right information from an image. Its second component, TPA, aligns sequential token-to-token transition probabilities, giving the student a training signal about the teacher’s evolving generation behavior. Together, these components address information selection and response construction.

The reported experiments show a 2.6% relative improvement over Vanilla KD. The distilled Align-TI-2B also outperforms the larger LLaVA-1.5-7B by a reported 7.0%. These comparisons support the value of transferring token interactions for efficient multimodal models, beyond simply reproducing isolated next-token outputs.
summary.tldr: Align-TI distills multimodal models by transferring instruction-relevant visual interactions and response-token transitions.

title: Beyond Next-Token Alignment: Distilling Multimodal Large Language Models via Token Interactions

abstract: Tokenization is the first point of contact between large language models (LLMs) and text data, yet it has not been viewed by many as a component of LLMs worth accelerating. During inference, tokenizers typically rely on simple dictionary lookups and are executed on CPUs as standard processes. This approach, however, introduces significant overhead from scheduling delays, core selection, data copying, and other system-level costs. These inefficiencies become problematic in latency-sensitive applications such as embedding, small language models, and agentic AI. In this paper, we present the Pinned Tokenizer (PinTok), a novel tokenizer architecture that reduces redundant hardware, operating system, and networking overhead through three key innovations: core and memory pinning, scheduling and context switch avoidance, and duplicate network packet copy and processing avoidance. Our implementation of PinTok can serve as a drop-in replacement for existing tokenizer deployments, delivering latency reductions of up to 95% (average), 97% (P50), 94% (P90), and 87% (P99) along with throughput improvements of up to 2,084%.

paragraphs: Tokenization converts text into the units a language model consumes, making it the first processing step for incoming text. Although tokenizer computation commonly uses simple CPU dictionary lookups, its surrounding system costs can be substantial. Scheduling delays, core selection, copying, and related overhead matter especially for latency-sensitive embedding services, small models, and agentic applications.

PinTok redesigns tokenizer deployment around dedicated CPU and memory resources. It combines core and memory pinning with avoidance of scheduling and context-switch costs, and removes duplicate network-packet copying and processing. The approach targets the machinery surrounding tokenization, treating resource placement and data movement as central parts of tokenizer performance.

The implementation can replace existing tokenizer deployments directly. Reported latency reductions reach up to 95% for average latency, 97% at P50, 94% at P90, and 87% at P99; throughput improvements reach up to 2,084%. These are upper-end reported improvements rather than uniform gains. The findings show that optimizing a seemingly lightweight preprocessing stage can produce substantial tokenizer-level efficiency benefits by reducing system overhead.
summary.tldr: PinTok accelerates tokenizer serving by pinning CPU and memory resources and removing redundant scheduling, copying, and network-processing overhead.

title: PinTok: Tokenizers Deserve Dedicated Pinned CPU-Compute and Memory

abstract: Search-integrated reasoning enables language agents to transcend static parametric knowledge by actively querying external sources. However, training these agents via reinforcement learning is hindered by the multi-scale credit assignment problem: existing methods typically rely on sparse, trajectory-level rewards that fail to distinguish between high-quality reasoning and fortuitous guesses, leading to redundant or misleading search behaviors. To address this, we propose Search-R2, a novel Actor–Refiner collaboration framework that enhances reasoning through targeted intervention, with both components jointly optimized during training. Our approach decomposes the generation process into an Actor, which produces initial reasoning trajectories, and a Meta-Refiner, which selectively diagnoses and repairs flawed steps via a “cut-and-regenerate” mechanism. To provide fine-grained supervision, we introduce a hybrid reward design that couples outcome correctness with a dense process reward quantifying the information density of retrieved evidence. Theoretically, we formalize the Actor–Refiner interaction as a smoothed mixture policy, proving that selective correction yields strict performance gains over strong baselines. Extensive experiments across various general and multi-hop QA datasets demonstrate that Search-R2 consistently outperforms strong RAG and RL-based baselines across model scales, achieving superior reasoning accuracy with minimal overhead.

paragraphs: Training search-enabled language agents from final-answer rewards makes it difficult to identify which reasoning and retrieval steps deserve credit. A correct answer can arise from strong evidence use or a lucky guess, while unnecessary searches may receive little direct feedback. Search-R2 addresses this credit-assignment problem through collaboration between an Actor and a Meta-Refiner.

The Actor generates an initial reasoning trajectory. The Meta-Refiner selectively identifies flawed steps and repairs them by cutting the trajectory and regenerating from the intervention point. Both components are optimized jointly. A hybrid reward combines answer correctness with a dense process signal based on the information density of retrieved evidence, providing feedback about the usefulness of the search process itself.

The authors formalize the interaction as a smoothed mixture policy and prove strict performance improvements from selective correction within that formulation. Experiments on general and multi-hop question answering show consistent gains over strong retrieval-augmented and reinforcement-learning baselines across model scales, with minimal overhead. The approach connects targeted repair with more detailed supervision, helping training distinguish useful reasoning from merely successful final outcomes.
summary.tldr: Search-R2 jointly trains an Actor and selective Refiner using answer and evidence-quality rewards to improve search-integrated reasoning.

title: Search-R2: Enhancing Search-Integrated Reasoning via Actor-Refiner Collaboration

abstract: Deep learning models for clinical event prediction on electronic health records (EHR) often suffer performance degradation when deployed under different data distributions. While domain adaptation (DA) methods can mitigate such shifts, their "black-box" nature prevents widespread adoption in clinical practice where transparency is essential for trust and safety. We propose ExtraCare to decompose patient representations into invariant and covariant components. By supervising these two components and enforcing their orthogonality during training, our model preserves label information while exposing domain-specific variation at the same time for more accurate predictions than most feature alignment models. More importantly, it offers human-understandable explanations by mapping sparse latent dimensions to medical concepts and quantifying their contributions via targeted ablations. ExtraCare is evaluated on two real-world EHR datasets across multiple domain partition settings, demonstrating superior performance along with enhanced transparency, as evidenced by its accurate predictions and explanations from extensive case studies.

paragraphs: Clinical prediction models can lose accuracy when the electronic health records encountered during deployment differ from their training data. Domain adaptation can help, but an opaque adaptation process makes predictions difficult to inspect. ExtraCare aims to improve prediction under distribution shifts while exposing how its internal representation relates to medical concepts.

The model separates patient representations into invariant and covariant components, distinguishing shared information from variation associated with the domain. Both components receive supervision, and training enforces orthogonality between them. This arrangement is intended to preserve information relevant to prediction while explicitly representing domain differences. For explanations, sparse latent dimensions are mapped to medical concepts, and targeted ablations measure their contributions to model predictions.

Evaluation on two real-world health-record datasets, using several domain partitions, reports strong predictive performance and improved transparency. Extensive case studies provide evidence for the explanations. The findings support treating domain variation as something to expose and structure, alongside learning transferable information, so that adaptation produces both useful predictions and inspectable accounts of their contributing concepts.
summary.tldr: ExtraCare separates shared and domain-varying patient information and connects predictions to medical concepts for more transparent healthcare adaptation.

title: Exploring Accurate and Transparent Domain Adaptation in Predictive Healthcare via Concept-Grounded Orthogonal Inference

abstract: We study an algorithm-independent, worst-case lower bound for the Gaussian process (GP) bandit problem in the frequentist setting, where the reward function is fixed and has a bounded norm in the known reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Specifically, we focus on the squared exponential (SE) kernel, one of the most widely used kernel functions in GP bandits. One of the remaining open questions for this problem is the gap in the dimension-dependent logarithmic factors between upper and lower bounds. This paper partially resolves this open question under a hyperspherical input domain. We show that any algorithm suffers $\Omega(\sqrt{T (\ln T)^{d} (\ln \ln T)^{-d}})$ cumulative regret, where $T$ and $d$ represent the total number of steps and the dimension of the hyperspherical domain, respectively. Regarding the simple regret, we show that any algorithm requires $\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}(\ln \frac{1}{\epsilon})^d (\ln \ln \frac{1}{\epsilon})^{-d})$ time steps to find an $\epsilon$-optimal point. We also provide the improved $O((\ln T)^{d+1}(\ln \ln T)^{-d})$ upper bound on the maximum information gain for the SE kernel. Our results guarantee the optimality of the existing best algorithm up to dimension-independent logarithmic factors under a hyperspherical input domain.

paragraphs: This paper studies fundamental limits for Gaussian-process bandit optimization with a squared-exponential kernel on a hyperspherical domain.
