The question is how closely existing algorithms approach the best performance any algorithm could guarantee.

The authors strengthen worst-case lower bounds on both cumulative regret and the number of observations needed to find an approximately optimal point. For horizon T and domain dimension d, cumulative regret is at least of order sqrt(T (ln T)^d / (ln ln T)^d). The corresponding sample requirement for epsilon accuracy is of order epsilon^-2 (ln(1/epsilon))^d / (ln ln(1/epsilon))^d.

They also improve the upper bound on maximum information gain to order (ln T)^(d+1) / (ln ln T)^d. Together, these results narrow the gap in dimension-dependent logarithmic factors. Under the stated domain and function assumptions, they establish that the existing best algorithm is optimal up to logarithmic factors that do not depend on dimension.
summary.tldr: Sharper bounds establish near-optimality of the best existing squared-exponential GP bandit algorithm on hyperspherical domains.

title: Tighter Regret Lower Bound for Gaussian Process Bandits with Squared Exponential Kernel in Hypersphere

abstract: We revisit the standard perturbation-based approach of Abernethy et al. (2008) in the context of unconstrained Bandit Linear Optimization (uBLO). We show the surprising result that in the unconstrained setting, this approach effectively reduces Bandit Linear Optimization (BLO) to a standard Online Linear Optimization (OLO) problem. Our framework improves on prior work in several ways. First, we derive expected-regret guarantees when our perturbation scheme is combined with comparator-adaptive OLO algorithms, leading to new insights about the impact of different adversarial models on the resulting comparator-adaptive rates. We also extend our analysis to dynamic regret, obtaining the first guarantees with optimal $\sqrt{P_T}$ path-length dependencies without prior knowledge of $P_T$. We then develop the first high-probability guarantees for both static and dynamic regret in uBLO. Finally, we discuss lower bounds on the static regret, and prove the folklore $\Omega(\sqrt{dT})$ rate for adversarial linear bandits on the Euclidean ball, which is of independent interest.

paragraphs: The paper studies unconstrained bandit linear optimization, where a learner makes repeated decisions with limited feedback and no constraint on its decision domain. Its central result revisits a standard perturbation method and shows that, in this setting, it effectively converts the bandit problem into an ordinary online linear optimization problem. This makes existing online optimization algorithms useful building blocks.

Combining the reduction with algorithms that adapt to the comparator yields expected-regret guarantees. Here, regret measures performance relative to a reference decision or sequence of decisions. The analysis explains how different adversarial models affect these guarantees. For a changing reference sequence, it obtains the first guarantees with optimal square-root dependence on path length, without requiring that path length in advance.

The authors also establish the first high-probability guarantees for both fixed and changing comparators in the unconstrained setting. Separately, they examine lower bounds and prove the previously folklore square-root-of-dimension-times-horizon bound for adversarial linear bandits on the Euclidean ball. Together, these results clarify both achievable performance and fundamental obstacles.
summary.tldr: A perturbation reduction connects unconstrained linear bandits to online linear optimization and yields new static and dynamic regret guarantees.

title: A Perturbation Approach to Unconstrained Linear Bandits

abstract: Most existing 3D assembly methods treat the problem as pure pose estimation, rearranging observed parts via rigid transformations. In contrast, human assembly naturally couples structural reasoning with holistic shape inference. Inspired by this intuition, we reformulate 3D assembly as a joint problem of assembly and generation. We show that these two processes are mutually reinforcing: assembly provides part-level structural priors for generation, while generation injects holistic shape context that resolves ambiguities in assembly. Unlike prior methods that cannot synthesize missing geometry, we propose CRAG, which simultaneously generates plausible complete shapes and predicts poses for input parts. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across in-the-wild objects with diverse geometries, varying part counts, and missing pieces. Our code and models will be released.

paragraphs: Most 3D assembly methods focus on finding the positions and orientations of available parts. CRAG broadens the task by jointly predicting those poses and generating a plausible complete object. The motivation is that understanding an object's overall shape can help determine how its pieces fit together, particularly when the observed parts leave the assembly ambiguous.

The two processes supply complementary information. Assembly contributes structural constraints from individual parts, helping guide shape generation. Generation supplies a holistic view of the object, helping resolve uncertainties about part placement. Because the method can synthesize geometry, it also addresses cases where some pieces are missing, rather than relying entirely on rearranging the geometry already supplied.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on objects with varied geometries, different numbers of parts, and missing pieces. These findings support treating generation and assembly as mutually useful tasks. The generated completion is described as plausible, so its role is to provide a coherent whole that informs assembly rather than establish that every missing detail has been recovered exactly.
summary.tldr: CRAG jointly assembles 3D parts and generates complete shapes, using each process to improve the other.

title: CRAG: Can 3D Generative Models Help 3D Assembly?

abstract: Autoregressive decoding becomes bandwidth-limited at long contexts, as generating each token requires reading all $n_k$ key and value vectors from KV cache. We present Stochastic Additive No-mulT Attention (SANTA), a method that sparsifies value-cache access by sampling $S \ll n_k$ indices from the post-softmax distribution and aggregates only those value rows. This yields an unbiased estimator of the post-softmax value aggregation while replacing value-stage multiply-accumulates with gather-and-add. We introduce stratified and systematic sampling to design variance-reduced, GPU-friendly variants. Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at 32k-token contexts, S$^2$ANTA matches baseline accuracy while achieving up to $1.5\times$ decode-step attention-kernel speedup over FlashInfer and FlashDecoding on an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada. In batched long-context generation, these kernel gains translate to up to $1.25\times$ end-to-end decode-latency speedup. Finally, we propose Bernoulli $qK^\mathsf{T}$ sampling as a complementary technique to sparsify the score stage, reducing key-feature access through stochastic ternary queries. Both methods are complementary to upstream quantization, low-rank projection, KV-cache compression, and KV-cache selection methods. Together, they point toward sparse, multiplier-free, and energy-efficient inference. We open-source our kernels at: https://github.com/OPUSLab/SANTA.git

summary.tldr: SANTA samples cached values to estimate attention efficiently, delivering measured kernel and end-to-end decoding speedups.

title: Stochastic Sparse Attention for Memory-Bound Inference

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) excel in many multimodal tasks but remain prone to a subtle yet impactful failure mode: they tend to overestimate dominant visual-textual cues while underestimating sparse but decision-critical contextual variables. This issue, which we term Contextual Variable Overestimation (CVE), becomes particularly evident in real-world applications such as predicting advertisement image preferences across diverse geographic markets. For instance, when a VLM (e.g., Qwen2-VL) is asked to choose between two product images tailored for different countries (e.g., Korea vs. France), it often defaults to a consistent output (e.g., always selects “A”), ignoring ground-truth regional variations. This collapse occurs because pervasive high-volume signals, such as product attributes and dense image patches, overwhelm the few but critical tokens that encode market-specific context (e.g., country names). To address CVE, we first collect a new multimodal dataset of real advertising creatives and their click-through performance across multiple countries. We then introduce GeoReward, a reward model designed to predict ad image preferences across diverse geographic markets. GeoReward integrates three purpose-built mechanisms: (1) Market-Aware Retrieval Augmentation, which retrieves and injects region-aligned preference signals during training to sharpen localization awareness. (2) Context-Guided Visual Modulation, a lightweight adapter that dynamically adjusts visual representations using textual country embeddings, enabling fine-grained regional adaptation. (3) Selective Sensitivity Loss, an objective that applies heightened penalties for context-specific mispredictions, sharpening the model’s focus on critical variables. Furthermore, we demonstrate how GeoReward can guide the fine-tuning of RL for a VLM to generate background designs for text-to-image models (e.g., SDXL), producing market-aware advertising creatives. Experiments validate that our framework mitigates CVE and outperforms existing baselines. This work not only diagnoses a systematic bias in VLMs toward dominant perceptual features but also delivers a targeted solution for applications where sparse contextual variables govern decision-making. Code is available at https://github.com/liushuo-hue/GeoReward.git.

summary.tldr: GeoReward strengthens the influence of geographic context so advertising preference predictions and generated designs better reflect market-specific differences.

title: GeoReward: Mitigating Contextual Variable Overestimation in Vision-Language Models for Cross-Market Preference Prediction

abstract: Point supervision has become a scalable solution to address dense annotation for infrared small target detection, but its performance is limited by two coupled bottlenecks: unstable pseudo-label evolution in cluttered, low-contrast infrared imagery and severe sample-distribution imbalance. In this paper, we present a more adaptive and stable framework to address these issues. Leveraging the intrinsic consistency between thermal radiation patterns and heat diffusion, we propose a physics-induced annotation strategy that expands single-point labels into reliable pseudo-masks. To further enhance supervision and alleviate sample imbalance, we develop a bi-level dual-update framework that jointly optimizes detector weights, sample weights, and diffusion parameters. A meta-classifier dynamically predicts sample-wise loss weights, while a differentiable diffusion module refines pseudo-labels with detection feedback, enabling adaptive interaction between training and hyperparameter optimization. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate five-fold annotation acceleration, superior detection accuracy, and comparable performance with 30% of the training data, validating the efficiency and practicality of our approach. Our code is available at https://github.com/yuanhang-yao/diffuse-to-detect.

paragraphs: Marking a single point on an infrared target requires less annotation work than outlining its full shape. However, training a detector from these points requires constructing fuller labels, which can become unstable in cluttered, low-contrast images. The paper addresses this problem together with severe imbalance in the distribution of training samples.

Its annotation strategy uses the consistency between thermal radiation patterns and heat diffusion to expand point labels into pseudo-masks. A bi-level optimization framework then jointly adjusts detector parameters, sample weights, and diffusion parameters. A meta-classifier predicts how much weight each sample's loss should receive, while a differentiable diffusion module uses detector feedback to refine the pseudo-labels.

This creates an adaptive relationship between what the detector learns, which examples receive emphasis, and how its training masks evolve. Across multiple datasets, the authors report five-fold faster annotation and superior detection accuracy. They also report comparable performance using 30% of the training data. These findings indicate that jointly improving supervision and sample weighting can make point-supervised infrared detection more efficient.
summary.tldr: The method turns infrared point labels into adaptive masks while jointly reweighting samples to improve detection and annotation efficiency.

title: Diffuse to Detect: Bi-Level Sample Rebalancing with Pseudo-Label Diffusion for Point-Supervised Infrared Small-Target Detection

abstract: Reasoning models enhance performance by tackling problems in a step-by-step manner, decomposing them into sub-problems and exploring long chains of thought before producing an answer. However, applying extended reasoning to every step introduces substantial redundancy, as sub-problems vary widely in difficulty and complexity: a small number of pivotal steps are genuinely challenging and decisive for the final answer, while many others only involve straightforward revisions or simple computations. Therefore, a natural idea is to endow reasoning models with the ability to adaptively respond to this variation, rather than treating all steps with the same level of elaboration. To this end, we propose MixReasoning, a framework that dynamically adjusts the depth of reasoning within a single response. MixReasoning enables fine-grained mode switching by training a lightweight concise LoRA adapter and control its strength to trigger switches based on reasoning difficulty estimated from sliding-window token confidence, yielding human-like transitions between fast and slow reasoning. The resulting chain of thought then becomes a mixture of detailed reasoning on difficult steps and concise inference on simpler ones. Experiments on AIME24, MATH-500, GPQA, and GSM8K demonstrate that MixReasoning shortens reasoning length by 13%–49% across benchmarks of varying difficulty, delivering consistent efficiency gains while maintaining performance.

paragraphs: MixReasoning addresses unnecessary elaboration inside long reasoning responses. A problem may contain a few difficult decisions alongside many straightforward calculations or revisions. Giving every step the same detailed treatment can waste output length. The framework changes reasoning depth within a single response so that easy and difficult portions receive different treatment.

The method trains a lightweight LoRA adapter that encourages concise reasoning. During generation, it estimates difficulty from token confidence measured over a sliding window and adjusts the adapter’s strength to switch modes. The resulting response can alternate between detailed reasoning for challenging steps and shorter inference for simpler ones, rather than committing to one style throughout.

Across AIME24, MATH-500, GPQA, and GSM8K, the authors report reasoning-length reductions of 13%–49% while maintaining performance. These are gains in the length of generated reasoning, with reductions varying across benchmarks. The findings support fine-grained control of elaboration as a practical way to improve reasoning efficiency while preserving the tested models’ answer performance.
summary.tldr: MixReasoning switches between concise and detailed reasoning within a response, reducing reported reasoning length by 13%–49% while maintaining performance.

title: MixReasoning: Switching Modes to Think

abstract: As policy catches up with the capabilities of generative AI, watermarking is central to content provenance efforts. Inference-time watermarks for autoregressive models are unfit for continuous modalities due to discretization inconsistencies. Existing methods overcome this by finetuning the modality tokenizers, nullifying the watermark’s training-free advantage. In this work, motivated by the vocabulary redundancy of discretization, we propose an elegant solution for powerful and robust watermarking of synthetic audio. We theoretically analyze the impact of token errors on watermark detection, and effectively mitigate them using a reduced vocabulary obtained via community detection. Thorough experiments showcase that our gradient-free method can boost detectability by several orders of magnitude, while also achieving built-in robustness to audio modifications. Broadly, we discover a new state-of-the-art for token-level watermarks in multimedia, which simply arises from the nature of discrete representation learning.

paragraphs: Token-level watermarks for synthetic audio must survive the imperfect mapping between continuous sound and discrete tokens. Existing solutions can require retraining the tokenizer, reducing the appeal of inference-time watermarking. This paper instead exploits redundancy within the learned token vocabulary.

The authors analyze how token errors affect watermark detection and use community detection to form a reduced vocabulary. Grouping related tokens mitigates inconsistencies introduced during audio reconstruction and retokenization. The method is gradient-free, avoiding the tokenizer fine-tuning required by some earlier approaches.

Experiments report improvements in detectability by several orders of magnitude and robustness to audio modifications. The contribution is a representation-aware watermarking strategy that turns vocabulary redundancy into a useful resource. The abstract does not specify every tested transformation or a guarantee against arbitrary editing, so robustness should be understood relative to the evaluated audio modifications and detection setup.
summary.tldr: Grouping redundant audio tokens enables gradient-free watermarks with stronger reported detection and resistance to audio modifications.

title: Hidden in Plain Tokens: Simply Robust, Gradient-Free Watermark for Synthetic Audio

abstract: In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) is an emerging RL paradigm where an agent, after pretraining, can adapt to out-of-distribution test tasks without any parameter updates, instead relying on an expanding context of interaction history. While ICRL has shown impressive generalization, safety during this adaptation process remains unexplored, limiting its applicability in real-world deployments where test-time behavior is expected to be safe. In this work, we propose SCARED: Safe Contextual Adaptive Reinforcement via Exact-penalty Dual, the first method that promotes safe adaptation of ICRL under the constrained Markov decision process framework. During the parameter-update-free adaptation process, our agent not only maximizes the reward but also keeps the accumulated cost within a user-specified safety budget. We also demonstrate that the agent actively reacts to the safety budget; with a higher safety budget, the agent behaves more aggressively, and with a lower safety budget the agent behaves more conservatively. Across challenging benchmarks, SCARED consistently enables safe and robust in-context adaptation, outperforming existing ICRL and safe meta-RL baselines.

paragraphs: In-context reinforcement learning lets a pretrained agent adapt to unfamiliar tasks using its growing interaction history, without updating model parameters. That makes test-time adaptation possible through context alone, but it also raises the question of whether the agent remains safe while adapting. SCARED brings an explicit safety budget into this process.

The method uses the constrained Markov decision process framework, where behavior is evaluated through both reward and accumulated cost. During adaptation, the agent seeks reward while keeping cost within a user-specified budget. Safety is therefore represented through the task’s cost constraint, giving the adaptation process an explicit quantity to manage alongside its performance objective.

The experiments show that the agent responds to different budgets: more permissive budgets produce more aggressive behavior, while tighter budgets produce more conservative behavior. Across challenging benchmarks, SCARED enables safe and robust adaptation and outperforms the compared in-context and safe meta-reinforcement-learning methods. These findings support budget-sensitive adaptation without parameter updates, with safety understood through the specified costs and constraints in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: SCARED enables in-context reinforcement-learning agents to adapt while managing a user-specified accumulated-cost budget.

title: Safe In-Context Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are fundamentally limited by representation collapse, a bottleneck that severely degrades long-context performance. We identify that existing approaches risk drifting into one of two pathological extremes: homogenization collapse (e.g., attention sinks causing rank deficiency) and isolation collapse (e.g., local attention causing context disconnection). Through spectral analysis of attention dynamics, we derive an intrinsic trade-off between mixing efficiency (spectral gap) and information capacity (effective rank) that standard mechanisms struggle to balance. To resolve this dilemma, we propose the Topologically Regularized Side-Path (TRSP), a non-invasive architectural intervention that achieves spectral balance. TRSP employs a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism, scaled by a lightweight, length-aware gate, to regularize the token interaction topology. By integrating proximal coupling to preserve effective rank and distal propagation to support non-degenerate mixing, TRSP promotes a geometrically healthier transition operator without altering core attention. Experiments show significant improvements across general capabilities and long-context benchmarks. Notably, on NoLiMa at $8\times$ the training length, TRSP retains $83%$ accuracy and surpasses the Differential Transformer and Gated Attention by approximately 30 and 50 percentage points, respectively. Code available at: https://github.com/Eziotao-tyd/TRSP.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes two ways language-model representations can deteriorate over long contexts. Excessive homogenization can erase distinctions between representations, while excessive isolation can disconnect parts of the context. Spectral analysis identifies a trade-off between efficient information mixing, measured by spectral gap, and information capacity, measured by effective rank.

The Topologically Regularized Side-Path adds a route for token interaction without changing core attention. It uses a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism controlled by a lightweight gate that accounts for sequence length. Nearby coupling helps preserve effective rank, while longer-range propagation supports mixing. These components aim to balance information exchange with preservation of distinct representations.

Experiments show improvements on general-capability and long-context benchmarks. On NoLiMa at eight times the training length, TRSP retains 83% accuracy, exceeding the Differential Transformer and Gated Attention by approximately 30 and 50 percentage points, respectively. The results support the proposed spectral balance as a useful architectural intervention for maintaining performance when context length grows beyond training conditions.
summary.tldr: TRSP adds a lightweight side path that balances information mixing and representation capacity, improving reported long-context performance.

title: The Devil is in the Spectrum: Mitigating Representation Collapse in LLMs via Topologically Regularized Side-Path

abstract: Transformer sequence models such as Decision Transformer can learn strong offline policies from logged trajectories, but they often suffer from causal confusion: reliance on spurious correlations that predict reward in the data but do not reflect the true causal mechanisms of the environment. We propose CSET (Counterfactual State Editing Transformer), which improves robustness in strictly offline reinforcement learning without learning environment transition dynamics. On the data side, CSET fits a causal reward model as a conditional variational autoencoder and uses a counterfactual state generator to propose minimally edited observations whose predicted reward matches the factual reward, under a normalized move-band constraint and an acceptance gate that enforce plausibility and reward consistency; augmentation replaces only the observation token to avoid synthetic successor transitions. On the model side, CSET uses a causally structured hybrid transformer: modality-specific convolutional encoders process return-to-go, state, and action streams, and a final attention block is softly supervised so action prediction focuses on its direct causal parents. Experiments on D4RL locomotion, AntMaze, and offline recommendation benchmarks show consistent gains within the DT family, and CSET remains substantially more robust than strong value-based and DT baselines under injected spurious distractors.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from existing trajectories, which can contain misleading correlations between observations and rewards. A sequence model may rely on those correlations even when they do not reflect how the environment works. CSET addresses this causal confusion through both edited training observations and a transformer designed to emphasize causal relationships.

A conditional variational autoencoder models reward, and a counterfactual generator proposes small observation changes whose predicted reward matches the original reward. A normalized move-band constraint and acceptance gate enforce plausibility and reward consistency. Only the observation token is replaced, avoiding invented successor transitions. The method therefore operates strictly offline without learning environment transition dynamics.

The model separately encodes return-to-go, state, and action streams, then softly supervises its final attention block toward the direct causal parents of action prediction. Experiments on locomotion, AntMaze, and offline recommendation show consistent gains within the Decision Transformer family. Under injected spurious distractors, CSET is substantially more robust than the strong value-based and Decision Transformer baselines evaluated.
summary.tldr: CSET combines reward-consistent observation edits with causally structured attention to improve offline policies and robustness to misleading distractors.

title: Reward-Preserving Counterfactual State Editing for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent progress in time-series forecasting has led to rapidly increasing architectural complexity, yet many reported State-of-the-Art gains are statistically fragile or misattributed. We argue that progress requires a shift from model selection to modular attribution, identifying which components truly drive performance. We propose CombinationTS, a self-contained probabilistic evaluation framework grounded in Evaluatology, the science of uncovering the effects. It decomposes forecasting models into orthogonal modules—Input Transformation, Embedding, Encoder, Decoder, and Output Transformation—and evaluates them under a shared evaluation condition space. By quantifying each component via marginalized performance ($\mu$) and stability ($\sigma$), CombinationTS enables robust attribution beyond fragile point estimates. Through large-scale paired evaluation, we uncover the Identity Paradox: once the data view (Embedding) is well-designed, a parameter-free Identity Encoder often matches or outperforms complex backbones.

paragraphs: CombinationTS asks which parts of a forecasting model actually account for its performance. The paper argues that increasingly complex architectures can receive credit for gains that are statistically fragile or caused by other components. Its proposed evaluation framework therefore shifts attention from ranking complete models to attributing effects to individual modules.

The framework separates a model into input transformation, embedding, encoder, decoder, and output transformation. It compares these modules within a shared space of evaluation conditions. Each component is described through marginalized performance and stability, so assessment reflects behavior across conditions rather than resting on a single favorable result. Large-scale paired evaluations support the comparisons.

The central finding is what the authors call the Identity Paradox: with a well-designed embedding, a parameter-free identity encoder often matches or exceeds complex backbones. This is a conditional empirical finding, not a claim that encoders never help. It suggests that the way data is presented to a model can explain gains otherwise attributed to its central processing architecture.
summary.tldr: CombinationTS attributes forecasting performance to individual modules and finds that good embeddings often let an identity encoder match complex backbones.

title: CombinationTS: A Modular Framework for Understanding Time-Series Forecasting Models

abstract: How should we analyze memory in deep RL? We introduce tools for analyzing policies under partial observability and revealing how agents use memory to make decisions. To utilize these tools, we present POPGym Arcade, a collection of Atari-inspired, hardware-accelerated environments sharing a single observation and action space. Each environment provides fully and partially observable variants, enabling counterfactual studies on observability. We find that controlled studies are necessary for fair comparisons and identify a pathology where value functions smear credit over irrelevant history. Using this pathology, we demonstrate how out-of-distribution scenarios can contaminate memory, perturbing the policy far into the future.

Each environment provides fully and partially observable variants, enabling counterfactual studies on observability. paragraphs: When an agent cannot observe the full state of its environment, earlier observations can help it choose an action. This paper develops tools for examining how reinforcement-learning policies actually use that memory. The emphasis is on analyzing the influence of history on decisions, rather than treating memory solely as an architectural feature.

To support controlled investigation, the authors introduce POPGym Arcade, a collection of Atari-inspired environments accelerated for hardware execution. The environments share observation and action spaces, and each offers fully observable and partially observable versions. These paired versions enable counterfactual studies of observability: researchers can examine how behavior changes when relevant information is available directly or must be recovered from history.

The study finds that controlled comparisons are necessary and identifies a failure in which value functions spread credit across irrelevant past events. Using that pathology, the authors show how out-of-distribution experiences can contaminate memory and continue perturbing decisions far into the future. The result highlights a specific way memory can transmit errors over time, alongside its intended role in carrying useful information.
summary.tldr: POPGym Arcade enables controlled studies of agent memory and reveals how irrelevant history can distort decisions long after an unusual experience.

title: Investigating Memory in Model-Free RL with POPGym Arcade

abstract: Inference time optimization techniques, such as repeated sampling, have significantly advanced the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, the critical role of model uncertainty remains largely underexplored in these optimization strategies. In this paper, we investigate the dynamics of confidence along reasoning trajectories and for first time reveal a surprising and unique pattern: correct answer traces tend to exhibit confidence improvement over time (positive confidence gain), while incorrect traces show attenuated or declining confidence as reasoning proceeds. Based on this observation, we propose Confidence Dynamic Gain (CDG) based voting, which incorporates how the confidence trajectory of the response evolves along the reasoning chain. Experiments across four open-source architectures (DeepSeek-R1, gpt-oss, Gemma-3, Qwen-QwQ) on the AIME24/25, HMMT25, and BRUMO25 benchmarks demonstrate that CDG yields a significant performance boost over baselines. These results demonstrate that our method provides a robust discriminative signal for improving answer selection in LLM reasoning. We also provide theoretical insights for this phenomenon. Code will be released at https://github.com/Accenture/CDG.git.

paragraphs: Generating several possible solutions can improve language-model reasoning, but the system still needs to choose among them. This paper studies whether the way confidence changes during a solution provides useful evidence for that choice. Its central observation concerns the trajectory of confidence, rather than confidence treated as a single fixed property of an answer.

The authors find that correct reasoning traces tend to become more confident as they progress. Incorrect traces tend to show weaker confidence growth or declining confidence. Based on this pattern, they propose Confidence Dynamic Gain voting, which incorporates confidence evolution along the reasoning chain into answer selection. The paper also provides theoretical insights into the observed phenomenon.

Experiments cover DeepSeek-R1, gpt-oss, Gemma-3, and Qwen-QwQ on AIME24/25, HMMT25, and BRUMO25. The method significantly improves performance over the evaluated baselines. These results support confidence change as a useful discriminative signal across those settings. The observed tendency supplies evidence for ranking answers; it does not establish that every increasingly confident trace is correct.
summary.tldr: Confidence Dynamic Gain voting improves answer selection by using the tendency of correct reasoning traces to gain confidence over time.

title: Inference Time Optimization with Confidence Dynamics

abstract: Recent advances in large language model (LLM) have empowered autonomous agents to perform multi-turn interactions with tools and environments. However, scaling such agent training is limited by the lack of diverse and reliable environments.In this paper, we propose Agent World Model (AWM), a fully synthetic environment generation pipeline. Using this pipeline, we scale to 1,000 environments covering everyday scenarios, in which agents can interact with rich toolsets and obtain high-quality observations. Notably, these environments are code-driven and backed by databases, providing more reliable and consistent state transitions than environments simulated by LLMs. Moreover, they enable more efficient agent interaction compared with collecting trajectories from realistic environments. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this resource, we perform large-scale reinforcement learning for multi-turn tool-use agents. Thanks to the fully executable environments and accessible database states, we can also design reliable reward functions. Experiments on three benchmarks show that training exclusively in synthetic environments, rather than benchmark-specific ones, yields strong out-of-distribution generalization. The code is available at https://github.com/Snowflake-Labs/agent-world-model.

paragraphs: Agents that use tools need environments where they can practice sequences of actions and observe the consequences. The paper identifies a shortage of diverse, reliable environments as a barrier to scaling this training. Agent World Model addresses that shortage with a fully synthetic generation pipeline producing 1,000 environments covering everyday scenarios.

The environments run on code and databases, with tools through which agents interact. This gives state changes an executable foundation and, according to the authors, makes them more reliable and consistent than environments simulated by language models. The authors also report more efficient interaction than collecting trajectories from realistic environments. Accessible database states help define reliable rewards for training.

The paper uses these environments for large-scale reinforcement learning of agents that perform multiple rounds of tool use. Across three benchmarks, training exclusively in synthetic environments produces strong generalization beyond the training distribution. The result supports executable synthetic environments as a useful training resource without requiring environments tailored to each evaluation benchmark.
summary.tldr: Training tool-using agents in 1,000 executable synthetic environments yields strong generalization across three benchmarks.

title: Agent World Model: Infinity Synthetic Environments for Agentic Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Learning-based whole-body controllers have become a key driver for humanoid robots, yet most existing approaches require robot-specific training. In this paper, we study the problem of cross-embodiment humanoid control and show that a single policy can robustly generalize across a wide range of humanoid robot designs with one-time training. We introduce XHugWBC, a novel cross-embodiment training framework that enables generalist humanoid control through: (1) physics-consistent morphological randomization, (2) semantically aligned observation and action spaces across diverse humanoid robots, and (3) effective policy architectures modeling morphological and dynamical properties. XHugWBC is not tied to any specific robot. Instead, it internalizes a broad distribution of morphological and dynamical characteristics during training. By learning motion priors from diverse randomized embodiments, the policy acquires a strong structural bias that supports zero-shot transfer to previously unseen robots. Experiments on twelve simulated humanoids and seven real-world robots demonstrate the strong generalization and robustness of the resulting universal controller.

paragraphs: XHugWBC studies whether one whole-body control policy can work across different humanoid robot designs after a single training process. Robot-specific training limits reuse when body structure or dynamics change. The proposed framework instead trains over a broad distribution of embodiments so that the controller learns patterns shared across different humanoids.

Three components support this transfer. Physics-consistent morphological randomization supplies diverse bodies during training. Semantically aligned observation and action spaces give corresponding information and commands consistent meanings across robots. Policy architectures also model morphological and dynamical properties. Together, these components let the policy learn motion priors from varied embodiments and develop a structural bias that supports transfer to previously unseen robots.

Experiments on twelve simulated humanoids and seven physical robots demonstrate strong generalization and robustness. The reported result is that a single trained policy can transfer across a wide range of designs, including zero-shot use on unseen embodiments. This provides evidence that training diversity and consistent interfaces can reduce dependence on separate controllers trained for each robot.
summary.tldr: XHugWBC trains one humanoid controller across varied bodies and dynamics, enabling robust transfer to previously unseen robot designs.

title: Scalable and General Whole-Body Control for Cross-Humanoid Locomotion

abstract: Real-world degradations, such as noise, blur, and low resolution, significantly impair the performance of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in document understanding tasks. Despite recent advancements, progress in this field remains stifled by two critical bottlenecks: the scarcity of large-scale, aligned training data necessary for learning robustness, and the lack of transferable restoration solutions across diverse MLLM architectures. To bridge the data gap, we first present DocRobust-VQA, a large-scale dataset explicitly constructed to support robustness training. Comprising 189K aligned clean/corrupted document image pairs and 417K QA pairs, it provides the first substantial corpus for fine-tuning MLLMs to handle varying degradation conditions. Leveraging this data, we propose Uni-DocRobust, a universal plug-and-play framework that decouples restoration capabilities from specific visual encoders. Our method employs a frozen Universal Restoration Core pre-trained in a canonical feature space via multi-teacher distillation, which can be seamlessly integrated into target MLLMs (e.g., Qwen-VL, InternVL) through lightweight Feature Adapters. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Uni-DocRobust significantly enhances robust performance on MLLMs and enables a cost-effective “pre-train once, deploy everywhere” paradigm for robust MLLM deployment.

DocRobust-VQA contains 189,000 aligned clean and corrupted document-image pairs and 417,000 question-answer pairs. Uni-DocRobust uses this data to build a restoration core in a shared feature space through multi-teacher distillation. The core remains frozen when integrated into target models, with lightweight feature adapters connecting it to different visual encoders, including those in Qwen-VL and InternVL.

This separation allows the central restoration capability to be pretrained once and adapted across models. Extensive experiments show significant improvements in robust document-understanding performance and support the cost-effective deployment approach described by the authors. The contribution joins aligned degradation training with a transferable feature-restoration design, addressing both the data needed to learn robustness and the architecture dependence that can impede its reuse.
summary.tldr: Uni-DocRobust pairs aligned document-corruption data with a reusable restoration core to improve robustness across multimodal language models.

title: Uni-DocRobust: Universal Plug-and-Play Robustness Enhancement for Multi-modal LLMs via Feature Restoration

abstract: Contemporary AI safety spans pre-training interventions, post-training alignment, deployment-time controls, monitoring, and red-teaming. These methods are necessary, but they primarily certify snapshots of system behavior. As AI systems become more capable, dynamic, embodied, and self-improving, this snapshot view becomes incomplete: safety depends not only on whether a system behaves acceptably now, but whether it remains correctable as it learns, adapts, acts, and modifies itself over time. This paper argues that safety should therefore be treated as an epistemic property of the evolving learner, not merely a behavioral property of the current policy. We introduce teachability as the capacity to preserve future corrective leverage under bounded human, institutional, or environmental intervention. We argue that advanced systems can retain visible competence while eroding the representational, algorithmic, or meta-decision conditions needed for future correction. Safe advanced AI systems must not only behave acceptably now; they must remain teachable later.

paragraphs: This paper argues that acceptable behavior today is an incomplete basis for judging the safety of systems that continue learning and changing. Existing interventions, monitoring, and adversarial testing remain necessary, but primarily assess particular states of a system. A capable agent may subsequently adapt, act in the world, or modify itself in ways that change whether people can still correct it.

The authors introduce teachability as the ability to preserve opportunities for future correction under limited human, institutional, or environmental intervention. Calling safety an epistemic property places attention on the evolving learner: how its internal organization and learning processes support continued correction. The relevant question extends beyond what the current policy visibly does.

The central concern is that apparent competence can persist while the conditions supporting correction deteriorate. Those conditions may involve representations, algorithms, or higher-level decisions about how the system changes. The paper therefore calls for safety thinking that considers whether corrective influence remains effective over time, alongside evaluations of present behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that advanced AI safety requires preserving the capacity for future correction as systems learn and change.

abstract: We address classification problems for which the training instances are governed by a distribution that is allowed to differ arbitrarily from the test distribution—problems also referred to as classification under covariate shift. We derive a solution that is purely discriminative: neither training nor test distribution are modeled explicitly. We formulate the general problem of learning under covariate shift as an integrated optimization problem. We derive a kernel logistic regression classifier for differing training and test distributions.
originalAbstract: We address classification problems for which the training instances are governed by a distribution that is allowed to differ arbitrarily from the test distribution—problems also referred to as classification under covariate shift. We derive a solution that is purely discriminative: neither training nor test distribution are modeled explicitly. We formulate the general problem of learning under covariate shift as an integrated optimization problem. We derive a kernel logistic regression classifier for differing training and test distributions.

paragraphs: A classification system may be trained on examples whose distribution differs from that of the examples it will later encounter. This paper addresses that situation under the heading of covariate shift. Within the stated setting, the distribution governing training instances is allowed to differ arbitrarily from the test distribution, making that mismatch part of the learning problem.

The proposed solution is purely discriminative: it learns a classifier without explicitly modeling either the training distribution or the test distribution. The authors formulate learning under covariate shift as an integrated optimization problem. This gives the distribution mismatch a place within the classifier's optimization rather than requiring explicit probability models of the two instance populations.

From that formulation, the paper derives a kernel logistic regression classifier for differing training and test distributions. Its stated contribution is a mathematical and algorithmic route to classification under covariate shift. The approach matters because it connects this mismatch problem with discriminative classifier training while avoiding the separate task of explicitly modeling both distributions.
summary.tldr: The paper derives a kernel logistic regression approach to covariate shift without explicitly modeling training or test distributions.

title: Discriminative learning for differing training and test distributions

abstract: This paper uses the notion of algorithmic stability to derive novel generalization bounds for several families of transductive regression algorithms, both by using convexity and closed-form solutions. Our analysis helps compare the stability of these algorithms. It suggests that several existing algorithms might not be stable but prescribes a technique to make them stable. It also reports the results of experiments with local transductive regression demonstrating the benefit of our stability bounds for model selection, in particular for determining the radius of the local neighborhood used by the algorithm.
originalAbstract: This paper uses the notion of algorithmic stability to derive novel generalization bounds for several families of transductive regression algorithms, both by using convexity and closed-form solutions. Our analysis helps compare the stability of these algorithms. It suggests that several existing algorithms might not be stable but prescribes a technique to make them stable. It also reports the results of experiments with local transductive regression demonstrating the benefit of our stability bounds for model selection, in particular for determining the radius of the local neighborhood used by the algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper uses algorithmic stability to study transductive regression. Stability concerns how sensitive a learning procedure is to changes in its training information. The authors use this perspective to derive generalization bounds for several families of algorithms, providing theoretical tools for assessing how their predictions may behave beyond the observed labels.

Their analysis draws on both convexity and closed-form solutions. It enables comparisons among the algorithms and suggests that some existing methods might lack stability. The authors also prescribe a technique for making them stable. The result is therefore both diagnostic and constructive: it helps identify potential sensitivity and offers a way to address it.

Experiments with local transductive regression demonstrate that the bounds can help with model selection. In particular, they support choosing the radius of the neighborhood used by the algorithm. This gives the theoretical analysis a concrete operational role. The paper connects stability guarantees to an actual modeling choice, showing how a bound can guide the scale of information used for local predictions.
summary.tldr: Stability analysis yields transductive regression bounds, a stabilization technique, and practical guidance for choosing local neighborhood size.

title: Stability of transductive regression algorithms

abstract: In inductive logic programming, theta-subsumption is a widely used coverage test. Unfortunately, testing theta-subsumption is NP-complete, which represents a crucial efficiency bottleneck for many relational learners. In this paper, we present a probabilistic estimator of clause coverage, based on a randomized restarted search strategy. Under a distribution assumption, our algorithm can estimate clause coverage without having to decide subsumption for all examples. We implement this algorithm in program ReCovEr. On generated graph data and real-world datasets, we show that ReCovEr provides reasonably accurate estimates while achieving dramatic runtimes improvements compared to a state-of-the-art algorithm.
originalAbstract: In inductive logic programming, theta-subsumption is a widely used coverage test. Unfortunately, testing theta-subsumption is NP-complete, which represents a crucial efficiency bottleneck for many relational learners. In this paper, we present a probabilistic estimator of clause coverage, based on a randomized restarted search strategy. Under a distribution assumption, our algorithm can estimate clause coverage without having to decide subsumption for all examples. We implement this algorithm in program ReCovEr. On generated graph data and real-world datasets, we show that ReCovEr provides reasonably accurate estimates while achieving dramatic runtimes improvements compared to a state-of-the-art algorithm.

paragraphs: Relational learning often needs to determine how many examples a logical clause covers. A widely used test, theta-subsumption, is NP-complete, making repeated exact coverage testing a major computational bottleneck. This paper develops a probabilistic estimator intended to obtain useful coverage information without completing that expensive decision process for every example.

The method uses randomized search with restarts and, under a distribution assumption, estimates clause coverage from the resulting search information. The title also identifies maximum likelihood as part of the estimation approach. The key change is the quantity being computed: the algorithm estimates overall coverage without requiring a definitive subsumption answer for all examples.

The authors implement the method in ReCovEr and evaluate it on generated graph data and real-world datasets. They report reasonably accurate estimates alongside dramatic runtime improvements over a state-of-the-art algorithm. These results support approximate coverage estimation as a practical way to reduce a relational learner's workload, with the distribution assumption remaining part of the method's stated basis.
summary.tldr: ReCovEr uses randomized restarted search to estimate clause coverage under a distribution assumption, achieving large reported runtime savings.

title: Fast estimation of first-order clause coverage through randomization and maximum likelihood

abstract: This paper addresses the problem of inferring a regular expression from a given set of strings that resembles, as closely as possible, the regular expression that a human expert would have written to identify the language. This is motivated by our goal of automating the task of postmasters of an email service who use regular expressions to describe and blacklist email spam campaigns. Training data contains batches of messages and corresponding regular expressions that an expert postmaster feels confident to blacklist. We model this task as a learning problem with structured output spaces and an appropriate loss function, derive a decoder and the resulting optimization problem, and a report on a case study conducted with an email service.
originalAbstract: This paper addresses the problem of inferring a regular expression from a given set of strings that resembles, as closely as possible, the regular expression that a human expert would have written to identify the language. This is motivated by our goal of automating the task of postmasters of an email service who use regular expressions to describe and blacklist email spam campaigns. Training data contains batches of messages and corresponding regular expressions that an expert postmaster feels confident to blacklist. We model this task as a learning problem with structured output spaces and an appropriate loss function, derive a decoder and the resulting optimization problem, and a report on a case study conducted with an email service.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to infer a regular expression from a collection of strings so that it resembles one a human expert would write. Its practical motivation is email administration, where postmasters create patterns to describe spam campaigns and decide which patterns they are confident enough to blacklist.

Training examples pair batches of messages with regular expressions supplied by an expert postmaster. The authors formulate the task as structured prediction: the output is an expression with internal structure, rather than a single category. They introduce a suitable loss function, derive a decoder for producing expressions, and formulate the corresponding optimization problem.

A case study with an email service examines the approach in its intended application. The target is expert-like campaign descriptions, so learning from the postmaster's chosen expressions is central to the problem definition. The work provides a learning formulation and algorithmic components for automating this pattern-writing task, with the case study connecting those components to email-service practice.
summary.tldr: Structured prediction learns to generate expert-like regular expressions for email campaigns from message batches paired with postmaster-written patterns.

title: Learning to Identify Regular Expressions that Describe Email Campaigns
